gabes: Gabès is the capital of the Gabès Governorate in Tunisia, on the Gulf of Gabès, 327 km south-east of Tunis and 113 km from Sfax. It lies at the delta of the Wadi Qabis, which rises 10 kilometres upstream at Ras al-Oued and is its main source of water. The ancient name Takapes is a Punic Numidian toponym. The prefix Ta, meaning the in Berber, was later dropped, and since Arabic lacks the sound p, Kapes became Kabes and then Gabès. It has a hot arid climate with low rainfall.

The town was a Carthaginian settlement known as Tacapae before it fell under Roman control, and it belonged to the Roman province of Tripolitania. Strabo calls it an important entrepôt of the Lesser Syrtis, and Pliny remarks that the water of a copious fountain there was divided among the cultivators, each having the use of it for a certain interval. Tacapae became a Christian bishopric, and three of its bishops are known: Dulcitius, at the Council of Carthage in 403 and the Conference of Carthage in 411; Servilius, exiled by Huneric in 484; and Caius or Gallus, at the Council of Carthage in 525.

The Umayyad Caliphate conquered the region in the 7th century, bringing Islam to Gabès, and the companion of the Prophet Muhammad Abu Lubaba al-Ansari settled in the city. The Banu Jami were among the dynasties that followed. In the 12th century al-Idrisi praised its economy, dense orchards and markets, and its dates, olives and leather goods. In the 14th century al-Tijani called it the paradise of the world and Little Damascus.

In 1574 it became part of the Eyalet of Tunis. It came under the French protectorate in 1881, which brought a railway, roads and a port. German forces held it in the World War II, until British forces retook it in 1943 in the Mareth Line operations. Tunisia became independent in 1956.

Gabès is a commercial centre and port with industries including chemicals, cement, brick and fishing, and a university. Its oasis is one of the last coastal oases in the world, and was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List on 28 May 2008. The Mosque of Sidi Boulbaba and the Mouradi school are its most notable historical and religious landmarks.
gaborone: Gaborone lies between Kgale Hill and Oodi Hill, near the confluence of the Notwane and Segoditshane rivers, in the south-eastern corner of Botswana and within 15 kilometres of the South African border. It stands at an elevation of 1,010 metres and has a hot semi-arid climate. Several neighbouring towns, among them Mogoditshane, Mochudi and Tlokweng across the river, are largely commuter towns for the city.

There have been inhabitants along the Notwane River for centuries. Around 1880 the Tlokwa left the Magaliesberg ranges to settle the area and called the settlement Moshaweng. The word Gaborone is said to mean "it does not fit badly" or "it is not unbecoming". Early European colonizers called the place Gaberones, a shortening of "Gaborone's Village", after Chief Gaborone of the Tlokwa, whose home village, now called Tlokweng, lay across the river from the Government Camp, the colonial government's headquarters. The nickname GC comes from Government Camp.

In 1890 Cecil John Rhodes picked Gaberones to house a colonial fort, where he planned the Jameson Raid. In the mid-1960s, when the Bechuanaland Protectorate became an independent nation, the city was planned as its capital. It was chosen because it was not affiliated with any specific indigenous group and was close to fresh water. The name changed from Gaberones to Gaborone in 1969. The city grew very fast, which has caused problems of housing and illegal settlement, and it dealt with conflicts spilling over from Zimbabwe and South Africa in the 1980s.

Gaborone is the capital and largest city of Botswana, with 246,325 inhabitants at the 2022 census, about 10 per cent of the national population. Its centre is a long commercial strip called the Main Mall, with a semicircular area of government offices to its east. It holds the Bank of Botswana, the Botswana Stock Exchange and the headquarters of the Southern African Development Community, formed in 1980. The National Museum and Art Gallery, which opened in 1968, has an exhibit on the San, the earliest inhabitants of southern Africa.
gabriele-dannunzio: Gabriele D'Annunzio was born in Pescara, in what is now the Italian region of Abruzzo, the son of Francesco Paolo Rapagnetta D'Annunzio, a wealthy landowner and mayor of the town, and Luisa de Benedictis. His father had been born Rapagnetta and was adopted at 13 by an aunt who had married a merchant and shipowner named D'Annunzio. A story that he was first baptised Gaetano is false; his birth and baptismal records both give Gabriele.

D'Annunzio published Canto novo in 1882, poems of youth, the sea and the Abruzzese landscape, followed by Terra vergine, stories of peasant life. With Intermezzo di rime in 1883 he began a more characteristic manner, expressing every subtle vibration of sensuous life. Critics divided: some called him a corrupter of public morals, others welcomed a breath of new vitality. He was linked with the Decadent movement and influenced by Friedrich Nietzsche. His novels include Il Piacere (1889) and Il fuoco (1900), and his plays La figlia di Jorio (1904). The censor banned his tragedy Francesca da Rimini in December 1901, three weeks into its run.

After the First World War began, D'Annunzio returned to Italy and spoke for entry on the side of the Triple Entente. He volunteered, became a fighter pilot and lost the sight of an eye in a flying accident. On 9 August 1918 he led nine planes on a round trip of 1,100 km to drop leaflets on Vienna.

Angered by the proposal at the Paris Peace Conference to hand over Fiume, now Rijeka, he led 186 grenadiers to seize the city on 12 September 1919. His force grew to some 2,500 men, and Italy refused to annex the city and blockaded it. With the syndicalist Alceste de Ambris he wrote the Charter of Carnaro, which set up a corporatist state with nine corporations and a tenth, D'Annunzio's own invention, for heroes, poets and prophets. It declared music the fundamental principle of the state. Afterwards he retired to Lake Garda, where he built the Vittoriale degli Italiani. Mussolini took up his balcony speeches and ceremonies, though D'Annunzio never joined the fascist government.
gadadhar-singha: Born Gadapani Konwar, and known by the Ahom name Supatphaa, he was the son of Gobar Roja, a descendant of the king Suhungmung. The minister Debera Borbarua made Gobar king in 1675; he reigned only twenty days and was executed after Debera's fall. In 1679 Laluk Sola Borphukan had the minister Atan Burhagohain murdered, installed Sulikphaa, called Lora Roja, as king and began to hunt down the Ahom princes eligible for the throne.

To escape, Gadapani became a fugitive in the Naga hills, perhaps near the present-day Mon district, among the Konyak Naga. During this time his wife Joymoti Konwari was tortured and killed by the henchmen of Sulikphaa and Laluk Sola Borphukan. Little is known of his two years in exile, though the hills are rich in lore and legend about him.

He was formally crowned in March 1682, and bound the leading nobles to himself by marrying their daughters. His first act was to equip an army against the Mughals at Guwahati: the forts at Bansbari and Kajali fell at the first assault, and a naval victory near the mouth of the Bar Nadi delivered the whole enemy fleet to the Ahoms. The campaign ended eighty years of Ahom–Mughal conflict. He also stopped Naga raids on the border villages, partly through marriage alliances with Naga chiefs.

He built roads, among them the Dhodar Ali, 211 km long from Kamargaon to Joypur, and two stone bridges, and had a number of tanks dug. The earliest known copper plates recording grants of land by Ahom kings to Brahmins or Hindu temples date from his reign. Having met the Mughal system of land measurement while hiding in Lower Assam, he brought surveyors from Koch Bihar and Bengal; the survey began in Sivasagar and was completed only after his death.

He died in February 1696 after a reign of fourteen and a half years, leaving two sons, Lai and Lechai. Lai succeeded him under the Hindu name Rudra Singha, and under him the Ahom kingdom reached its zenith; the Tungkhungia house ruled until the end of the kingdom in 1826. Gadadhar Singha was buried at Charaideo. The American Baptist missionary Nathan Brown, who saw the royal tombs there dug open, reckoned his about ninety feet high and so natural in appearance that a stranger would have taken it for an ordinary hill.
gaeta: Gaeta lies in the province of Latina in Lazio, on a promontory stretching towards the Gulf of Gaeta, 133 kilometres south of Rome and 96.5 kilometres north of Naples. In antiquity the site, then called Caieta, was inhabited by the Oscan-speaking Aurunci, and in 345 BCE its territory came under Roman influence. Its mild climate made it a place for seaside villas of the Roman elite, owned by figures such as Scipio Africanus and Gaius Laelius. Lucius Munatius Plancus, consul in 42 BCE, had a villa on Monte Orlando, and his cylindrical travertine mausoleum still stands on the summit. The Emperor Antoninus Pius restored the port.

After the Lombard invasion Gaeta remained under Byzantine suzerainty, but like Amalfi, Sorrento and Naples it became practically independent and traded with the Levant. Around 830 it became a lordship ruled by hereditary hypati. The first, Constantine, helped Pope Leo IV in the naval fight at Ostia in 847, and John I helped crush the Saracens at the Garigliano in 915. Docibilis II first took the title of duke, and after his death in 954 the duchy declined. Pandulf IV of Capua captured the city in 1032, and in 1140 Roger II definitively annexed it to the Kingdom of Sicily.

Because of its strategic position Gaeta was repeatedly attacked in wars for the Kingdom of Naples. Frederick II strengthened its castle in 1227, and Charles I of Anjou rebuilt it in 1279. King Alfonso V of Aragon besieged and took the city in 1435 as his base for conquering the kingdom. A new wall around Monte Orlando followed after 1528. The French took it in 1806 under André Masséna after a defence, and the Austrians in 1815. Pope Pius IX took refuge there after fleeing the Roman Republic. In 1860 to 1861 King Francis II of the Two Sicilies defended the fortress with 12,000 men, and capitulated on 13 February 1861 when the withdrawal of the French fleet made bombardment from the sea possible.

Gaeta is a fishing port and seaside resort with beaches such as Serapo. Its main sights include the Angevine-Aragonese Castle and the cathedral, whose Romanesque marble Paschal candelabrum carries 48 reliefs of the life of Jesus. Its bell tower, 57 metres high, was completed in 1279. The Sixth Fleet of the United States Navy has had its flagship based at Gaeta since 1967. Local cooking includes the tiella, a pie resembling a pizza, and a Latin text of 997 found in the town contains the earliest known use of the word pizza. After Italy surrendered to the Allies, German troops occupied the city and expelled most of its population.
gaius-maecenas: Gaius Cilnius Maecenas was a friend and political adviser to Octavian, who later reigned as the emperor Augustus. He prided himself on an ancient Etruscan lineage and claimed descent from the princely house of the Cilnii of Arretium. Horace alludes to this in the opening of his Odes with the phrase "atavis edite regibus", descendant of kings. Tacitus calls him Cilnius Maecenas, and it is possible that Cilnius was his mother's family name, or that Maecenas was a cognomen. His wealth may have been partly inherited, but he owed his position to his connection with Augustus. Despite his wealth and power he chose not to enter the Senate and remained of equestrian rank.

Maecenas first appears in 40 BCE, when Octavian employed him to arrange his marriage with Scribonia and to help negotiate the Treaty of Brundisium and the reconciliation with Mark Antony. In 37 BCE he and Marcus Cocceius Nerva patched up a reconciliation between the two claimants to power by the Treaty of Tarentum. During the Sicilian war against Sextus Pompeius in 36 BCE he held supreme administrative control of Rome and Italy, and he acted for Octavian again before the Battle of Actium, when he crushed the conspiracy of Lepidus the Younger. In his last years he fell somewhat out of favour with Augustus. He died in 8 BCE, leaving Augustus sole heir to his wealth.

Maecenas is best known for supporting young poets, and in many languages his name means a patron of the arts, as in French mécène and German Mäzen. Virgil wrote the Georgics in his honour and introduced Horace to him in 38 BCE. Maecenas gave Horace financial support and an estate in the Sabine Mountains, and Propertius and Varius Rufus were also among his protégés. Some see the patronage as serving the state, reconciling minds to the new order. He wrote prose and verse himself, now lost apart from about twenty fragments, and Augustus, Seneca and Quintilian mocked his strange style. His gardens on the Esquiline Hill, the first of their kind in Rome, became imperial property after his death.
gaius-marius: Marius was born about 157 BCE in Cereatae, a village near Arpinum in south-east Latium, a town that had received full Roman citizenship only in 188 BCE. Plutarch calls his father a labourer, which is almost certainly false: Marius had ties with the nobility in Rome and Arpinum, and came from a locally important family of equestrian status with inherited wealth, probably from large landholdings. His younger brother Marcus Marius also entered public life.

He gained military experience under Scipio Aemilianus at the Siege of Numantia in 134 BCE, was elected tribune of the plebs in 119 BCE and passed a law limiting aristocratic interference in elections. He was barely elected praetor in 115 BCE and then governed Further Spain, campaigning against bandits.

In 109 BCE Marius joined the consul Quintus Caecilius Metellus as a legate in the Jugurthine War, probably as his senior subordinate. By 108 BCE he wished to stand for the consulship. Metellus refused his blessing, but Marius won the respect of the troops by sharing their labours, and Italian traders wrote home that he could end the war quickly. Elected consul for 107 BCE, he took volunteers, among them men without property, the capite censi, and sailed to Africa, leaving his cavalry with his quaestor Lucius Cornelius Sulla.

After a series of Roman defeats by the Cimbri and their allies, Marius was elected consul again for 105 BCE and held the office each year from 104 to 100 BCE. He defeated the Teutones at Aquae Sextiae and the Cimbri at Vercellae.

In his sixth consulship, in 100 BCE, the tribune Lucius Appuleius Saturninus pushed laws that gave land to Marius's veterans, and Marius then withdrew from active public life. In 88 BCE a conflict with Sulla, elected consul and given the command against Mithridates of Pontus, led to Marius's exile to Africa. He returned during the War of Octavius, joined Cinna, seized Rome and purged his opponents. He was elected consul for the seventh time and died on 13 January 86 BCE, within weeks.

Since the 1840s Marius has been credited with sweeping army reforms, but specialists now increasingly dismiss these Marian reforms as a construct of modern scholarship. His lasting example lies elsewhere: his successive consulships gave one man unprecedented power, and his use of the assemblies to overturn senatorial assignments of commands set a pattern for later rivals.
galapagos-islands: The archipelago lies on the equator in the Eastern Pacific and consists of 127 islands, islets and rocks, of which 19 are large islands with an area over one square kilometre. Isabela, at 4,588 square kilometres, makes up close to three-fifths of the land area, and its Volcán Wolf, at 1,700 metres, is the highest point. The islands rest on the Nazca plate and above the Galápagos hotspot, where a mantle plume creates volcanoes. The cold Humboldt Current brings frequent drizzle.

Whether Polynesians or the Indigenous peoples of South America ever reached the islands is disputed. European discovery is recorded on 10 March 1535, when Tomás de Berlanga, bishop of Panama, sailing to Peru, drifted off course in the Doldrums. The islands were so arid that two men and ten horses died for lack of fresh water, and he left them unclaimed. The name comes from the giant tortoises, galápagos in Spanish, and appears on Abraham Ortelius's map of 1570.

Pirates, mostly English, used the islands as a hideout until the early nineteenth century to attack Spanish treasure fleets from Peru. William Ambrosia Cowley mapped them in 1684 and gave English names to 16 of them. The first known permanent resident was Patrick Watkins, an Irish sailor marooned on Floreana from 1807 to 1809. Ecuador formally occupied the islands on 12 February 1832, and José de Villamil led the settlement. In 1892 the group was renamed the Colón or Columbus Archipelago, still its official name on Ecuadorian maps.

In the early twentieth century the United States wished to buy the islands to guard the Panama Canal, and Chilean diplomacy supported Ecuador's resistance. Protective legislation began in 1930, and the Galápagos Province was created by decree on 18 February 1973.

The islands form Ecuador's Galápagos Province, with Puerto Baquerizo Moreno as capital and a population slightly over 33,450 in 2020. All the islands are part of Galápagos National Park and Marine Reserve. Their endemic species include giant tortoises, finches, flightless cormorants and marine iguanas, and about 180 vascular plant species are endemic. Introduced goats, cats, cattle and plants remain the chief threat to native life.
galata-tower: In 1267 the Genoese, allied with the Byzantine Empire, founded a colony called Pera in Galata, north of the Golden Horn. They later expanded without authorization toward the hill to the north-east and between 1335 and 1349 built walls and towers surrounded by moats on its slopes. The tower now known as the Galata Tower was built in 1348. It was a watchtower and the principal tower of the fortifications meant to protect the colony's coastal section against a siege by land. A cross stood at its summit. A war between the Byzantines and Genoese broke out in August 1348 and ended in 1349, and a decree of Emperor John VI transferred the hill to the Genoese.

After the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople on 29 May 1453, the Genoese of Pera surrendered the colony without resistance. Damage to the tower's summit was halted by an edict of Sultan Mehmed II. Under restoration led by Zağanos Pasha the cross was replaced with the Ottoman flag. An earthquake in 1509 damaged it, and repairs under Mimar Hayreddin were complete by mid-1510. In the 16th century the tower and others along the walls housed Christian prisoners of war working at the Kasımpaşa shipyards. In the 17th century Evliya Çelebi wrote that it had been a dungeon and in his time a supply warehouse. From the 18th century the Mehterhane corps and fire watchers used it as a lookout for fires.

A fire of 27 July 1794 forced repairs that shortened the tower, and its upper section became a coffeehouse, with a drum to announce fires and a dovecote in the attic. Another fire in 1831 led to further repairs. After the roof collapsed in a storm in 1875, two floors were added above the top, again for watching fires. After the republic was proclaimed in 1923 the fire brigade and the Turkish Naval Forces still used it. A restoration between 1965 and 1967 made it a tourist facility, and it has served as a museum and exhibition venue since work in 2020.

The Galata Tower is a cylindrical masonry tower in the Romanesque style, 62.59 m tall to the tip of its roof. It stands on a hill 35 m above sea level in the Beyoğlu district of Istanbul. It has eleven floors, including a basement, ground floor and mezzanine. An elevator runs to the sixth floor, and the eighth floor is an observation terrace. A poem by Pertev above the entrance commemorates repairs of 1831 and 1832. The tower is a symbolic landmark of Beyoğlu and Istanbul, and was included on UNESCO's Tentative List of World Heritage Sites in 2013.
galati: Galați lies in south-eastern Romania, on the left bank of the Danube at the junction of the Siret and the Prut, about 80 kilometres from the Black Sea. It is the capital of Galați County in the historical region of Western Moldavia and one of the larger cities on the Danube. The nearest town is Brăila, 15 kilometres to the south, and the two have long been rivals. The city is built on three terraces, from the low Valley City area to the old town, now the centre, and the higher modern city.

The area was occupied in the Neolithic period, and the town developed from a Dacian settlement of the sixth and fifth centuries BCE beside a ford over the Danube. After the Dacian wars against the Romans in 101 to 102 and 105 to 106, the area became part of the Roman empire, and a strong fortress was built at Barboși to defend the ford. A document signed by Stephen II of Moldavia mentions Galați in 1445, and after the Ottomans conquered Chilia in 1484 it remained Moldavia's only port, for trade with Turkey and Poland.

Tatars plundered the town in 1710, Russia opened a consulate in 1775, and Russian troops under General Mikhail Kamensky burned it during the Russo-Turkish War of 1787–92. After Russia annexed half of Moldavia in 1812, Galați was left as Moldavia's only port, and warships were built there. After the Second World War it was rebuilt on communist lines; the steel works began construction in 1960 and opened in 1966, when the population was 151,000.

Galați is an economic centre based on its port, its naval shipyard, the largest in Romania, and the largest steel works in the country, still commonly called Sidex. The University of Galați was founded in 1974. The Archdiocesan Cathedral of the Lower Danube was begun in 1906 and built over eleven years, and the Roman and Dacian site of Tirighina-Barboși has been excavated. The 2021 census counted 217,851 inhabitants. In Bram Stoker's novel Dracula, Galați, spelled Galatz, is the port where the Count lands on his way back to Transylvania.
galba: Servius Sulpicius Galba was born near Terracina on 24 December 3 BCE into a wealthy and distinguished noble family unrelated to the Julio-Claudian dynasty. One ancestor had been consul in 200 BCE and another in 144 BCE, and his father and elder brother, both named Gaius, held the office in 5 BCE and 22 CE. His stepmother Livia Ocellina adopted him, and he took the name Lucius Livius Ocella Sulpicius Galba, which he gave up on becoming emperor. He married Aemilia Lepida and had two sons, but she and the sons died in the early years of Claudius, and he never remarried.

Galba became praetor about 30, governed Aquitania for about a year and was consul in 33. In 39, after a plot against Caligula involving the general Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Gaetulicus, Caligula put Galba in command of the legions of Germania Superior, where he gained a reputation as a disciplinarian. He governed Africa from 44 or 45 and retired at an uncertain date under Claudius, possibly in 49. Nero recalled him in 59 or 60 to govern Hispania.

In 68 Gaius Julius Vindex rebelled against Nero in Gaul. Galba also rebelled, rejecting the title General of Caesar for General of the Senate and People of Rome. On the night of 8 June the official Nymphidius Sabinus falsely told the Praetorian Guard that Nero had fled to Egypt, and Galba was proclaimed emperor. Nero killed himself with help from his secretary.

Galba, who suffered from chronic gout, relied on a circle of advisers: the general Titus Vinius, the praetorian prefect Cornelius Laco and his freedman Icelus. He seized property, dismissed his Germanic bodyguards and did not pay the Praetorians or the soldiers who had fought Vindex, and he became unpopular. Suetonius, who gives the fullest account, reports a double reputation for cruelty and avarice, and Tacitus judged that he seemed equal to the imperial office until he held it.

On 1 January 69 two legions of Germania Superior refused to swear loyalty and the soldiers of Germania Inferior proclaimed their governor Aulus Vitellius emperor. Galba adopted Lucius Calpurnius Piso Licinianus as his successor, but Marcus Salvius Otho, angered at being passed over, plotted with a few Praetorian Guards. Galba was killed on 15 January 69 near the Lacus Curtius in the Forum; Piso and Vinius also died, and Laco and Icelus did not survive Otho's reign. His body was taken to a tomb in his private gardens on the Aurelian Way. Otho became emperor.
galeazzo-ciano: Galeazzo Ciano was born in Livorno on 18 March 1903, the son of Admiral Costanzo Ciano, a hero of the First World War, a founding member of the National Fascist Party and the reorganiser of the Italian merchant navy in the 1920s. Father and son both took part in Mussolini's March on Rome in 1922. Galeazzo studied the philosophy of law at the University of Rome, worked briefly as a journalist and then entered the diplomatic service. On 24 April 1930 he married Benito Mussolini's daughter Edda, and they had three children. He then served at the Italian Legation in Beijing and as consul in Shanghai.

On his return to Italy in 1935 Ciano became minister of press and propaganda. He volunteered for the invasion of Ethiopia as a bomber squadron commander and won two silver medals of valour. In 1936 Mussolini made him foreign minister, and he began his diary soon afterwards. He negotiated the formal alliance with Germany, the Pact of Steel, in Berlin in May 1939.

In early August 1939 Mussolini sent him to Germany to explain that Italy was not ready for a large war. When Italy declared war on France in 1940 he wrote in his diary, "I am sad, very sad. The adventure begins. May God help Italy!"

Ciano became disenchanted with Nazi Germany, but he went along with the ill-advised parallel war and the badly executed invasion of Greece. After the Axis defeat in North Africa he pressed for Italy's exit from the war, and on 5 February 1943 he was removed from the foreign ministry with the rest of the cabinet. He then became ambassador to the Holy See, presenting his credentials to Pope Pius XII on 1 March 1943.

On 24 July 1943 the Fascist Grand Council voted 19 to 8 for Dino Grandi's resolution asking the king to resume his constitutional powers, and Ciano voted in favour. The king dismissed Mussolini the next day and had him arrested. Ciano and Edda fled with their children to Germany on 27 August 1943. The Germans, furious at his vote, turned him over to Mussolini's Italian Social Republic, which arrested him for treason. After the Verona trial he was shot on 11 January 1944 with four others who had voted against Mussolini, all tied to chairs.

His diaries of 1937 to 1943, survived because Edda smuggled five of them to Switzerland. They were first published in English in 1946 and were used by the prosecution against Joachim von Ribbentrop at the Nuremberg trials.
galen: Galen was born in September 129 in Pergamon, in present-day Bergama, Turkey, the son of Aelius Nicon, a wealthy Greek architect with scholarly interests. His Latin name implies that he held Roman citizenship. At sixteen he began medical studies at the healing temple, or asclepeion, of Pergamon, where he served as an attendant for four years. He then travelled widely, exposing himself to a variety of medical theories, before settling in Rome in 162, where he made his mark as a practising physician. His public demonstrations and impatience with other views brought him into conflict with other doctors.

Galen was in Rome when the Antonine Plague struck in 166, and he described its symptoms and his treatment of it. His account is enough to identify the disease as related to smallpox. He became personal physician to several emperors, and Marcus Aurelius is reported to have called him first among doctors and unique among philosophers. A fire in the Temple of Peace in 191 or 192 destroyed many of his works, particularly treatises on philosophy.

The date of his death is debated: a later Greek lexicon implies about 199, but Arabic sources say he died in Sicily at the age of 87, which would mean about 216, and scholars including Nutton and Boudon-Millot favour that date.

Galen followed the theory of the four humours, black bile, yellow bile, blood and phlegm, and linked an imbalance of each to a temperament. Roman law had prohibited human dissection since roughly 150 BCE, so he dissected animals, mostly primates, and urged his students to look at dead gladiators. He showed that the larynx generates the voice, and was among the first to use experiments in medical research. In On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato he placed the parts of the soul in the brain, heart and liver, an idea now called localization of function.

He may have written as many as 500 treatises, of which less than a third survive. In the 9th century Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated 129 of his works into Arabic. From the 11th century Latin translations carried Galenism to the West, where he was called the Medical Pope of the Middle Ages. His anatomy stood until Andreas Vesalius published his work in 1543.
galerius: Galerius was of Dacian origin and was born in the Danube provinces, either near Serdica or at the place where he later built a palace named after his mother, Felix Romuliana (Gamzigrad). His mother Romula had left Roman Dacia because of attacks by the Carpi. He followed his father's occupation as a herdsman and was nicknamed Armentarius, from the Latin for herd. He served with distinction under the emperors Aurelian and Probus, and married Diocletian's daughter Valeria. In 293, at the establishment of the Tetrarchy, he was named Caesar together with Constantius Chlorus and was entrusted with the Illyrian provinces.

After campaigning against Sarmatians and Goths on the Danube, he took command on the eastern frontier. The Sasanian king Narseh inflicted a severe defeat on him between Carrhae and Callinicum. Diocletian then made him walk a mile ahead of the imperial cart in his purple robes, which some scholars read as blame, while another sees ordinary procedure. In 298 Galerius reinforced his army and defeated Narseh in two battles, the second at Satala, where the Romans seized Narseh's camp, treasury and wife. The Peace of Nisibis of 299 made the Tigris the boundary, returned Armenia to Roman influence and gave Rome control of five satrapies. Galerius also defeated the Carpi in 297 and 300.

He was promoted to Augustus when Diocletian abdicated in 305. After Constantius died in 306 Galerius reluctantly accepted Constantine as Caesar, and when Maxentius rebelled in Italy he invaded but had to withdraw. At the conference at Carnuntum in 308 it was agreed that Licinius would be Augustus in the West. Seven claimants to power eventually existed, and Galerius spent his later years on public works such as a logging and drainage project at Lake Balaton.

Galerius was a fierce advocate of the old gods, and Christians credited the persecution beginning with the edict of 24 February 303 to his work. Some historians claim he provoked Diocletian into it, although the fire in the palace he is said to have started is unproven. In April 311 at Serdica he issued an edict of toleration, apparently during his last illness, and asked Christians to pray for him and the state. This ended official persecution, and Constantine and Licinius legalised Christianity two years later in the Edict of Milan.

He died in late April or early May 311 of a painful illness described by Eusebius and Lactantius. He was buried in a mausoleum at Gamzigrad-Romuliana, which was inscribed on the World Heritage List in June 2007. Lactantius, a Christian and adviser to Constantine, portrays him as hostile to Rome, but Timothy Barnes and others suspect he tailored the facts to his thesis.
galilean-moons: With a telescope he had improved to a magnification of 20 times, Galileo Galilei observed the moons in January 1610. On 7 January he wrote a letter that mentions them for the first time. He saw only three, and took them for fixed stars near Jupiter. The next night he noticed that they had moved, on 13 January he saw all four at once, and by 15 January he concluded that they were bodies orbiting Jupiter. Simon Marius claimed an earlier sighting, but his first observation, once his Julian dates are converted, falls on 8 January 1610, a day after Galileo's.

Galileo had been tutor to Cosimo de' Medici, who became Grand Duke Cosimo II of Tuscany in 1609, and he used the discovery to seek the family's patronage. He first called the moons Cosimo's stars, then, on the advice of the Grand Duke's secretary, the Medician stars, honouring all four Medici brothers. The Sidereus Nuncius, published in Venice in March 1610, used that name.

Ganymede, Callisto, Io and Europa are listed in descending order of size. Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System and is larger than the planet Mercury, though with about half its mass. Callisto is slightly smaller than Mercury, and Io and Europa are about the size of the Earth's Moon. The three inner moons are locked in an orbital resonance of 4:2:1. Io has more than 400 active volcanoes, and an ocean of water is thought to lie beneath Europa's icy surface. The four are bright enough to be seen with binoculars, though their closeness to Jupiter makes naked-eye observation very difficult.

The names now in use come from Marius, who proposed in his Mundus Jovialis of 1614, at the suggestion of Johannes Kepler, to name the moons after lovers of Zeus: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. Galileo refused them and numbered the moons I to IV outward from Jupiter. The numbers stayed in use until the middle of the 20th century, when other inner moons were found and Marius's names became widely used.

Bodies circling something other than the Earth dealt a serious blow to the Ptolemaic system, in which everything orbits the Earth. Galileo also proposed finding longitude at sea from the timing of the moons' eclipses, and in 1616 he applied for the Spanish prize of 6,000 gold ducats. Observing from a moving ship proved too hard, but on land Giovanni Domenico Cassini and Jean Picard used the method to re-map France.
galilee: Galilee is a region of northern Israel and southern Lebanon, made up of the Upper Galilee and the Lower Galilee, with the Western Galilee and the Galilee Panhandle as further sub-regions. It lies north of the Mount Carmel and Mount Gilboa ridge and south of the east-west stretch of the Litani River, and runs from the Mediterranean coast near Acre to the Jordan Valley, with Dan at the foot of Mount Hermon in the north-east. Some definitions include the Jezreel Valley, the Beit She'an Valley, the Hula Valley and the Sea of Galilee.

The name appears in Egyptian inscriptions of the 15th century BCE recording the campaigns of Tuthmosis III. In Biblical Hebrew gālíl means district or circle, and Isaiah calls the region Galilee of the nations, a reference to the gentiles who settled there.

In the Iron Age II Galilee was part of the Kingdom of Israel, which fell to the Assyrians. The local Israelite population was carried off to Assyria after 732 BCE. Before the Hasmonean conquest the region was sparsely populated, and the first Hasmonean king, Aristobulus I, annexed much of it in 104 to 103 BCE, after which Jewish settlement grew. By the early Roman period it was predominantly Jewish, with towns such as Tiberias, and an economy of olives, fishing and pottery; salted and pickled fish were exported from Magdala.

After the Muslim conquest of the 630s Galilee belonged to Jund al-Urdunn, with Tiberias as its capital, and underwent Arabization and Islamization. In the Ottoman period Jews expelled from Spain settled in Safed, which became a centre of weaving and learning. The Druze emir Fakhr al-Din Ma'n governed the region from 1602, and in 1620 he allowed the Franciscans to re-establish a church at the site of the Annunciation in Nazareth. It came under British rule after the First World War, as part of Mandatory Palestine from 1923, and after the 1948 war nearly the whole of Galilee came under Israeli control.

Galilee has many small villages, and agriculture and tourism are the main livelihoods. The largest cities include Acre, Nahariya, Nazareth, Safed, Karmiel, Afula and Tiberias, and Haifa is the commercial centre of the region. The population includes Muslims, Druze, Christians, Jews, Bedouins and Circassians.

Christian pilgrims visit the shores of the Sea of Galilee, where the New Testament places many miracles of Jesus, and sites such as Megiddo, Mount Tabor and Hazor. Safed remains one of Judaism's four holy cities and a centre for kabbalah.
galileo-galilei: Galileo was born in Pisa, then part of the Duchy of Florence, on 15 February 1564, the first of six children of Vincenzo Galilei, a leading lutenist, composer and music theorist, and Giulia Ammannati. His family moved to Florence when he was eight, though he stayed in Pisa for two years more. From 1575 to 1578 he was educated, particularly in logic, at the Vallombrosa Abbey. He seriously considered the priesthood, but in 1580 enrolled at the University of Pisa for a medical degree at his father's urging.

He had been deliberately kept from mathematics, since a physician earned more than a mathematician, but after accidentally attending a lecture on geometry he persuaded his reluctant father to let him study mathematics and natural philosophy instead.

Galileo made original contributions to the science of motion by combining experiments and mathematics. He was one of the first modern thinkers to state clearly that the laws of nature are mathematical. In The Assayer he wrote that philosophy is written in the book of the universe in the language of mathematics, whose characters are triangles, circles and other geometric figures. With an improved telescope he observed the Milky Way, the phases of Venus, the four largest satellites of Jupiter, Saturn's rings, lunar craters and sunspots.

His Starry Messenger of 1610 was the first scientific treatise published on observations made through a telescope. His Letters on Sunspots of 1613 suggested that the Sun and heavens are changeable. His championing of Copernican heliocentrism met opposition within the Catholic Church and from some astronomers. The Roman Inquisition investigated the matter in 1615 and concluded that his opinions contradicted accepted Biblical interpretations.

His Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems of 1632 appeared to dispute and satirise Pope Urban VIII, alienating both the Pope and the Jesuits. He was tried by the Inquisition, found vehemently suspect of heresy and forced to recant, and spent the rest of his life under house arrest. During this time he wrote Two New Sciences, published in 1638, on kinematics and the strength of materials. He died on 8 January 1642, aged 77, following a fever and heart palpitations.

Grand Duke Ferdinando II wished to bury him in the main body of the Basilica of Santa Croce, but plans were dropped after protests from Pope Urban VIII and Cardinal Francesco Barberini. He was reburied in the main body in 1737.
galle: Galle lies on the south-western tip of Sri Lanka, 119 km south of Colombo. In ancient times it was known as Gimhathiththa, thought to mean a port near the River Gin. The Sinhalese name Gālla is believed to come from a word for a place where cattle are herded, because bullock carts sheltered there after long journeys; another theory derives the name from the Latin gallus or Portuguese galo, meaning rooster, which the Dutch used as the symbol of Galle. The hill of Rumassala forms a natural barrier east of the harbour, and local tradition links it with events of the Ramayana.

Galle was a prominent seaport long before European rule, and Persians, Arabs, Greeks, Romans, Malays, Indians and Chinese traded through it. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta, who called it Qali, visited in 1342. In the 12th and 13th centuries Sinhalese refugees fleeing Tamil armies from the north settled in and near the town. In 1411 the Galle Trilingual Inscription, in Chinese, Tamil and Persian, was set up to commemorate the second visit to Ceylon of the Chinese admiral Zheng He.

In 1502 a small Portuguese fleet under Lourenço de Almeida, blown off course on its way to the Maldives, stopped briefly at Galle before going on to the king at Kotte. In 1640 the Portuguese surrendered to the Dutch East India Company, whose fort, with a granite wall and three bastions named Sun, Moon and Star, still stands. After the British took over the country from the Dutch in 1796, they kept the fort unchanged and used it as the district's administrative centre.

Galle is the provincial capital and largest city of Southern Province and the capital of Galle District, with a population mostly Sinhalese and with many Muslims, particularly in the fort area. Its fort is a World Heritage Site and the largest remaining fortress in Asia built by European occupiers. Other landmarks include the natural harbour, the National Maritime Museum and St Mary's Cathedral. The city was devastated by the tsunami of 26 December 2004. A railway and the Galle Road link it to Colombo.
galleon: The English word galleon is probably borrowed from the Italian galeone or galione, later reinforced by the Spanish galeón. These forms go back to galea, a galley, with an augmenting suffix. The term is thought to come from gallioni, Venetian oared vessels used on rivers in the fifteenth century. The galleons of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries were fully developed sailing ships, which emerged in the early 16th century in Portugal and Spain from ships such as the caravel and the carrack. The name was used notably in Spain, Portugal and Venice. English shipwrights built galleon-type vessels but simply called them ships.

A lowering of the carrack's forecastle and a longer hull gave ocean-going ships more stability and less wind resistance at the front. The galleon differed from the carrack mainly by being longer, lower and narrower, with a square tuck stern instead of a round one and a snout or head projecting from the bows below the forecastle. It carried three or four masts, with a lateen sail on the rear ones. Some Portuguese carracks exceeded 1,000 tons, while galleons were usually under 500 tons, although some Manila galleons reached 2,000 tons. The Spanish captains Pedro Menéndez de Avilés and Álvaro de Bazán designed the definitive long, narrow-hulled galleon in the 1550s.

Galleons were built of oak for the keel, pine for the masts and various hardwoods for the hull and decking, usually carvel-built. Hundreds of tradesmen worked for months on one, and groups of wealthy businessmen often pooled the cost, so most galleons were first built for trade. The most common gun was the demi-culverin.

Galleons were first used by Europeans as armed cargo carriers and were the principal vessels drafted as warships until the Anglo-Dutch Wars of the mid-17th century. Carracks were lightly armed and became almost exclusively cargo ships, while galleons were more heavily armed and cheaper to build for the same displacement: five galleons could cost about as much as three carracks. They served in the Spanish treasure fleet and as the Manila galleons, which sailed between Manila and Acapulco from 1565 to 1815.

Galleons also appeared in the Mediterranean, where rowed galleys were usually more practical. Spain used them at least since the conquest of Tunis in 1535, and in 1616 a Spanish sailing fleet led by galleons repulsed a large Ottoman galley fleet at Cape Gelidonya. The Vasa, which sank in 1628 and was raised in 1961, is the only original galleon preserved.
galley: A galley is a ship optimised for propulsion by oars. It developed in the Mediterranean world during antiquity and lasted in various forms until the early 19th century. The English word is attested from about 1300 and comes from the Medieval Greek galea, a smaller version of the dromon, the main warship of the Byzantine navy. The first evidence of craft regarded as prototypes of galleys comes from Egypt in the Old Kingdom, when under Pepi I such vessels carried troops to raid the Levantine coast.

A galley typically had a long, slender hull, a shallow draft and a low freeboard. Most also carried sails, square ones until the early Middle Ages and lateen sails later, but relied on oars to move independently of winds and currents. Ancient galleys had oars in 15 to 30 pairs, from monoremes to triremes with three tiers, which by the 5th century BCE were in use in the eastern Mediterranean. From the 12th century the war galley took the form that lasted to the late 18th century, with a length-to-breadth ratio of at least 8:1, a projecting outrigger for the oars and benches in a herringbone pattern. A mid-17th-century galley had 25 pairs of oars and about 500 men.

Contrary to the popular image of chained rowers, there is no evidence that ancient navies regularly used condemned criminals or slaves as oarsmen. Greek and Roman navies relied on paid labour or ordinary soldiers, and slaves rowed only in crises. The later a scaloccio method, with several rowers on one large oar, suited forced labour, both galley slaves and convicts.

Galleys were the primary warships of the Phoenicians, Greeks and Romans and the dominant warship in the Mediterranean until the early modern period. They carried out landing raids, ferried troops and fought mainly by boarding, with rams until late antiquity, Greek fire in the early Middle Ages and cannon from the 15th century. They also carried high-value goods and Christian pilgrims. Around 1450 the Ottomans, Venice and Habsburg Spain used them as primary weapons in the eastern, central and western Mediterranean.

Galleys were unsuitable far from land and in rough weather. In the 16th century Ottoman galleys contested the Portuguese intrusion into the Indian Ocean but failed against the high-sided Portuguese carracks, whose heavy iron guns outmatched the short-ranged, low Turkish galleys. French galley numbers peaked in the 1690s, with more than 50 vessels, and the corps was abolished in 1748.
gallic-wars: The tribes of Gaul belonged to the La Tène culture. Many had contact with Roman merchants, struck coins and traded iron, grain and slaves with Rome, and some, such as the Aedui, had enjoyed stable alliances with Rome.

Caesar had incurred significant debts as consul in 59 BCE. Through the First Triumvirate, with Marcus Licinius Crassus and Pompey, he secured the governorship of Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum, and Transalpine Gaul was added when its governor died, for a term of five years. Caesar portrayed the invasion as defensive, but historians agree that he fought chiefly to boost his career and pay off his debts.

The wars began in 58 BCE with the migration of the Helvetii, a confederation of tribes on the Swiss plateau, which drew in neighbouring tribes and the Germanic Suebi. By 57 BCE Caesar had resolved to conquer all of Gaul, and he marched against the Belgae. In 56 BCE he defeated the Veneti in a naval battle and took most of northwest Gaul. In 55 BCE he made the first Roman expeditions across the Rhine and the English Channel, partly to keep himself in the public eye; Rome hailed him as a hero, although he had achieved little beyond landing. He returned to Britain the next year and extracted tribute from the locals.

In winter 54 BCE the Eburones under Ambiorix destroyed a Roman force under Quintus Titurius Sabinus and Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta, and only a handful of Romans survived. A brutal pacification campaign followed in 53 BCE. In 52 BCE Vercingetorix led a major revolt. The Gauls won a notable victory at Gergovia, but the Roman siege works at the Battle of Alesia crushed the Gallic coalition. Resistance in 51 and 50 BCE was limited.

The wars have no precise end date. The coming Roman Civil War led Caesar to withdraw his troops in 50 BCE. They made him wealthy and gave him a great reputation, and were a key factor in his ability to win the civil war and make himself dictator. Gaul was made formally into Roman provinces only under Augustus in 27 BCE.

The main source is Caesar's own Commentarii de Bello Gallico, which was largely taken as accurate until the 20th century. Modern historians consider it propaganda prone to exaggeration: Caesar claims to have killed over a million Gauls while reporting almost no Roman casualties, and modern historians believe the Gallic forces were far smaller than he claimed. The campaigns were exceptionally brutal, and untold numbers of Gauls were killed, enslaved or mutilated, including many civilians.
gallienus: Gallienus was born into a wealthy and traditional senatorial family, the son of Valerian and Mariniana. His exact birth date is unknown, but two late sources give his age at death as about 50, which puts it around 218. About ten years before his accession he married Cornelia Salonina, and they had three sons. When Valerian was proclaimed emperor in September 253, he had the Senate raise Gallienus to the rank of Augustus. Father and son divided the empire, as Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus had done a century earlier: Valerian went east to meet the Persian threat, and Gallienus stayed in the west to repel Germanic tribes on the Rhine and Danube.

Between 258 and 260 Gallienus defeated the usurper Ingenuus in the Balkans, but his absence left the Rhine open. The Franks broke into Gaul, some reaching southern Spain, and the Alemanni crossed the Alps in the first invasion of the Italian peninsula since Hannibal, 500 years before. An improvised army raised by the Senate repelled them from the outskirts of Rome, and Gallienus's army defeated them at Mediolanum. They did not trouble the empire again for ten years.

In 260 Valerian was defeated and captured at Edessa by Shapur I of the Sasanian Empire, and control of the whole empire passed to Gallienus. He defeated the eastern usurpers Macrianus Major and Lucius Mussius Aemilianus in 261 and 262, but the general Postumus took Britain, Spain, Germania and much of Gaul as the Gallic Empire, which stayed independent until 274, and Palmyra under Odaenathus became independent in nearly every respect. In 267 to 269 the Heruli and others invaded by sea and ravaged Greek cities, among them Athens and Sparta.

In 268 the cavalry commander Aureolus proclaimed himself emperor at Mediolanum, was defeated and besieged in the city, and during the siege Gallienus was stabbed to death by the officer Cecropius. The sources agree that most of his officials wanted him dead. Ancient historians treated him badly, and the Historia Augusta, largely fictional, makes him a lover of luxury; this hostility was partly due to the loss of Gaul and Palmyra.

He was the first to commission primarily cavalry units, the Comitatenses, which could be sent anywhere in the empire quickly, and Aurelius Victor reports that he forbade senators to become military commanders. He also issued the first official declaration of tolerance of Christians, restoring their places of worship and cemeteries. Some historians now see him more favourably.
gallipoli: The Gallipoli Peninsula lies in the southern part of East Thrace, with the Aegean Sea to the west and the Dardanelles to the east. Gallipoli is the Italian form of the Greek name Kallípolis, meaning beautiful city, the original name of the modern town of Gelibolu. In antiquity the peninsula was protected by the Long Wall across its narrowest part, an isthmus of about 6.5 km, and it was known for its wheat. It lay on the main route between Europe and Asia and controlled the shipping route from Crimea. The city of Sestos was the main crossing point on the Hellespont.

According to Herodotus the Thracian Dolonci held the peninsula before Greek settlers, mainly Ionian and Aeolian, founded about twelve cities there in the 7th century BCE. Miltiades the Elder founded a major Athenian colony around 560 BCE. Athens enrolled the peninsula in the Delian League in 478 BCE, and it was ceded to Philip II of Macedon in 338 BCE. Lysimachus later made Lysimachia his capital there. The Romans took it and gave it to Eumenes II of Pergamon in 188 BCE; from 129 BCE it belonged to the Roman province of Asia. It was part of the Eastern Roman Empire from 395, and Attila the Hun captured Callipolis and Sestus in 443.

An earthquake destroyed the town and its walls on the night of 1 and 2 March 1354. Within a month the Ottomans besieged and captured it, making it their first stronghold in Europe and the staging area for expansion across the Balkans. The Savoyard Crusade recaptured it for Byzantium in 1366, but it was handed back in September 1376. British and French forces used it as an encampment during the Crimean War in 1854. In 1915 the Ottoman Empire deported Greek residents from Gallipoli and the surrounding region before the Allied landings.

During the First World War, French, British and other forces fought the Gallipoli campaign of 1915 and 1916 to secure a sea route to Russia. The first Australian troops landed at ANZAC Cove on 25 April 1915, and the last Allied soldiers withdrew by 9 January 1916. Turks regard the campaign as a defining moment in their national history, and 25 April is ANZAC Day in Australia and New Zealand. Greek troops occupied the town on 4 August 1920 during the Greco-Turkish War, and it returned to Turkish rule on 26 November 1922. From November 1920 to May 1922 a camp near Gelibolu held White Russian exiles, 26,590 of them transferred from Constantinople.

Between 1923 and 1926 Gallipoli was the centre of Gelibolu Province. It later became a district centre in Çanakkale Province. The Gallipoli Peninsula Historical National Park preserves battlefields, cemeteries and memorials of the campaign.
gallipoli-campaign: The Ottoman Empire entered the First World War on 31 October 1914 after the Black Sea raid. Allied planners wanted to take control of the Turkish straits, expose Constantinople to bombardment by warships and cut it off from the Asian part of the empire. Success could have opened the Bosphorus and Dardanelles to Allied supplies for Russia and given Western control of the Suez Canal. The campaign began on 19 February 1915 with an Anglo-French bombardment of the Dardanelles forts. On 18 March the Entente fleet of 18 battleships tried to force the narrowest point. The French battleship Bouvet struck a mine and capsized in two minutes, and the battleships Irresistible and Ocean were also lost.

After the naval failure, General Sir Ian Hamilton was appointed to command 78,000 men of the Mediterranean Expeditionary Force. Landings were made on 25 April 1915 at five beaches. The 29th Division landed at Cape Helles, while the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps landed north of Gaba Tepe at a place that became known as ANZAC. The French made a diversion at Kum Kale. The Ottoman 5th Army, a conscript force commanded by Sanders, held the high ground, and Lieutenant Colonel Mustafa Kemal had predicted the likely landing areas. The Allies were checked at Krithia in three battles, and trench warfare followed.

A force of 42,000 Ottoman troops attacked Anzac on 19 May and suffered about 13,000 casualties. In August the Allies tried a new offensive at Sari Bair and Suvla, which failed. Criticism of Hamilton's performance was smuggled out by journalists, and he was replaced by Sir Charles Monro. Autumn and winter brought gales, blizzards and flooding. The Allies evacuated the peninsula, and the campaign ended on 9 January 1916.

Casualty figures vary. Edward J. Erickson wrote in 2001 that over 100,000 men were killed, including 56,000 to 68,000 Ottoman soldiers and around 53,000 British and French. Fisher resigned in May 1915, and the crisis led H. H. Asquith to form a coalition government with the Conservatives. Churchill was demoted from First Lord of the Admiralty, and the Dardanelles Commission investigated the failure.

In Turkey the campaign is regarded as a defining moment, and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, who rose to prominence at Gallipoli, became the first president of the Republic of Turkey in 1923. In Australia and New Zealand it is regarded as a baptism of fire, linked to the emergence of a national identity and the Anzac spirit, and 25 April is Anzac Day. About 50,000 Australians and 16,000 to 17,000 New Zealanders served there. Analysis of the campaign led many to believe that amphibious assaults could not succeed against modern defences.
galway: Galway, in Irish Gaillimh, lies on the River Corrib between Lough Corrib and Galway Bay, and is the county town of County Galway. Its name comes from the river, which formed the western boundary of the earliest settlement, Dún Gaillimhe, the fort at the mouth of the Gaillimh. Residents are called Galwegians, and the Latin name of the city is Galvia. It bears the nickname City of the Tribes, from the fourteen merchant families who led it in its Hiberno-Norman period. The climate is oceanic, mild, moist and changeable, with about 1,156 mm of rain a year spread through the seasons.

During the Norman invasion of Connacht in the 1230s, Dún Gaillimhe was captured by Richard Mor de Burgh, who had led the invasion. As the de Burghs eventually became Gaelicised, the merchants of the town, the Tribes of Galway, pushed for greater control over the walled city. A municipal charter of 1484 allowed the citizens to form a council and mayoralty, and the first mayor, Peirce Lynch Fitzjohn, was elected in 1485. Controlled largely by the merchant families, the city grew into a trading port, before a period of decline.

Local government changed several times in the twentieth century. In 1937 the Urban District of Galway became the Borough of Galway, remaining part of County Galway; in 1986 it became the County Borough of Galway and ceased to be part of the county; and in 2001 it was renamed Galway City. Queen's College, Galway, was founded in 1845 and is now the University of Galway. The patron saint of the city since the 14th century has been St Nicholas of Myra, and the Roman Catholic diocese of Galway was created in 1831.

Galway is the capital of Connacht and, with a population of 85,910 at the 2022 census, the most populous settlement in the province. St. Nicholas' Collegiate Church, founded in 1320 and enlarged in the following two centuries, is the largest medieval church still in everyday use in Ireland. Lynch's Castle on Shop Street is a medieval townhouse built by the Lynch family in the 16th century, and Galway Cathedral, built on the site of the old gaol, was consecrated in 1965.

The city has a reputation for the Irish language, music, song and dance, and the Galway Gaeltacht lies on its doorstep. It holds many festivals, among them the Galway Arts Festival, and the Galway Races, first held in the 1860s. UNESCO designated it a City of Film in 2014.
gamprin: Gamprin is a municipality of Liechtenstein, on the Rhine, on the border with the Swiss municipality of Sennwald. It lies in the hilly landscape west of the Eschnerberg and consists of the villages of Gamprin and Bendern, in a scattered settlement that includes the old hamlets of Au, Bühl, Badäl, Salums and Gölla. It covers 6.188 square kilometres. It also has an exclave on the Nendler Berg, and its Gampriner Seele, a lake of 2.6 hectares, is the only lake in Liechtenstein. A flood of the Rhine in 1927 created it.

Settlement here goes back to the Stone, Bronze and Iron Ages, and the archaeological site of Lutzengüetle lies within the parish. The name comes from the Old Romansh camp Rin, a field on the Rhine. It was first mentioned about 1150 as Camporin, and in 1253 as Gamperin. The Bendern Parish Church, dedicated to Mary, has a nave dating from the 8th or 9th century, enlarged in the 14th century, and a Gothic chancel inaugurated in 1481. In 1499, during the Swabian War, Swiss Confederates pillaged the village. The oldest surviving village charter, of 1643, describes the villagers' rights and duties in using pastures and forests, and in 1699 the men of the Unterland swore allegiance to the Prince at Bendern.

In the 18th and 19th centuries Bendern ran one of the five ferries on the Liechtenstein stretch of the Rhine, linking it with Haag on the opposite bank. A wooden bridge was built across the river in 1867–68.

Until 1950 Gamprin had neither a coat of arms nor an official flag. A committee designed them, and the municipality adopted them in 1958. The yellow ribbon stands for the Rhine, and the roses come from the arms of the knight Rüdiger von Limpach, who owned property in Gamprin in the Middle Ages. The municipality contains the Liechtenstein Institute and the LGT Group.
ganapati-kakatiya: Ganapati's father Mahadeva was killed in a conflict with the Seuna, or Yadava, kingdom in 1198–1199, and Ganapati himself was taken captive. During his captivity the kingdom suffered revolts and invasions, and the commander-in-chief Rudra of the Recherla Reddi family appears to have governed in his name. An inscription at Manthena dated 26 December 1199 calls Ganapati the establisher of all the kingdom, which suggests that he had been freed by then. Yadava inscriptions claim that their king Jaitrapala released him out of compassion; the Yadavas may rather have wanted a quiet eastern border while they fought the Hoysalas.

Helped by the decline of the Kalyani Chalukya and Chola empires, Ganapati first turned to coastal Andhra, which the Kakatiyas had lost. The Krishna delta was conquered by 1201, and his general Chaunda plundered the island of Divi, whose Ayya chiefs submitted; Ganapati married two daughters of their chief, and their brother Jayapa became his commander. The Velanati Choda ruler Prithvishvara probably died fighting the Kakatiyas about 1206, and by 1209 Vela-nadu and Kamma-nadu were annexed. At Nellore Ganapati installed the Telugu Choda chief Tikka on the throne.

Repeated campaigns in Kalinga and Vengi from 1212 against the Eastern Ganga kings Ananga Bhima III and Narasimha I had mixed results, and Kakatiya control was probably limited to the land south of the Godavari River. In 1250 an army under Samanta Bhoja won a decisive victory at Palaiyaru and restored Tikka's son Manuma-siddhi II at Nellore. Around 1257, however, the Pandya king Jatavarman Sundara I attacked; the Pandyas captured Nellore and killed Manuma-siddhi II at the Battle of Muttukuru in 1263.

Ganapati continued the removal of the capital from Anumakonda to Orugallu, where he built a fortification of 75 bastions, each protected by a nayaka, comprising a stone fort and a mud fort one within the other. He also subdued the petty chiefs who had been harassing foreign merchants at the port of Motupalli.

Ganapati apparently retired after his defeats by the Pandyas in the late 1250s. He had no male heir and two daughters, Rudrama-devi, married to the Vengi Chalukya prince Virabhadra, and Ganapama-devi. Rudrama began to rule as co-regent in 1259–1260 under the regnal name Rudra-deva Maharaja, though an inscription at Duggi shows that Ganapati was alive at least until 1269. The 17th-century Pratapa-charita says that two sons of his by junior queens, Hari-hara and Murari-deva, rebelled against her; no other source knows these sons. Inscriptions listing distant kings as his vassals follow literary convention and can be dismissed.
gandaki-river: The Gandaki drains a catchment of 46,300 square kilometres, most of it in Nepal. Its upper course, the Kali Gandaki, rises at the Nhubine Himal Glacier in the Mustang region at 6,268 metres, on the border with Tibet. It then runs south through the Kali Gandaki Gorge between Dhaulagiri (8,167 metres) and Annapurna (8,091 metres), one of the deepest canyons in the world, and the river is older than the Himalayas, cutting through the mountains as they rise. Near Devghat the Kali Gandaki is joined by the Trishuli, a larger tributary.

Below Gaindakot the river is called the Narayani or Sapt Gandaki, the Seven Gandakis, after seven tributaries that rise in the Himalaya. In India it enters Uttar Pradesh, passes Kushinagar District and flows about 300 kilometres south-east across Bihar, building an immense megafan across eastern Uttar Pradesh and north-western Bihar.

The river is mentioned as Sadanira in the Shatapatha Brahmana, and in the Mahabharata. Its origin is told in the Shiva Purana. Between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna it flows past Muktinath, whose stones, the saligrama silas found in the riverbed, are of great significance to Hindus, who regard them as a representation of Narayana. Srivaishnavas and followers of Madhvacharya count the Muktinath temple among the 108 Divyakshetrams.

Along the river lie places of archaeological interest. At Lauriya-Nandangarh stands a lion pillar of Ashoka, a single block of polished sandstone 11 metres high, believed to be over 2,300 years old, beside brick stupas said to hold ashes from the Buddha's funeral pyre. Near the Kali Gandaki in Upper Mustang some 10,000 man-made caves have yielded partly mummified bodies and skeletons at least 2,000 to 3,000 years old, and religious paintings, sculptures and manuscripts of the 12th to 14th century. Mahatma Gandhi began the Champaran Satyagraha from his ashram at Bhitiharawa near the river.

Under an agreement signed on 4 December 1959 between Nepal and India, the Gandak Barrage was built at Valmikinagar in 1968–69 to supply irrigation to Nepal, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Chitwan National Park in Nepal, established in 1973 and a World Heritage Site since 1984, lies beside India's Valmiki National Park around the barrage. The river's valleys also have many hydroelectric stations.
ganesha: Ganesha is mentioned in Hindu texts between the 1st century BCE and the 2nd century CE, and a few images from the 4th and 5th centuries CE have been documented. An elephant-headed figure on Indo-Greek coins of the 1st century BCE has been proposed as an early depiction, but this is strongly contested. The first terracotta images date from the 1st century CE, and the earliest stone icons were carved at Mathura in Kushan times. The title gaṇapati appears twice in the Rig Veda, but there it refers to Brahmanaspati and Indra, not to Ganesha. The detailed stories of his birth and elephant head come from the later Puranas, composed from about 600 onwards.

Ganesha is identified by his elephant head and four arms. He is also called Ganapati, Vinayaka and Pillaiyar. Hindu texts name him as the son of Shiva and Parvati, though the Puranas give different accounts of his birth. In the most recurrent story Parvati made him from clay to guard her, and Shiva beheaded him when he came between them and replaced the head with an elephant's.

Devotees honour him as Vighneshvara, the Lord of Obstacles, held both to place obstacles in the way of those who need to be checked and to remove them for those who begin something new. He is also the patron of letters and learning. In the Ganapatya tradition he is the Supreme Being, and the Ganesha Purana and Mudgala Purana are its principal texts.

Hindus of all denominations invoke Ganesha at the beginning of prayers and ceremonies, and dancers and musicians, particularly in southern India, begin performances with a prayer to him. He is placed at the doorway of many temples, and the Ashtavinayak, eight shrines near Pune, are dedicated to him. The ten-day festival of Ganesh Chaturthi begins with the bringing in of clay idols, which are immersed in water at its end. In 1893 Lokmanya Tilak turned it from private family celebrations into a public event, to build unity against British rule in Maharashtra.

From about the 10th century he became the principal deity of traders. In Mahayana Buddhism he appears as the god Vināyaka, often dancing. Some Jains worship him, and the earliest known Jain statue dates to about the 9th century.
gangtok: Gangtok stands at an elevation of 1,650 m in the lower Himalayas, on the side of a hill. A promenade called The Ridge runs between the Raj Bhawan, the governor's residence, at one end and the palace at the other. Two streams, the Roro Chu and the Ranikhola, flank the city and flow south to join the Teesta at Singtam. Mount Kanchenjunga is visible to the west. The slopes are prone to landslides, and in June 1997 a landslide disaster killed 38 people and destroyed hundreds of buildings. Most agree that the name means hill top in Tibetan.

Little is known of Gangtok's early history. The earliest records date from the building of a hermitic monastery in 1716, and the town remained a small hamlet until the Enchey Monastery, built in 1840, made it a pilgrimage centre. After the English conquest of Sikkim in the mid-19th century it became the capital of what was left of Sikkim, and after the British defeated the Tibetans it became a major stopover in the trade between Tibet and British India. In 1894 Thutob Namgyal, the Sikkimese monarch under British rule, shifted the capital from Tumlong to Gangtok, and a new palace and other state buildings were built.

After India's independence in 1947 Sikkim became a nation-state under Indian suzerainty, by a treaty that gave India control of its external affairs. Trade through the Nathula and Jelepla passes flourished, but it declined after 1959 and the passes were sealed after the Sino-Indian War of 1962. In 1975, after years of political uncertainty including riots, the monarchy was abolished and, following a referendum, Sikkim became India's twenty-second state, with Gangtok as its capital.

Gangtok is the capital of Sikkim and the seat of the Sikkim High Court. Its residents include Nepalis, who settled in the region under British rule and form the majority, Lepchas, who are native to the land, Bhutias and Tibetans. Hinduism and Buddhism are the most significant religions. The Enchey Monastery is the city's oldest and the seat of the Nyingma order, and the Rumtek Monastery on the outskirts, built in the 1960s on the model of one in Lhasa, is the seat of the Kagyu order. Tourism is the main part of the city's economy.
ganja-azerbaijan: Ganja lies 400 to 450 metres above sea level on the Ganja-Dashkasan plain in the west of Azerbaijan, 375 km from Baku. It stands at the north-eastern foothills of the Lesser Caucasus on the Ganjachay river. The name comes from the Persian word ganj, meaning treasure or treasury; Arabic sources call the city Janza and Armenian sources Gandzak. The tale that its founder found treasure nearby is considered a folk etymology.

The anonymous Arabic history Tarikh Bab al-abwab says Ganja was founded in 859–60 by Muhammad ibn Khalid, the Arab governor of the region under the caliph Al-Mutawakkil, after he unearthed a treasure there. The medieval Armenian historian Movses Kaghankatvatsi supports a 9th-century Arab foundation, while the Persian name suggests an older pre-Islamic town. From the 9th to the 12th century the area was known as Arran, and its urban population mainly spoke Persian. The city was damaged by an earthquake in September 1139, when King Demetrius I of Georgia took it and carried off its gates, and again by the Mongol invasion of 1231. It revived after the Safavids came to power in 1501 and was occupied briefly by the Ottomans in 1578–1606 and 1723–1735.

After the death of Nader Shah in 1747 Ganja became the centre of the Ganja Khanate, whose khans were subordinate to the rule of Iran. Russia, after annexing eastern Georgia in 1801, met strong opposition at Ganja. In 1804 Russian forces under General Pavel Tsitsianov invaded and sacked the city, sparking the Russo-Persian War of 1804–1813. Some western sources claim that up to 3,000 inhabitants were massacred. The Treaty of Gulistan forced Iran to cede the khanate, and the Treaty of Turkmenchay of 1828 made its inclusion in the Russian Empire permanent. It was renamed Yelizavetpol after Alexander I's wife, Elizabeth, and became capital of the Elizavetpol Governorate in 1868, though local Azerbaijanis continued to call it Ganja.

In 1918 Ganja was the temporary capital of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic. The Red Army occupied Azerbaijan in April 1920, and in May an anti-Soviet rebellion in Ganja was put down, heavily damaging the city. In 1935 it was renamed Kirovabad after Sergei Kirov, and it regained its original name in 1989. A pogrom in November 1988 forced the local Armenian population to leave.

Ganja is a major city of western Azerbaijan, divided into the Kapaz and Nizami districts, which were established in 1980. The poet Nizami Ganjavi was born there, and its old landmarks include the Nizami Mausoleum, the Shah Abbas Caravanserai, the Imamzadeh complex and the Chokak Hamam. Most of its people are Muslim, mainly Shia, and most of its Armenians, Slavs, Jews and Germans have emigrated. The city is known for Ganja silk, and metallurgical and food industries operate there.
gansu: Gansu lies between the Tibetan Plateau and the Loess Plateau, bordering Xinjiang and Qinghai to the west, Sichuan to the south, Shaanxi to the east and Inner Mongolia and Ningxia to the north. The Yellow River passes through the south of the province and flows through Lanzhou. The Qilian Mountains rise in the south, and parts of the Gobi Desert lie within the province. The Hexi Corridor, a natural passage of some 1,000 kilometres from Lanzhou to the Jade Gate, runs between the Gobi to the north and the Qilian Mountains to the south.

The name Gansu is a compound of Ganzhou, around Zhangye, and Suzhou, around Jiuquan, two prefectures of the Sui and Tang periods; the compound was first used under the Song dynasty. Before that the region was known as Longxi or Longyou, after Mount Liupan.

In prehistoric times Gansu was home to Neolithic cultures. The Dadiwan culture flourished in the east from about 6000 BCE to about 3000 BCE, and the Majiayao and Qijia cultures took root there in later millennia. The Yuezhi lived in the far west until the Xiongnu forced them to emigrate around 177 BCE. The state of Qin grew out of the south-east, around Tianshui, and Qin tombs and artefacts have been excavated at Fangmatan.

The Han dynasty extended the Great Wall across the corridor and built the fort towns of Yumenguan and Yangguan along it. The Ming dynasty built the Jiayuguan outpost, begun around 1372 and then at the western edge of China. By the Qingshui treaty of 823 between the Tibetan Empire and the Tang dynasty, China lost much of western Gansu for a significant period. Uyghurs who had migrated from their fallen khaganate set up the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom, which lasted from 848 to 1036, and the Western Xia later controlled much of the province.

Along the Silk Road, Gansu was both an economic route and a path of cultural transmission. The Mogao Caves near Dunhuang were begun in 366 CE, when a monk named Le Zun is said to have had a vision and carved the first grotto. The Bingling and Maijishan grottoes also date from the early centuries of Buddhist art. The Dungan Revolt of 1862–77 began in Gansu, and an earthquake on 16 December 1920 killed some 180,000 people.

Gansu is a province of north-western China with Lanzhou as its capital and largest city. Its population is about 26 million, mostly Han, with Hui, Dongxiang and Tibetan minorities. Labrang Monastery, built in 1710 in the south, is one of the six great monasteries of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, and the Jiayuguan pass preserves a section of the Great Wall.
gao: Gao lies on the eastern bank of the Niger River, 320 km east-southeast of Timbuktu, at the junction with the Tilemsi Valley. The climate is arid, with rain only from June to September, and almost all local agriculture depends on the river's annual flood, which reaches Gao later than the upper river and peaks in December. In flood the river is 4 km wide at the city.

Excavations at Gao-Saney show that the site was occupied by about 700 CE, as a centre of manufacturing, iron smelting and trade reaching as far as Mesopotamia. Al-Khwārizmī gives the earliest written mention in the first half of the 9th century, and about 872 al-Yaqubi called the kingdom of Kawkaw the most important and most powerful of the realms of the Sūdān. By the 10th century the ruler was said to be a Muslim and the city had two towns. More than 100 medieval Arabic inscriptions survive from Gao and Gao-Saney, the oldest dated 1042. Towards the end of the 13th century Gao became part of the Mali Empire, and Ibn Battuta stayed there in 1352–53.

In the first half of the 15th century Sunni Sulayman Dama threw off Malian rule, and his successor Sunni Ali Ber, who ruled from 1464 to 1492, expanded Songhai territory and made Gao his capital. Leo Africanus, who visited between 1506 and 1510 under Askiya Muhammad I, found a large town without a wall, full of rich merchants, with a market where many slaves were sold. A survey under Askiya Al-Hajj, who reigned from 1582 to 1586, counted 7,626 houses, suggesting about 45,000 people. After the Moroccan invasion of 1591 the invaders made Timbuktu their capital, and Gao declined. When Heinrich Barth visited in 1854 he found a poor village of about 300 huts.

Gao is the capital of the Gao Region and the largest town in eastern Mali. The Tomb of Askia, a World Heritage Site, is a mosque tomb of some 2,500 square metres with a minaret 12 metres high. The town also has a mosque associated with Kankou Moussa, a museum of the Sahel and the sand dune La Dune Rose. Most people speak Koyraboro Senni, and the population includes Bozo, Fulani, Tuareg, Arab and Bambara groups. The city is regarded as a Songhay cultural capital.
garden-of-the-hesperides: In Greek mythology the Hesperides are the nymphs who tend the garden in which grow the trees of Hera that bear golden apples. They were also called the Atlantides, from their reputed father Atlas. Their name means originating from Hesperos, the evening, which also shares a root with the English word west. Their parents, number and names vary between sources. They are listed as daughters of Night, of Atlas and Hesperis, of Phorcys and Ceto, or of Zeus and Themis. Apollonius of Rhodes gives three, Aigle, Erytheis and Hespere, while Apollodorus gives four, Aigle, Erytheia, Hesperia and Arethusa. Euripides calls them minstrel maids for their sweet song.

The garden is Hera's orchard in the far west, near the Atlas Mountains, at the edge of the ocean of Oceanus. According to the legend, the goddess Gaia brought branches bearing golden apples as a wedding gift when Zeus and Hera married, and Hera had them planted in her gardens, which extended as far as Mount Atlas. The Hesperides tended the grove, and Hera set the immortal, never-sleeping, hundred-headed dragon Ladon to guard the apples. Pliny the Elder places the garden at Lixus in modern Morocco, and elsewhere says the Hesperides live on two islands in the Atlantic. Diodorus gives a variant in which the Hesperides had flocks of sheep so beautiful that the poets called them golden apples, guarded by a shepherd named Dracon.

Euesperides, modern Benghazi, might have mythological associations with the garden. Diodorus gives a variant in which the Hesperides had flocks of sheep so beautiful that the poets called them golden apples, guarded by a shepherd named Dracon.

The eleventh Labour of Heracles was to steal the apples. In one version Heracles tricked Atlas into fetching them by offering to hold up the heavens for a while, and then walked away with them; in another he killed Ladon.
