According to Apollodorus, Eurystheus gave the apples back to Heracles, and Athena returned them to the garden. The Argonauts came to the Hesperian plain the next day, and the Hesperides directed them to a spring that Heracles had struck from a rock near Lake Triton. Heracles appears sitting in bliss in the garden on Attic pottery, especially from the late fifth century BCE.

By Roman times the garden had dwindled to a poetic convention. It returned in Renaissance poetry, where Robert Greene, Shakespeare and John Milton mention it, and Robert Herrick's collection of verse, Hesperides, was published in 1647. Later it was thought the golden apples might have been oranges, and the Greek botanical name for citrus species is Hesperidoeidē.
garonne: The Garonne flows from the central Spanish Pyrenees to the Gironde estuary at the French port of Bordeaux, a length of 529 km, of which 47 km lies in the Val d'Aran in Spain. Its basin covers 56,000 square kilometres. The name comes from Garumna, a Latin form of an Aquitanian name meaning stony river. Three places have been proposed as its source, and by the usual convention of the United States Geological Survey and others it is the Ratera-Saboredo cirque, the most distant point of the basin.

The river follows the Aran Valley northwards into France and passes Toulouse and Agen on its way to Bordeaux. The Ariège, the Tarn and the Lot join it, and just after Bordeaux it meets the Dordogne at the Bec d'Ambès to form the Gironde estuary, which runs about 100 km to the Atlantic. It is one of the few rivers in the world with a tidal bore. The European sea sturgeon, critically endangered, breeds only in its basin.

Umayyad and Aquitanian forces fought the Battle of the River Garonne in 732 beside the river near present-day Bordeaux. The river has long served shipping. Seagoing vessels reach Bordeaux, and it forms part of the Canal des Deux Mers between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Before the lateral canal was built between 1838 and 1856, shallow-draught boats used the river as far as Toulouse, though navigation on the upper river was uncertain. The canal now takes boats through 53 locks to Toulouse, where it meets the Canal du Midi.

Floods have been recorded since around 1177, with others in 1220, 1258 and many later years. At Toulouse, where the left bank is inhabited, they were frequent. In 1827 the river rose four metres above its usual level and filled the arches of the Pont de Pierre and Pont Neuf, and the floods of 1835, 1855 and 1875 were higher.

The river passes Vielha, Saint-Gaudens, Muret, Toulouse, Agen, Marmande, Langon and Bordeaux. Upstream of Toulouse it depends mainly on snow and snow melt, and downstream it is fed by rain, as are its main tributaries. The Saint-Martory canal and the lateral canal both draw water from the river.
gascony: Gascony was a province of south-western France that succeeded the Duchy of Gascony, dated 602 to 1453. The region is vaguely defined: it lies between the Atlantic Ocean and the Pyrenees and extends north to the Garonne, with the Adour as its other main river. Most definitions put it east and south of Bordeaux. Its historical capital was Auch. Gascony was historically inhabited by Basque-related people, and the Gascon language, usually classified as a variety of Occitan, has been spoken there from the Middle Ages. The name comes from the same root as the word Basque, through Vasconia, Wasconia and Gasconia.

Before Roman rule the inhabitants were the Aquitanians, who spoke a language related to Basque. Julius Caesar's lieutenants conquered Aquitania in the 50s BCE. In 297 Emperor Diocletian made the territory south of the Garonne the province of Novempopulania, the land of the nine tribes, which corresponds mostly to modern Gascony. It was given to the Visigoths in 416 to 418 and passed to the Franks after their victory in 507. Viking raiders devastated towns including Bayonne and Dax in 842 to 844, until Duke William II Sánchez defeated them at Taller in 982. The duchy then splintered into counties and viscounties such as Fézensac, Armagnac, Astarac, Bigorre and Béarn.

The 1152 marriage of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine gave Henry control of Aquitaine and Gascony. The duchy functioned as an overseas English possession, sometimes called England's first colony. Philip IV of France confiscated it in 1294, beginning the Gascon War, and Edward I's three expeditions of 1294 to 1298 failed to recover it before the Treaty of Paris in 1303. In 1337 Philip VI of France took Gascony back into his hands, which precipitated the Hundred Years' War. The English were finally defeated at the Battle of Castillon on 17 July 1453, and Gascony remained French. From the 17th century its government was united with Guyenne, with its capital at Bordeaux, until 1792.

Gascony is divided between the region of Nouvelle-Aquitaine, with the departments of Landes, Pyrénées-Atlantiques, south-western Gironde and southern Lot-et-Garonne, and the region of Occitanie, with Gers, Hautes-Pyrénées, south-western Tarn-et-Garonne and western Haute-Garonne. Its towns include Auch, Bayonne, Dax, Lourdes, Mont-de-Marsan, Pau and Tarbes. It was the home of Henry III of Navarre, who became king of France in 1594, and it is the land of d'Artagnan, who inspired the character in Alexandre Dumas's The Three Musketeers.
gaul: Little is written about the peoples of Gaul before the Romans, so their early history rests largely on archaeology. Eastern and southern France shared in the Urnfield culture of the Late Bronze Age, from which the Hallstatt culture developed. The La Tène culture arose in the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, probably under Greek, Phoenician and Etruscan influence, and spread across the whole of Gaul by the late 5th century BCE. In the 4th and early 3rd centuries BCE Gallic tribal confederations expanded into northern Italy, Transylvania and Asia Minor.

Rome intervened in southern Gaul in 154 BCE and again in 125 BCE, when it stayed, and by 121 BCE it held the Mediterranean region called Provincia. Julius Caesar entered Gaul in 58 BCE, ostensibly to help Rome's allies against the migrating Helvetii, and conquered nearly all of it. Vercingetorix tried to unite the Gauls and checked Caesar at Gergovia, but Caesar captured him at the Battle of Alesia in September 52 BCE. The Gallic Wars are said to have killed as many as a million people, probably one in twelve of the Gauls, and to have enslaved another million.

Gaul's inhabitants gradually adopted Roman culture, producing a Gallo-Roman culture, and all received citizenship in 212 CE. From 260 to 273 the Gallic Empire broke away from Rome. After Frankish victories in 486, 507 and 532, Gaul except for Brittany and Septimania came under the Merovingians, the first kings of France.

The basic unit of Gallic politics was the tribe or civitas, which had a council of elders and at first a king; later the executive was an annually elected magistrate. The Gauls were seldom united. Caesar divided the people of Gallia Comata into the Aquitani, the Belgae and the Celtae. The druids presided over sacrifices, kept the agricultural calendar, educated the aristocracy and claimed the right to decide questions of war and peace. The Gaulish language is thought to have survived into the 6th century and helped shape the Vulgar Latin that became French.
gauls: The Gauls were a group of Celtic peoples of mainland Europe in the Iron Age and the Roman period, roughly from the 5th century BCE to the 5th century CE, and they spoke Gaulish, a Continental Celtic language. Their culture developed over the first millennium BCE, from the Urnfield culture through the Hallstatt culture of the 8th century BCE to the La Tène culture from around the 5th century BCE. By the 4th century BCE they were spread over much of what is now France, Belgium, Switzerland, southern Germany, Austria and the Czech Republic, controlling trade routes along the Rhône, Seine, Rhine and Danube. Their name Galli is generally derived from a Celtic root meaning power or ability.

Gallic invaders settled the Po Valley in the 4th century BCE and defeated Roman forces under Brennus in 390 BCE. In the early 3rd century BCE they expanded into the Balkans, and in 279 BCE they defeated the Macedonians and killed King Ptolemy Keraunos. Those who crossed to Asia Minor settled in Galatia, and the Seleucid king Antiochus I checked them with war elephants in 275 BCE. Many Gauls served as mercenaries in the armies of Carthage, and Hannibal used them in his invasion of Italy, including at Cannae.

Roman pressure grew after the First Punic War. The Battle of Telamon in 225 BCE began a gradual decline of Gallic power. The Romans conquered the area later called Gallia Narbonensis by 121 BCE, and the Cisalpine Gauls were subdued in the early 2nd century BCE. In 58 BCE Julius Caesar began the Gallic Wars, and a mixed Gallo-Roman culture emerged after the annexation. In the crisis of the third century a Gallic Empire briefly broke away under the Batavian general Postumus.

Gaul was never united under a single ruler. The fundamental unit of politics was the tribe, each with a council of elders and at first a king, later an annually elected magistrate. Among the Aedui the executive was called a Vergobret. Many tribes built large fortified settlements called oppida, such as Bibracte, Gergovia and Alesia, and minted their own coins. They imported Mediterranean wine in large quantities, as the Vix grave's 1.63 m vessel shows. Their religion was polytheistic and overseen by druids, and they produced the Coligny calendar.

The Roman civitates, based on the tribes, later became the basis of the French dioceses, which lasted until the French Revolution. In modern France the Gauls have been evoked as ancestors, in the phrase of Ernest Lavisse's school textbook, our ancestors the Gauls.
gautama-buddha: Siddhartha Gautama was a wandering religious teacher of the eastern Indo-Gangetic Plains who lived in the 6th or 5th century BCE. Buddhist legends place his birth at Lumbini, in what is now Nepal, to royal parents of the Shakya clan. Most scholars accept that he lived, taught and founded a monastic order during the reign of Bimbisara of Magadha and died in the reign of Bimbisara's successor Ajatashatru, making him a contemporary of Mahavira, the Jain tirthankara.

His dates are uncertain. The long chronology of the Sri Lankan chronicles gives 624 to 544 BCE, while most scholars who accept it but date Ashoka's coronation to about 268 BCE put his life at 566 to 486 BCE. The oldest surviving written mention of the Buddha is from the middle of the 3rd century BCE, in the Edicts of Ashoka, whose Lumbini pillar inscription commemorates the emperor's pilgrimage to the birthplace. The earliest biographies already contain supernatural elements, and the scholar Rupert Gethin holds that the life story is not history, nor meant to be.

According to Buddhist tradition, he renounced home life to live as a wandering ascetic and attained nirvana at Bodh Gaya in what is now Bihar. He then taught across the lower Indo-Gangetic Plain and built a monastic order, the sangha. Tradition describes a Middle Way between sensual indulgence and severe asceticism, summarised in the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path. The earliest biographical material in the Pali Nikayas describes a forty-five-year career as a teacher.

He left no writings. His teachings were compiled by the Buddhist community as the Vinaya Pitaka, on monastic discipline, and the Sutra Pitaka, discourses attributed to him, passed down orally in Middle Indo-Aryan dialects. How far later doctrine reflects his own words is disputed. Scholars such as Richard Gombrich and A. K. Warder hold that early texts contain material traceable to him, while others doubt that the beliefs of pre-sectarian Buddhism can be recovered.

Buddhist tradition holds that he died at Kushinagar, in modern Uttar Pradesh, and reached parinirvana. Buddhism later developed into the Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions and spread beyond the Indian subcontinent. It declined in India and largely disappeared there after the 8th century CE, but became more prominent in Southeast and East Asia. Mahayana sutras present Shakyamuni as a transcendent being, and the Hindu tradition incorporated the Buddha as the ninth avatar of Vishnu.

The earliest artistic depictions, at Bharhut and Sanchi, are aniconic, showing an empty throne, footprints, a Dharma wheel or a Bodhi tree. Images in human form became widespread after the first century CE, and those of Gandharan and Central Asian Buddhism were influenced by Hellenistic art, a style known as Greco-Buddhist art.
gauteng: Gauteng lies on the Highveld, a high-altitude grassland at about 1,500 m above sea level. Its southern border is the Vaal River, which separates it from the Free State, and it also borders North West, Limpopo and Mpumalanga. It is the only landlocked South African province without a foreign border. Between Johannesburg and Pretoria lie low parallel ridges and undulating hills, part of the Magaliesberg Mountains and the Witwatersrand. The Witwatersrand area, also called the Rand or the Reef after its gold reefs, is a conurbation about 120 km wide, historically divided into the East Rand, Central Rand and West Rand. The name comes from the Sotho-Tswana word gauta, meaning gold.

At the Sterkfontein caves some of the oldest hominid fossils have been found, including Mrs Ples and Little Foot. Events in the area were not written down until the 19th century. The first records are from the early 19th century, when settlers from the Cape Colony defeated the chief Mzilikazi and began to establish villages. Pretoria, founded in 1855 as capital of the South African Republic, grew rapidly until the discovery of gold on the Witwatersrand in 1886 led to the founding of Johannesburg. Pretoria remained significant, notably in the Second Boer War. In 1905 the Cullinan Diamond, the largest diamond ever found, was mined at the nearby town of Cullinan.

Many events of the anti-apartheid struggle took place in what is now Gauteng: the Freedom Charter of 1955, the Women's March of 1956, the Sharpeville massacre of 1960, the Rivonia Trial of 1963 and 1964, the Soweto uprising of 1976 and the Boipatong massacre of 1992. The Apartheid Museum documents this era. The province was formed from part of the old Transvaal after South Africa's first multiracial elections on 27 April 1994, first as Pretoria–Witwatersrand–Vereeniging, and was renamed Gauteng on 28 June 1995.

Gauteng is the smallest of South Africa's nine provinces by land area and the most populous. Its capital, Johannesburg, is the country's largest city, and Pretoria is the administrative capital. Soweto is its largest township. The province is governed by a 73-member provincial legislature, and the Constitutional Court sits in Johannesburg. Its southern half is a financial and commercial centre and is home to the Johannesburg Stock Exchange. The Cradle of Humankind, which includes the Sterkfontein caves, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The first FIFA world cup match on African soil took place at Soccer City on 11 June 2010.
gavrilo-princip: Gavrilo Princip was born on 25 July 1894 in the hamlet of Obljaj, near Bosansko Grahovo, in western Bosnia, the second of nine children, six of whom died in infancy. His parents, Petar and Marija, were poor Serb farmers who gave a third of their income to a landlord. At thirteen he went to Sarajevo, where his brother Jovan paid for his schooling at the Merchants' School and then the Sarajevo Gymnasium.

Bosnia had been annexed by Austria-Hungary in 1908, and student groups there took up nationalist and anti-imperial ideas. In 1911 Princip joined Young Bosnia, a secret society with Serb, Croat and Muslim members that sought the liberation of Bosnia and the unification of the South Slavs. After taking part in a demonstration in February 1912 he was expelled from school and walked to Belgrade.

In 1914 Nedeljko Čabrinović showed Princip a newspaper cutting announcing Archduke Franz Ferdinand's visit to Sarajevo. Princip drew Čabrinović and Trifko Grabež into a plot. Milan Ciganović, an associate of the Serbian secret society known as the Black Hand, obtained five Browning pistols, six grenades and vials of poison for them and trained them in Belgrade. The three crossed into Bosnia, and Danilo Ilić recruited further conspirators in Sarajevo.

On 28 June 1914 the conspirators stood along the Appel Quay. Čabrinović threw a grenade that wounded occupants of another car, and the motorcade sped on. After the Archduke decided to visit the injured in hospital, his driver took a wrong turn into a side street where Princip stood. As the car stalled, Princip fired twice, killing Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July, and the conflict widened to the First World War.

Tried with twenty-four others in October 1914, Princip said he was a Yugoslav nationalist and that he regretted the death of the Duchess. He was too young to be executed, being twenty-seven days short of twenty, and received a sentence of twenty years. Held in the Small Fortress at Theresienstadt, he developed tuberculosis, which led to the amputation of his right arm, and he died on 28 April 1918. In 1920 he and the other conspirators were reburied in Sarajevo.

His memory remains contested. The Habsburg monarchy saw a terrorist, the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and socialist Yugoslavia a hero, and many Serbs still honour him, while many Bosniaks and Croats regard him as a terrorist.
gdansk: Gdańsk lies at the mouth of the Motława River on the southern edge of Gdańsk Bay. The low-lying Lower Terrace covers part of the Vistula Fens, while the Upper Terrace is an area of uneven highlands that belongs to the Kashubian Lake District. The name most likely comes from Gdania, the old name of the Motława. Its German form, Danzig, developed from forms such as Danzc and Danczk.

The first written mention is in a biography of Saint Adalbert, which records his visit in 997 to a town called Gyddanyzc, then ruled by Bolesław I the Brave of Poland. The city grew into a trading town and later joined the Hanseatic League. In 1308 the Teutonic Knights, called in to relieve the Polish garrison, seized the town and killed many of its inhabitants; estimates of the dead range from about 60 to about 1,000. In 1454 the Prussian Confederation rejected the authority of the Teutonic Order and appealed to King Casimir IV of Poland, which led to the Thirteen Years' War, and on 16 June 1454 the king granted Danzig extensive privileges.

With considerable autonomy it served as the Polish Crown's main seaport and largest city until the early 18th century. Prussia annexed it in 1793 in the Second Partition of Poland, and it joined the German Empire in 1871. It was a free city from 1807 to 1814 and again from 1920 to 1939. A military clash at Westerplatte on 1 September 1939 was one of the first events of the Second World War. After 1945 the German population fled or was expelled and Poles settled in their place. The Solidarity trade union began in the city in the 1980s.

Gdańsk is the capital of the Pomeranian Voivodeship and Poland's sixth-largest city, with a population of 486,492, and a major seaport. With Gdynia and Sopot it forms a metropolitan area called the Tricity. Parts of the old city destroyed in the war were rebuilt in the 1950s and 1960s. Its landmarks include the Town Hall, the Green Gate, Artus Court, Neptune's Fountain and St. Mary's Church, one of the largest brick churches in the world. St. Dominic's Fair, which dates back to 1260, is still held there.
gdynia: Gdynia is historically and culturally part of Kashubia and Eastern Pomerania. It lies in a conurbation with the spa town of Sopot and the city of Gdańsk, which together form the Tricity, a metropolitan area of around a million inhabitants. In prehistoric times the area was the centre of the Oksywie culture. In the late 10th century the region was united with the emerging state of Poland by Mieszko I, and the district of Oksywie was first mentioned in 1209, as Oxhöft. For centuries Gdynia remained a small fishing village, and by the 20th century it attracted visitors as a seaside resort.

The Polish government decided to build a major seaport at Gdynia in the winter of 1920, during the Polish–Soviet War. German dockworkers in the Free City of Danzig had struck and refused to unload military supplies sent from the West to aid the Polish army, and Poland concluded that it needed a port it controlled economically and politically. A special committee began building the city in 1925, city rights were granted in 1926 and tax privileges for investors in 1927. Growth became rapid after 1928, with a new railway station and post office, and by 1939 the population had grown to over 120,000.

Gdynia was the site of fierce Polish defence during the German invasion of September 1939. The Germans captured the whole city on 14 September and occupied it until 1945, carrying out mass arrests of some 7,000 Poles on 15 and 16 September. The occupiers set up prisons and camps, and Poles were deported to concentration camps or executed. The Red Army captured the city on 28 March 1945 and it was restored to Poland. Settlers arrived from destroyed Warsaw and from Wilno and Lwów, and Greek refugees from the Greek Civil War also came through the port. Protests in and around Gdynia in 1970 contributed to the rise of the Solidarity movement in Gdańsk.

Gdynia is a seaport on the Baltic coast of northern Poland, and the largest city in Poland that is not a voivodeship capital. Its modernist centre, laid out in 1926 by Adam Kuncewicz and Roman Feliński as a grand maritime façade for the newly independent state, is built around an axis that runs from 10 Lutego Street through Kościuszko Square to the Southern Pier. Its architecture shows monumentalism, early functionalism and interwar modernism. The oldest building is the 13th-century church of St Michael the Archangel in Oksywie, and two museum ships, the destroyer ORP Błyskawica and the sailing ship Dar Pomorza, are moored in the harbour. The port is the home of the 3rd Ship Flotilla of the Polish Navy.
gebhard-leberecht-von-blucher: Blücher was born on 16 December 1742 in Rostock, then in the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, the son of a retired army captain from an old landowning noble family. At sixteen he joined the Swedish Army as a hussar. Prussian hussars captured him in a skirmish in 1760, and the colonel of their regiment, Wilhelm Sebastian von Belling, a distant relative, had him join it.

In peacetime his ardent spirit led him into excesses, including the mock execution of a priest in 1772. Passed over for promotion, he sent a rude letter of resignation in 1773, and Frederick the Great replied, "Captain Blücher can take himself to the devil". He farmed until Frederick died in 1786, then returned as a major in 1787.

He received the Pour le Mérite in 1789 and became a major general in 1794 after his victory at Kirrweiler. As a cavalry general in 1806 he fought at Auerstedt, but he was defeated at Lübeck and surrendered at Ratekau on 7 November, insisting that the document record a lack of provisions and ammunition. In 1813, aged 71, he returned to high command.

As commander-in-chief of the Army of Silesia he defeated Marshal MacDonald at the Katzbach and Marshal Marmont at Möckern, and his army stormed Leipzig on the last day of the Battle of the Nations. He was made field marshal on 16 October 1813 and, with his chief staff officers, pressed the Coalition sovereigns to carry the war into France.

In 1814 he suffered defeats at Champaubert, Vauchamps and Montmirail, then won at Laon on 9 and 10 March, after which a breakdown cost him his sight for a time. The allies entered Paris, and Frederick William III made him Prince of Wahlstatt. When Napoleon returned in 1815 Blücher commanded the Army of the Lower Rhine. At Ligny on 16 June he lay trapped for hours under his dead horse and the Prussians retreated, but he led his army to join Wellington at Waterloo, where its arrival was decisive. The two armies entered Paris on 7 July.

Blücher retired to Krieblowitz in Silesia and died there on 12 September 1819, aged 76. Napoleon called him very brave but no talent as a general, and admired his readiness to rise again after a defeat. Later Prussian soldiers spoke of a Prussian way of war built on the quick, decisive battle. He was made an honorary citizen of Berlin, Hamburg and Rostock, and statues were raised at Berlin, Breslau, Rostock and Kaub, where his troops crossed the Rhine.
geez: Geʽez, sometimes called Classical Ethiopic in scholarly writing, is an ancient South Semitic language from what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea. Most linguists believe that it is not the common ancestor of the modern Ethio-Semitic languages but separated early from another unattested common language. Inscriptions in Sabaic have been found in the kingdom of Dʿmt from the middle of the first millennium BCE, and Semitic languages have been present in Eritrea since about 2000 BCE. Geʽez is not regarded as an offshoot of Sabaic. The earliest Geʽez inscriptions, from the Kingdom of Aksum, date to as early as the 4th century, and the oldest known example of the script is on the Hawulti obelisk in Matara, Eritrea. It is unvocalised and contains pagan references.

Geʽez is written with the Ethiopic script, an abugida first developed for this language and called fidäl in languages such as Amharic and Tigrinya that use it. It is read from left to right. The script has been adapted for other languages, chiefly Amharic and Tigrinya, and Tigre in Eritrea. The language distinguishes two genders and two numbers, and nouns have an unmarked nominative and an accusative marked with final -a. The normal word order of a declarative sentence has the verb first. Because it is no longer spoken in daily life by large communities, the early pronunciation of some consonants is uncertain.

Surviving Geʽez literature properly begins in the 4th century with the Christianization of Aksum, during the reign of Ezana. Almost all texts from the early Aksumite period are Christian and translated from Greek, producing an Ethiopic Bible of 81 books. The Book of Enoch survives complete in no other language. The oldest surviving Geʽez manuscript is thought to be the second of the Garima Gospels, dating to the 5th or 6th century. After the decline of Aksum, Geʽez was no longer a living language, replaced by Amharic in the south and by Tigrinya and Tigre in the north. It remained the official written language until the 19th century, in a position compared to that of Medieval Latin in Europe.

In the 14th century the Kebra Nagast, retelling the story of the Queen of Sheba, King Solomon and their son Menelik I, was written, and the first royal chronicles date to the reign of Amda Seyon I. Literature flourished especially under Emperor Zara Yaqob, who himself wrote the Book of Light and the Book of the Nativity. The Fetha Negest, the Laws of the Kings, was translated into Geʽez around 1450 and served as supreme law until a modern constitution replaced it in 1931. Geʽez remains the liturgical language of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Churches and of the Beta Israel.
generalitat-de-catalunya: The Generalitat has its roots in the General Court of Catalonia, which under James I the Conqueror came to be convoked by the king as representatives of the estates. Under Peter the Great the Courts gained institutional status when the king obliged himself to hold a General Court each year. It sat in three branches, the clergy, the nobility and the towns under direct royal rule, and the union of the three was called Lo General de Cathalunya. The Courts passed the Constitutions of Catalonia, the first being those of 1283. Behind them lay the eleventh-century Peace and Truce of God, a Church movement against feudal violence whose first Catalan assembly met at Toluges in 1027.

The Diputació del General de Catalunya was a permanent council of deputies set up by the Courts in 1359 to collect a new tax of the General, a tribute for the king. It gained considerable political power over the following centuries and took on tasks such as that of prosecutor. In the early 18th century, after the Catalan defeat in the War of the Spanish Succession, the Nueva Planta Decrees abolished it with the Principality's other institutions.

It was restored in 1931, when Francesc Macià declared a Catalan Republic and then agreed with Spanish ministers that it be renamed the Generalitat of Catalonia, the self-government of Catalonia within the Spanish Republic. A statute of autonomy of 1932 gave it a parliament, a presidency and an executive council. Macià presided until 1933 and Lluís Companys from 1933 to 1940. Abolished when the Civil War ended, it continued in exile; Companys was executed on 15 October 1940, and Josep Tarradellas, president in exile, returned in 1977 and was recognised by the Spanish government.

The Generalitat is the whole system of Catalan self-government: the Parliament, the President and the Executive Council. The Parliament is unicameral, with 135 members elected for four years. The Generalitat holds wide powers over culture, environment, communications, transport, commerce and public safety, and shares jurisdiction with Spain over education, health and justice. Catalonia has its own police force, the Mossos d'Esquadra. Its seat is the Palau de la Generalitat in Barcelona, and its powers rest on the Statute of Autonomy of 2006.
geneva: Geneva lies at the south-western end of Lake Geneva, at 46°12' North, 6°09' East, where the Rhône flows out of the lake. Three mountain chains belonging to the Jura surround it: the Jura main range to the north-west, the Vuache to the south and the Salève to the south-east. The city covers 15.93 square kilometres, and about 91.8 per cent of that land is built up.

The Canton of Geneva covers 282 square kilometres and has a border of only 4.5 kilometres with the rest of Switzerland. Of its 107.5 kilometres of border, 103 are shared with France. The name appears in Latin texts, in Caesar's spelling Genava, and probably comes from a Celtic stem meaning mouth, in the sense of an estuary.

Geneva was an Allobrogian border town, fortified against the Helvetii tribe, when the Roman Republic took it in 121 BCE. It became Christian under the Late Roman Empire. It was connected to the Bishopric of Vienne in the 4th century and acquired its own first bishop in the 5th century.

The medieval county of Geneva was known in Middle Latin as the pagus major Genevensis. After 1400 it became the Genevois province of Savoy, although the province did not extend to the city itself until the reformation of the seat of the Bishop of Geneva. A local holiday, the Jeûne genevois, falls on the first Thursday after the first Sunday in September and by tradition commemorates the day news of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre of Huguenots reached the city.

Geneva is the second most populous city in Switzerland and the most populous in French-speaking Romandy. It is the capital of the Republic and Canton of Geneva. Its municipal population was 203,856 in January 2021.

The city is the European headquarters of the United Nations, in the Palace of Nations, up the hill from the headquarters of the former League of Nations. It also hosts the World Health Organization, the International Labour Organization, the International Committee of the Red Cross and CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research. The whole old city is part of the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and 82 buildings or sites are listed of national significance, among them the Cathédrale St-Pierre.
genghis-khan: Temüjin was born between 1155 and 1167, and historians favour different dates: 1155, 1162 or 1167, with 1162 accepted by most. He was the eldest child of Yesügei, a chieftain of the Borjigin clan, and Hö'elün. When he was eight his father died and his family was abandoned by its tribe. He married Börte around 1178, and when Merkit raiders kidnapped her he recovered her with armies lent by Toghrul, khan of the Kerait, and his childhood sworn brother Jamukha.

Later his relationship with Jamukha deteriorated into open warfare, and he was badly defeated around 1187. After he reappeared in 1196 he swiftly gained power, overpowered Toghrul after a surprise attack in 1203, defeated the Naiman tribe and executed Jamukha, becoming sole ruler of the Mongolian steppe.

In 1206, at a kurultai, or assembly, at the source of the Onon River, Temüjin adopted the title Genghis Khan, whose meaning is much debated. He set out to suppress tribal loyalties in favour of unconditional loyalty to the khan and the ruling family, raising his own family, the Golden Family, to the highest tier of the Mongol hierarchy.

He led a raid against the Western Xia in 1209 and fought the Jin dynasty for four years until the capture of its capital, Zhongdu, in 1215. His general Jebe annexed Qara Khitai in 1218. In 1219 Genghis invaded the Khwarazmian Empire after his envoys were executed; the campaign toppled the state and devastated Transoxiana and Khorasan, while Jebe and Subutai led an expedition that reached Georgia and Kievan Rus'. The Mongol army under him killed millions of people, yet his conquests also facilitated commercial and cultural exchange over a vast area.

Genghis fell from his horse while hunting in the winter of 1226 to 1227 and grew ill during the siege of Zhongxing, the Western Xia capital. He died on 18 or 25 August 1227, and Zhongxing fell the following month, its population treated with extreme savagery. He was buried on or near Burkhan Khaldun in the Khentii Mountains, a site he had chosen years before.

His son Ögedei acceded in 1229. The division of the empire into appanages, meant to ensure stability, had the opposite effect, and in the late 1200s it split into the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate and the Yuan dynasty. He is remembered as a savage tyrant in Russia and the Arab world, while modern Mongolians recognise him as the founding father of their nation.
genocide-convention: The Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide was conceived largely in response to the Second World War and atrocities such as the Holocaust, which lacked an adequate legal description. The Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin coined the term genocide in 1944 to describe Nazi policies in occupied Europe and the Armenian genocide, and he campaigned for its recognition as a crime under international law. He also linked colonialism with genocide. In a resolution of 1946 the United Nations General Assembly recognized genocide as an international crime and called for a binding treaty. The Convention was the first human rights treaty adopted unanimously by the General Assembly, on 9 December 1948, and it entered into force on 12 January 1951.

Article 2 defines genocide as any of five acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such: killing members of the group, causing them serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction, imposing measures intended to prevent births, and forcibly transferring children to another group. Article 3 also punishes conspiracy, direct and public incitement, attempt and complicity. Perpetrators are to be tried whether they are private individuals, public officials or political leaders.

Political groups were first included in the draft and then removed in a diplomatic compromise, since several states argued that such groups are voluntary and that inclusion could invite outside interference. Early drafts also contained acts of cultural genocide, which former colonial powers and some settler countries opposed. In 2007 the International Court of Justice read the words in whole or in part to mean at least a substantial part of the group.

The definition has been adopted by international and hybrid tribunals, including the International Criminal Court, and incorporated into the law of several countries. Its provisions are widely considered customary law, binding on states whether or not they are parties. Most states are parties. The United States, whose delegates helped draft it, ratified only in 1988, with reservations, after Senator William Proxmire spoke for the treaty in the Senate every day it sat between 1967 and 1986.

One early petition, We Charge Genocide, presented to the United Nations in December 1951 by William Patterson, Paul Robeson and W. E. B. Du Bois, accused the United States of genocide against Black Americans and was rejected. In Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro the International Court of Justice ruled on 26 February 2007 that Serbia had failed to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica in 1995.
geoffrey-chaucer: Geoffrey Chaucer was born in London, most likely in the early 1340s; his monument gives 1343, but the precise date and place are unknown. His father, John Chaucer, rose to be an important wine merchant with a royal appointment, and earlier generations of the family had been vintners and merchants in Ipswich. The surname derives from the French chaucier, a maker of shoes, boots or leggings. In 1357 the first of the Chaucer Life Records shows him as a page in the household of Elizabeth de Burgh, Countess of Ulster, whose husband Lionel of Antwerp was a son of Edward III; the post brought him into the court circle in which he stayed for the rest of his life.

Chaucer was a public servant whose official life is very well documented, with nearly 500 written items. He worked as a courtier, a diplomat and a civil servant, sat in the Parliament of England as shire knight for Kent, and was Clerk of the King's Works from 1389 to 1391. He was a close friend of John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, and served under his patronage; in 1366 he married Philippa de Roet, and when Lancaster married her sister Katherine Swynford in 1396 the two men became brothers-in-law.

His first major work was The Book of the Duchess, an elegy for Blanche of Lancaster, who died in 1368. He wrote many of his major works while he was customs comptroller for London, from 1374 to 1386, among them the Parlement of Foules, The Legend of Good Women and Troilus and Criseyde, and he is believed to have begun The Canterbury Tales in the 1380s. He also translated Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy and wrote A Treatise on the Astrolabe for his ten-year-old son Lewis.

Chaucer died on 25 October 1400 and was the first writer buried in what has since become Poets' Corner in Westminster Abbey. He invented the rhyme royal and was one of the first English poets to use the five-stress line. His contemporary Thomas Hoccleve called him the first finder of our fair language, and almost two thousand English words are first attested in his manuscripts. Eighty-three manuscripts of The Canterbury Tales survive, in whole or part, and William Caxton, the first English printer, published two folio editions of it, in 1478 and 1483.
geoffrey-of-monmouth: Geoffrey was born between about 1090 and 1100, in Wales or the Welsh Marches. He called himself Galfridus Monemutensis, which points to a significant connection with Monmouth, and his contemporaries knew him as Galfridus Arturus. Earlier scholars assumed that he spoke Welsh, but his knowledge of the language appears to have been slight, and there is no evidence that he was of Welsh descent. He may have belonged to the French-speaking elite of the border country, and some suggest that his parents were among the Bretons who took part in the Norman Conquest, since Monmouth had been in the hands of Breton lords since 1075 or 1086. His ethnicity remains debated.

Geoffrey had reached the age of majority by 1129, when he is recorded as witnessing a charter. Most of his adult life appears to have been spent outside Wales. Between 1129 and 1151 his name appears on six charters in the Oxford area, sometimes with the title magister, teacher, and he was probably a secular canon of St George's college. On 24 February 1152 Archbishop Theobald of Bec consecrated him Bishop of St Asaph at Lambeth, having ordained him a priest at Westminster ten days earlier. There is no evidence that he ever visited his see. He appears to have died between 25 December 1154 and 24 December 1155, when his successor took office.

His major work, the Historia Regum Britanniae, or History of the Kings of Britain, relates the purported history of Britain from its settlement by Brutus of Troy to the death of Cadwaladr in the 7th century, taking in Julius Caesar's invasions, the kings Leir and Cymbeline and one of the earliest developed narratives of King Arthur. In his dedication he claims to have translated an ancient book in the British language given to him by Walter, Archdeacon of Oxford, but modern historians dismiss the claim. He drew on the Historia Britonum, Bede and Gildas, with oral tradition and his own imagination.

Some contemporaries doubted the History, and William of Newburgh wrote around 1190 that everything in it about Arthur and his successors had been made up. It was nevertheless widely copied, with 186 manuscripts listed in 1929, and was adapted by Wace, Layamon and in the Middle Welsh Brut y Brenhinedd. Robert of Torigny and Henry of Huntingdon used it as history. Geoffrey also wrote the Prophecies of Merlin, before 1135, and the poem Life of Merlin.
georg-buchner: Georg Büchner was born on 17 October 1813 at Goddelau, now part of Riedstadt, in the Grand Duchy of Hesse, the son of a physician. He attended the humanistic gymnasium in Darmstadt, and in 1828 he became interested in politics and joined a circle of Shakespeare enthusiasts. This circle probably later became the Giessen and Darmstadt section of the Society for Human Rights. At 18 he began to study medicine at Strasbourg, where he immersed himself in French literature and political thought and was influenced by the utopian communist theories of François-Noël Babeuf and Claude Henri de Saint-Simon. In 1833 he moved to Giessen and continued his studies at the university there.

At Giessen Büchner established a secret society devoted to the revolutionary cause. In July 1834, with the help of the theologian Friedrich Ludwig Weidig, he published the leaflet Der Hessische Landbote, a revolutionary pamphlet criticising social injustice in Hesse. It has been called the most revolutionary manifesto of the nineteenth century before The Communist Manifesto. The authorities charged the authors with treason. Weidig was arrested, tortured and later died in prison in Darmstadt, while Büchner fled to Strasbourg, where he wrote most of his literary work.

His first play, Dantons Tod, about the French Revolution, was published in 1835, and the novella Lenz, based on the life of the Sturm und Drang poet Jakob Michael Reinhold Lenz, appeared in part in a journal that was quickly banned. His comedy Leonce and Lena of 1836 satirised the nobility. His unfinished and best-known play, Woyzeck, exists only in fragments and was published after his death. He also translated two plays by Victor Hugo.

Büchner's medical dissertation on the nervous system of the barbel was published in 1836. In October 1836, after receiving his doctorate and an appointment as lecturer in anatomy at the University of Zürich, he moved there. He spent his last months writing and teaching until he died of typhus on 19 February 1837, aged 23. By the 1870s he was nearly forgotten in Germany, until Karl Emil Franzos edited his works, which then influenced the naturalist and expressionist movements. Arnold Zweig described Lenz as the beginning of modern European prose. Alban Berg's opera Wozzeck premiered in 1925, and the Georg Büchner Prize was created in 1923.
georg-philipp-telemann: Georg Philipp Telemann was born in Magdeburg and was almost completely self-taught in music. His father, a deacon, died when he was four. He had his first lessons at ten, and although his mother and relatives forbade musical activity, he studied and composed in secret, even writing an opera at the age of 12. At the Gymnasium Andreanum in Hildesheim he taught himself flute, oboe, violin, viola da gamba, recorder and double bass. In 1701 he went to Leipzig to study law but became a professional musician, writing for the Nikolaikirche and the Thomaskirche. In 1702 he became director of the municipal opera house, and he supplied a wealth of music for Leipzig, including his first major opera, Germanicus.

Telemann left Leipzig in 1705 to be Kapellmeister at the court of Count Erdmann II of Promnitz at Sorau, but the Great Northern War cut his time there short. He then entered the service of Duke Johann Wilhelm at Eisenach, where Johann Sebastian Bach had been born, and rose from Konzertmeister to Kapellmeister. In 1712 he moved to Frankfurt as city music director, where he gained his mature personal style and published his first works, including the Frankfurt Sonatas of 1715 and the Brockes Passion of 1716. In 1721 he took the post in Hamburg of Kantor of the Johanneum Lateinschule and Kapellmeister of the five largest churches.

The next year, when Johann Kuhnau died, Telemann was approved as his successor at Leipzig but declined after Hamburg gave him a raise, and the post went to Bach. He travelled to Paris in 1737 and stayed eight months, and after hearing Rameau's Castor et Pollux he added French operatic style to his vocal works. He was married twice. His first wife died soon after the birth of their daughter, and his second wife, Maria Catharina Textor, bore nine children but later accumulated large gambling debts. He died on 25 June 1767, aged 86.

Telemann composed more than 3,000 works, half of them lost, including 1,043 sacred cantatas and 600 overture-suites between 1708 and 1750. He combined German, French, Italian and Polish styles in what is called the German mixed style. His contemporaries rated him highly, and Bach and Handel bought and studied his published works. By pursuing exclusive publication rights, he set an early precedent for treating music as the intellectual property of the composer. In the early 19th century his reputation fell, and critics called him a Vielschreiber, someone for whom quantity came before quality. The last performance of a substantial work, Der Tod Jesu, took place in 1832. Interest revived in the 20th century and led to the Bärenreiter critical edition of the 1950s.
georg-wilhelm-friedrich-hegel: Hegel was born on 27 August 1770 in Stuttgart, capital of the Duchy of Württemberg. His father, Georg Ludwig Hegel, was secretary to the revenue office at the court of Karl Eugen, Duke of Württemberg. His mother died of bilious fever when he was thirteen; he and his father also caught the disease but narrowly survived. At Stuttgart's Eberhard-Ludwigs-Gymnasium, which he entered in 1776, he read voraciously. His first biographer, Karl Rosenkranz, wrote that the school belonged entirely to the Enlightenment in principle and entirely to classical antiquity in curriculum. Entering the Tübingen seminary in 1788, he was more devoted to the classics than to anything modern, and the Greeks, especially Plato, came first.

In 1801 Hegel came to Jena at the encouragement of Schelling and became a Privatdozent after submitting the dissertation De Orbitis Planetarum. In 1802 he and Schelling founded the Critical Journal of Philosophy, a collaboration that ended when Schelling left for Würzburg in 1803. In 1805 he was promoted to an unsalaried extraordinary professorship. With his finances failing, he was finishing the Phenomenology of Spirit as Napoleon engaged Prussian troops in the Battle of Jena on 14 October 1806. The book appeared in 1807 and was poorly understood even by his contemporaries.

His academic career culminated in the chair of philosophy at the University of Berlin, where he remained a prominent figure until his death on 14 November 1831. From 1818 he lectured there on the philosophy of art as an autonomous subject.

His system has three parts: the science of logic, the philosophy of nature and the philosophy of spirit, a structure drawn from Proclus's triad of remaining, procession and return and from the Christian Trinity. Geist, usually rendered spirit, denotes the human mind and its products, and Hegel held that the essence of spirit is freedom. His method, often called dialectical, he usually called speculative. The scheme of thesis, antithesis and synthesis comes from Fichte; Walter Kaufmann notes that Hegel never used the three terms together.

History was central to his philosophy: a culture is more advanced the more it is permeated by awareness of freedom. After his death his followers split into Right and Left Hegelians. The Left, including Ludwig Feuerbach and Karl Marx, adapted his method for materialist critiques of religion and society.
george-armstrong-custer: George Armstrong Custer was born in New Rumley, Ohio, on 5 December 1839, the son of Emanuel Henry Custer, a farmer and blacksmith, and Marie Ward Kirkpatrick. According to family letters he was named after a minister, George Armstrong, in his devout mother's hope that he might join the clergy. He graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point, last in his class. On 9 February 1864 he married Elizabeth Clift Bacon, known as Libbie, whose father had at first disapproved of a blacksmith's son.

Commissioned a second lieutenant, Custer served at the First Battle of Bull Run on 21 July 1861. In June 1863 the cavalry commander Alfred Pleasonton, looking for aggressive officers, promoted him to brigadier general of volunteers at the age of 23, commanding the Michigan Cavalry Brigade. He fought at Gettysburg, where his brigade defeated J. E. B. Stuart's attack at East Cavalry Field. In 1864 he served under Philip Sheridan in the Overland Campaign and in the Shenandoah Valley, defeating Jubal Early at Cedar Creek, and in April 1865 his division blocked Robert E. Lee's retreat and received the first Confederate flag of truce.

After the war he commanded cavalry in Texas, and in July 1866 he became lieutenant colonel of the newly created 7th Cavalry Regiment at Fort Riley, Kansas. By the time of his Black Hills Expedition of 1874, tension between the United States and the Lakota and Cheyenne was very high. The United States wanted to take possession of the Black Hills and its gold deposits, and in 1875 the Grant administration tried to buy the region. When the Sioux refused, they were ordered to report to reservations by 31 January 1876, a deadline that winter conditions made impossible to meet.

In the spring of 1876 Custer was to command one of three columns, marching west from Fort Abraham Lincoln. On 25 June 1876, at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in the Montana Territory, he was killed together with every soldier of the five companies he led. The Cheyenne warriors did not know Custer was in the fight until weeks later. The assignment of blame continues: Major Marcus Reno's flight to the timber and Captain Frederick Benteen's late arrival have both been cited.

His widow Libbie published several books about him and did much to build what is called the Custer myth, which the secrecy of the 1879 Court of Inquiry record, released only in 1951, also supported. The reaction to his life remains divided.
george-c-marshall: George Catlett Marshall Jr. was born in Uniontown, Pennsylvania, the youngest of three children of George Catlett Marshall, who was active in the coal and coke business, and Laura Emily Bradford Marshall. He graduated from the Virginia Military Institute in 1901 and was commissioned a second lieutenant of Infantry in February 1902. Within days he married, and he sailed to the Philippines to serve during the Philippine–American War.

After the United States entered the First World War in 1917 Marshall served on the staff of the 1st Division in France and later became a key planner of American operations, including the Meuse-Argonne Offensive. From 1919 he was an aide to General John J. Pershing, and in 1927 he became assistant commandant of the Infantry School at Fort Benning, where he modernised command and staff processes.

As Chief of Staff of the Army from 1939 he organised the largest military expansion in American history, from a Regular Army of 189,000 men to more than eight million soldiers by 1942. Rapid training left some units unprepared, and the army suffered early reverses against German armoured units in Africa. At the Arcadia Conference he persuaded the British to accept a strategy of defeating Germany first.

In December 1945 President Truman sent him to China to broker a coalition between Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists and Mao Zedong's Communists. Both sides rejected his proposals, and the Communists won the war in 1949. As Secretary of State from 1947 to 1949 he lent his prestige to the plan to rebuild Europe, the Marshall Plan. In September 1950 Truman named him Secretary of Defense, which required a congressional waiver, to restore morale during the Korean War.

Marshall retired in September 1951 to Dodona Manor in Leesburg, Virginia, and chaired the American Battle Monuments Commission. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953. He died at Walter Reed Hospital on 16 October 1959 and was buried at Arlington National Cemetery. Historians describe him as the best-known and most selfless American leader of the early Cold War, noting also his defeats: the failed mission to China, the rejection of his proposal for universal military service, and his unsuccessful opposition to recognising Israel.
george-eliot: Mary Ann Evans was born on 22 November 1819 at South Farm on the Arbury Hall estate near Nuneaton, Warwickshire, the third child of Robert Evans, the estate's manager. Her father invested in an education not often afforded to women. After sixteen she educated herself, with access to the library of Arbury Hall. When she was twenty-one she and her father moved to Foleshill near Coventry, where she became friends with the free-thinking Charles and Cara Bray. Their circle introduced her to liberal and agnostic theology, and she translated David Strauss's The Life of Jesus, Critically Examined, published in 1846. She also translated Ludwig Feuerbach's The Essence of Christianity in 1854.

After her father died in 1849 she moved to London in 1850 and began to call herself Marian Evans. She became assistant editor of the radical journal The Westminster Review in 1851 under John Chapman. She met the philosopher and critic George Henry Lewes in 1851. He was married to Agnes Jervis, but by 1854 he and Evans had decided to live together, and she called him her husband. The refusal to conceal the relationship attracted considerable disapproval.

Resolving to become a novelist, she took the pen name George Eliot, George being Lewes's forename. The first of the Scenes of Clerical Life appeared in Blackwood's Magazine in 1857. Adam Bede (1859) was an instant success, and The Mill on the Floss (1860) and Silas Marner (1861) followed, then Romola, Felix Holt, the Radical (1866), Middlemarch (1871–1872) and Daniel Deronda (1876).

Lewes died on 30 November 1878. On 16 May 1880 Eliot married John Walter Cross, twenty years her junior. She fell ill with a throat infection, which together with kidney disease led to her death on 22 December 1880, aged sixty-one. Because she denied the Christian faith and had lived with Lewes, she was not buried in Westminster Abbey but in Highgate Cemetery, beside Lewes. Middlemarch, set on the eve of the Reform Bill of 1832, is notable for its psychological insight, and Virginia Woolf described it as one of the few English novels written for grown-up people.
george-frideric-handel: Handel was born in 1685 in Halle, in the Duchy of Magdeburg, then part of Brandenburg-Prussia, in the same year as Johann Sebastian Bach and Domenico Scarlatti. His father, Georg Händel, was an eminent barber-surgeon who served the court of Saxe-Weissenfels. Almost everything known of his childhood comes from his first biographer, John Mainwaring, who often relates misinformation, including the portrait of the father as implacably opposed to a musical education.

Between the ages of seven and nine Handel went with his father to Weissenfels, where Duke Johann Adolf I heard him play the court organ and recommended that he be taught. His only teacher was Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow, organist of the Halle parish church. His father died on 11 February 1697, and in 1702 Handel matriculated at the University of Halle. By July 1703 he was in Hamburg, and he then went to Italy.

In June 1710 Handel became Kapellmeister to George, the Elector of Hanover, but left at the end of the year for London, where his opera Rinaldo was a great success. He settled there in 1712. In 1717 he became house composer at Cannons in Middlesex, where he wrote the Chandos Anthems and Acis and Galatea. From 1719 he engaged singers for the Royal Academy of Music, founded by aristocrats to secure a steady supply of Italian opera. By 1723 he lived at 25 Brook Street, now the Handel House Museum.

He started three commercial opera companies, the third at Covent Garden in 1734. In 1737 he suffered a physical breakdown and turned towards English choral works, and after the success of Messiah in 1742 he never composed an Italian opera again. In 1749 he wrote Music for the Royal Fireworks, whose first performance drew 12,000 people, and in 1750 he arranged a performance of Messiah for the Foundling Hospital. He died on 14 April 1759, aged 74, and was given a state funeral at Westminster Abbey.

Handel's compositions include 42 operas, 24 oratorios, more than 120 cantatas, 18 concerti grossi and 12 organ concertos. His first oratorio, an allegory, was composed in Italy in 1707. One of his four coronation anthems, Zadok the Priest, has been performed at every British coronation since 1727. His music was admired by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven.
george-i-of-great-britain: George was born on 28 May 1660 in Hanover, the eldest son of Ernest Augustus, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and Sophia of the Palatinate, a granddaughter of King James VI and I. His inheritance was at first uncertain because his uncles might have sons of their own, and at fifteen he was taken on campaign in the Franco-Dutch War to be tested and trained. In 1682 he married his cousin Sophia Dorothea of Celle, which brought extra income and helped the eventual unification of Hanover and Celle. They divorced in 1694.

Ernest Augustus died on 23 January 1698, leaving George his territories except the Prince-Bishopric of Osnabrück. His court at Hanover included the philosopher Gottfried Leibniz and the composer George Frideric Händel. The Act of Settlement of 1701 named his mother Sophia heir to the English throne as the closest Protestant relative of the royal family, bypassing fifty-six Catholics with stronger claims, and the Treaty of Union of 1707 confirmed this for Great Britain. George inherited the throne on 1 August 1714, after the deaths of Sophia and Queen Anne.

The Whigs won the election of 1715 by a wide margin. The Jacobites, who wanted Anne's Catholic half-brother James Francis Edward Stuart on the throne, rose that year under John Erskine, Earl of Mar, but the rebellion collapsed and James fled to France in February 1716. George moderated the government's response and spent the income from forfeited estates on schools for Scotland. The Septennial Act of 1715 extended Parliaments to seven years, and the Tories did not return to power for half a century.

George spoke little English, took little interest in daily affairs and rarely attended cabinet. In Hanover he ruled as an absolute monarch within the laws of the Empire, but in Britain he governed through Parliament, and Robert Walpole, who grew powerful, is regarded as Britain's first de facto prime minister. The South Sea Bubble of 1720 ruined many investors, the king among them.

George suffered a stroke on 9 June 1727 on his sixth journey to Hanover as king and died on 11 June at the palace of his brother Ernest Augustus, Prince-Bishop of Osnabrück. He was buried in Hanover, and is the most recent British monarch buried outside Britain. His accession secured the Protestant succession, though he was widely disliked as a foreigner.
george-i-of-greece: He was born Prince William of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg-Glücksburg on 24 December 1845 at the Yellow Palace in Copenhagen, the second son of Prince Christian and Princess Louise of Hesse-Kassel. The family was relatively obscure until 1852, when his father was designated heir to the childless Frederick VII of Denmark. William entered the Royal Danish Navy as a cadet.

After the expulsion of Otto in October 1862 the Greeks held a plebiscite in which Prince Alfred, Duke of Edinburgh, a son of Queen Victoria, received over 95 per cent of the 240,000 votes; William received six. The ruling families of the great powers were barred from the Greek crown, and the choice fell on the Danish prince. The Greek National Assembly elected him unanimously on 30 March 1863.

George reached Athens on 30 October 1863, learned Greek quickly and was often seen informally in the streets. He sent home Danish advisers who had become unpopular, and in October 1864 pressed the Assembly to finish its work; on 28 November he swore to a constitution that created a single chamber, the Vouli, elected by direct, secret, universal male suffrage. Governments were short-lived: 21 between 1864 and 1874. After Charilaos Trikoupis blamed the king in a newspaper article for imposing minority governments, George declared in 1875 that the leader of the parliamentary majority would in future be appointed prime minister.

Trikoupis and Theodoros Deligiannis alternated in office between 1882 and 1897. In 1896 the king presided over the opening of the revived Olympic Games in Athens. A revolt in Crete led in 1897 to a war with the Ottoman Empire that was lost by the end of April; Greece paid an indemnity of 4 million Turkish pounds and Crete passed to international administration. George considered abdication, but regained esteem after he and his daughter Maria survived an attack by two riflemen on 27 February 1898.

In August 1909 a league of army officers demanded that the royal family lose their military commissions and attempted a coup. George gave way to calls for a revising assembly, and Eleftherios Venizelos became prime minister in 1910. King and minister agreed on rebuilding the army, which entered Thessaloniki on 9 November 1912 under Crown Prince Constantine. On 18 March 1913, walking near the White Tower without meaningful protection, George was shot in the back by Alexandros Schinas and died at once. Schinas fell to his death from a police station window six weeks later. The dynasty he founded reigned, with breaks, until the monarchy was abolished in 1973.
george-ii-of-great-britain: George Augustus was born in the city of Hanover. His parents, George Louis, later George I, and Sophia Dorothea of Celle, both committed adultery, and in 1694 the marriage was dissolved on the pretext that she had abandoned her husband. George spoke only French until the age of four, then learned German, English and Italian.

In June 1705 he visited the Ansbach court under the false name Monsieur de Busch to see Princess Caroline of Brandenburg-Ansbach, and was so taken by her good character that he would think of nobody else. They married on 2 September 1705 at Herrenhausen Palace and had eight children. When his father became King in 1714, George was made Prince of Wales; quarrelling with the King, he became associated with the opposition, and his residence at Leicester House was a meeting place for Sir Robert Walpole and Lord Townshend.

George I died on 22 June 1727 and George II succeeded him as king and elector. He did not go to Germany for the funeral, which the English took as proof of his fondness for England, and he suppressed his father's will, which tried to split the Hanoverian succession. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 22 October 1727. He exercised little control over domestic policy, which Parliament largely controlled, and he spent twelve summers in Hanover.

Britain reopened hostilities with Spain in 1739, in the War of Jenkins' Ear, which became part of the War of the Austrian Succession. George took part in the Battle of Dettingen and was the most recent British monarch to lead an army in battle. The Jacobite rising of 1745 failed to depose the King. His son Frederick, Prince of Wales, supported the opposition and died in 1751. In 1756 a French invasion of Minorca began the Seven Years' War.

On 25 October 1760 George rose at six, drank hot chocolate, and was found on the floor of his closet; he was dead before his daughter Amelia arrived. At nearly seventy-seven he had lived longer than any English or British predecessor, and his grandson George III succeeded him.

He donated the royal library to the British Museum in 1757, founded the University of Göttingen in 1737. The province of Georgia, chartered in 1732, was named after him. For two centuries historians tended to view him with disdain, concentrating on his mistresses, short temper and boorishness, but later scholars conclude that he exercised more influence in foreign policy and military appointments than was thought.
george-ii-of-greece: George was born on 19 July 1890 at the royal villa at Tatoi, near Athens, the eldest son of Crown Prince Constantine and Sophia of Prussia. He was a great-grandson of both King Christian IX of Denmark and Queen Victoria. He trained with the Prussian Guard at the age of 18 and served in the Balkan Wars. His grandfather George I was assassinated at Thessaloniki on 18 March 1913, and Constantine became king, making George crown prince at 23. He followed his father into exile in Switzerland in 1917, after the National Schism, and he was in Romania when his younger brother Alexander died in 1920. A rigged referendum restored Constantine that year, and he abdicated again in 1922.

George became king on 27 September 1922, but he was not warmly received. Greece was unstable after a coup, and many refugees were arriving from Asia Minor after the war. He and his wife Elisabeth, daughter of the Romanian king Ferdinand I, were confined to Tatoi and closely watched. After a failed royalist coup in October 1923 he went to Romania. The Second Hellenic Republic was proclaimed on 25 March 1924, and the royal family was banished and stripped of Greek citizenship.

In the next ten years Greece had twenty-three governments and thirteen coups. The monarchy was restored after a rigged referendum, and George returned in November 1935. On 4 August 1936 he endorsed the dictatorship of Ioannis Metaxas, signing decrees that dissolved parliament, banned political parties and abolished the constitution. He ruled jointly with Metaxas, kept full control of the army and was largely responsible for foreign policy, though he distrusted Metaxas's growing power.

Italy began a propaganda campaign against Greece in 1940, and when Hitler suggested George abdicate in return for a guarantee against an Italian attack, the king refused. Metaxas rejected an Italian ultimatum on 28 October 1940, and Greece repelled the invasion and occupied the southern half of Italian Albania. After the German invasion of April 1941 George left for Crete, then Egypt and London, where he headed the government in exile. A referendum on 1 September 1946 gave 68.4 per cent in favour of his return, although Allied observers acknowledged significant fraud. George died of arteriosclerosis on 1 April 1947, aged 56. He had no children, and his younger brother Paul succeeded him.
george-iii: George was born on 4 June 1738 at Norfolk House in St James's Square, London, two months prematurely and so weak that he was baptised the same day. He was the eldest son of Frederick, Prince of Wales, and Princess Augusta of Saxe-Gotha. After his father's death in 1751 he became Prince of Wales. He was the first monarch of the House of Hanover to be born in Great Britain, to speak English as his first language and never to visit Hanover. In his accession speech in 1760 he declared, "Born and educated in this country, I glory in the name of Britain." He married Princess Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, and they had 15 children.

The early years were politically unstable, chiefly because of disagreements over the Seven Years' War. The Peace of Paris in 1763 gave Britain Canada and the part of Louisiana east of the Mississippi. At home George insisted on the Royal Marriages Act 1772, after his brothers made marriages he disapproved of.

After the Boston Tea Party of 1773 opinion hardened in Britain, and fighting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775. The King and Parliament ignored the petitions of the Second Continental Congress, and George declared the American leaders traitors. Thomas Paine's Common Sense called him the Royal Brute of Great Britain. Britain later fought revolutionary and Napoleonic France from 1793, and the Acts of Union 1800 created the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. The slave trade was banned in the British Empire in 1807, although the King supported planters who sought to delay abolition.

George suffered from recurrent mental illness. Until the mid-20th century it was thought psychological; in 1966 Ida Macalpine and Richard Hunter proposed porphyria, a view that gained wide acceptance. Since 2010 it has been challenged, and recent scholarship holds that the illness was psychiatric, most probably bipolar disorder. In late 1810, nearly blind from cataracts, he relapsed. The Regency Act 1811 made the Prince of Wales regent, and George lived in seclusion at Windsor Castle until his death on 29 January 1820.

He had reigned for 59 years and 96 days, longer than any earlier king. Two of his sons, George IV and William IV, succeeded him in turn, and the throne then passed to Victoria, the only legitimate child of his fourth son.
george-iv-of-the-united-kingdom: George Augustus Frederick was born on 12 August 1762 at St James's Palace, the eldest child of King George III and Queen Charlotte. He was created Prince of Wales a few days after his birth. At eighteen he was given a separate establishment and threw himself into heavy drinking, mistresses and spending. On reaching twenty-one in 1783 he received a grant of £60,000 from Parliament and an annual income of £50,000 from his father, which was far too little for his wants. He quarrelled with his conservative father and allied himself with the Whig Charles James Fox.

When the King's mental health failed in 1788, Fox argued that the Prince was automatically entitled to rule, while William Pitt the Younger held that Parliament alone could choose a regent. In 1795, with his debts rising and his father refusing to help unless he married, he wed his cousin Princess Caroline of Brunswick. They separated after the birth of their only child, Princess Charlotte, in 1796.

After the King's final breakdown, the Prince became Prince Regent on 5 February 1811 under the Regency Act 1811. He left his ministers in full charge of government, and the principle that the prime minister is the person supported by a majority in the House of Commons became established. Lord Liverpool controlled the government for most of the regency and reign, presiding over victory over Napoleon and the peace settlement.

George became king on the death of George III in 1820, obese and possibly addicted to laudanum. He refused to recognise Caroline as queen and had her name omitted from the Book of Common Prayer. He asked for the Pains and Penalties Bill, which would have annulled the marriage, but it proved so unpopular that it was withdrawn. Caroline was excluded from the coronation at Westminster Abbey on 19 July 1821, which cost about £243,000, and she died on 7 August. After Liverpool's retirement, he was forced to accept Catholic emancipation, which he opposed.

His health declined in the late 1820s from gout and dropsy, and by December 1828 he was almost blind. He died on 26 June 1830. His only legitimate child, Charlotte, had died in 1817, and his brother Frederick in 1827, so the throne passed to another brother, William IV.

Called the first gentleman of England for his style and manners, he was widely held in contempt for his way of life, and the prestige of the monarchy dimmed. The Duke of Wellington described him in harsh terms, and in his eulogy as the most accomplished man of his age.
george-orwell: Eric Arthur Blair was born on 25 June 1903 in Motihari, Bengal Presidency, British India, into what he described as a lower-upper-middle-class family. His father, Richard Walmesley Blair, worked in the Opium Department of the Indian Civil Service, and his mother, Ida Mabel Blair, grew up in Moulmein, Burma. When he was one year old his mother took him and his sister Marjorie to England, and in 1904 she settled at Henley-on-Thames. Apart from a brief visit in mid-1907, he did not see his father until 1912.

He attended a convent school in Henley run by French Ursuline nuns, and then, through a scholarship, St Cyprian's School in Eastbourne from September 1911. He hated the school and later wrote the essay Such, Such Were the Joys about it, published after his death. He met Cyril Connolly there. He went on to win a scholarship to Eton. As a child he took a keen interest in natural history, in butterflies, birds and fishing, and his adult diaries are full of observations of nature.

Blair wrote under the pen name George Orwell. For most of his career he was best known for journalism, in essays, reviews, columns and books of reportage: Down and Out in Paris and London, The Road to Wigan Pier (1937), on the living conditions of the poor in northern England, and Homage to Catalonia (1938), on his experiences soldiering for the Republican side in the Spanish Civil War. He later called that war his watershed political experience, and said that everything he had written since 1936 was directed against totalitarianism and for democratic socialism.

Modern readers meet him more often as a novelist, through the allegorical novella Animal Farm (1945), often thought to reflect the degeneration of the Soviet Union and the rise of Stalinism, and Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), on life under totalitarian rule. Many of his coinages, such as Big Brother, Thought Police, Room 101, Newspeak and doublethink, entered the English language. He was an atheist who identified with the humanist outlook, yet he took part in the life of the Church of England. His works are widely studied in schools in England, and his political legacy is contested, with critics on both left and right claiming or attacking him.
george-seferis: Georgios Seferiadis, who wrote as Giorgos Seferis, was born on 13 March 1900 (28 February in the old style) in the Aidin Vilayet of the Ottoman Empire. His father, Stelios Seferiadis, was a lawyer and later a professor at the University of Athens, as well as a poet and translator, a Venizelist and a supporter of demotic Greek over the formal katharevousa. In 1914 the family moved to Athens, and from 1918 to 1925 Seferis studied law at the Sorbonne in Paris.

In September 1922, while he was in Paris, Smyrna was taken by the Turkish Army after a two-year Greek campaign in Anatolia, and many Greeks, including his family, fled. He did not visit Smyrna again until 1950. The sense of exile from his childhood home shaped much of his poetry, notably his interest in the story of Odysseus.

Seferis entered the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 1926 and held posts in the United Kingdom from 1931 to 1934 and Albania from 1936 to 1938. In the Second World War he accompanied the Greek government-in-exile to Crete, Egypt, South Africa and Italy and returned to liberated Athens in 1944. Later postings included Ankara, London, a ministry to Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and Iraq, and the embassy in London, his last post before retirement.

His collections began with Strophe in 1931 and Mythistorema in 1935, and Log Book III in 1955. He first visited Cyprus in November 1953 and was struck by its likeness to his childhood summer home at Skala. Log Book III, mostly written there, ended six or seven years without poems. In the dispute among the United Kingdom, Greece and Turkey over the island's status he worked through his diplomatic post for a settlement.

In 1963 Seferis received the Nobel Prize for Literature for his eminent lyrical writing, inspired by a deep feeling for the Hellenic world of culture. He was the first Greek to win it. His Hellenism lay in a unifying strand of humanism in the continuity of Greek literature rather than in nationalism.

After the Regime of the Colonels took power in 1967, he made a statement on the BBC World Service on 28 March 1969, declaring that this anomaly must end. He died in Athens on 20 September 1971, of pneumonia aggravated by a stroke, and did not see the junta fall. Crowds at his funeral sang Mikis Theodorakis's setting of his poem Denial, then banned.
george-town-penang: George Town is the capital of the Malaysian state of Penang. Its jurisdiction covers about 306 square kilometres, the whole of Penang Island and nine surrounding islets. The island is mountainous down the middle, and the city centre lies on the largest coastal plain, at the north-eastern cape. Before the British arrived the cape was known as Tanjung Penaga after the penaga laut trees that grew there, and the city was named for King George III.

In 1771 Francis Light, a former Royal Navy captain, was instructed by the East India Company to establish trade relations in the Malay Peninsula. The sultan of Kedah, a Siamese vassal state threatened by the Bugis of Selangor, offered Penang Island in exchange for British military protection. Light saw it as a convenient magazine for trade that could check Dutch and French ambitions, and he established George Town as an entrepôt in 1786, the first British settlement in Southeast Asia. As a free port and a conduit for the spice trade it grew rapidly and drew trade from Dutch posts. During the Napoleonic Wars the British enlarged Fort Cornwallis against the threat of French invasion.

George Town became capital of the Straits Settlements in 1826 and lost that status to Singapore in 1832. Immigrants came from across Asia, and by the 1891 census about 68 per cent of its 51,627 people were ethnic Chinese. The Penang High Court was established in 1808 and Penang Free School, the oldest English school in Southeast Asia, in 1816. The first newspaper in Malaysia, the Prince of Wales Island Gazette, appeared there in 1806. After the Second World War the British dissolved the Straits Settlements in 1946, and the Penang Secessionist Committee formed in 1948 to resist merger with Malaya, fearing for the free port. George Town was declared a city shortly before independence in 1957, the first in the country.

At the 2020 census the city had 794,313 inhabitants and the wider conurbation 2,843,344. Malay, English, Hokkien, Mandarin and Tamil are in common use, and Penang Hokkien is the unofficial lingua franca. In 2008 UNESCO designated nearly 260 hectares of the city centre a World Heritage Site for its unique architectural and cultural townscape. The city is known for its street food and for the Chingay procession introduced in 1919.
