george-v: George was born on 3 June 1865 at Marlborough House, London, the second son of Albert Edward, Prince of Wales, and Alexandra, a daughter of King Christian IX of Denmark. As a younger son he was not expected to become king. In 1877 he and his elder brother, Prince Albert Victor, joined the training ship HMS Britannia, and he served in the Royal Navy until 1892. Albert Victor's death in January 1892 made George second in line to the throne, and the next year he married his brother's former fiancée, Princess Victoria Mary of Teck. After his father became Edward VII in 1901, George was created Prince of Wales.

George became king on 6 May 1910. He insisted that his wife be called Queen Mary, and he objected to the anti-Catholic wording of the Accession Declaration, which Parliament shortened. The Parliament Act 1911 established the supremacy of the House of Commons.

He held a council on 4 August 1914 to declare war on Germany, whose Kaiser, Wilhelm II, was his first cousin. Because of anti-German feeling he changed the name of the royal house in 1917 from Saxe-Coburg and Gotha to Windsor. The monarchies of Russia, Austria-Hungary, Germany, Greece and Spain fell to war and revolution. On 22 June 1921, at the opening of the Parliament of Northern Ireland, he appealed for conciliation, and a truce followed within weeks. He appointed the first Labour ministry in 1924.

George was seriously injured in a fall from his horse in France in October 1915, and heavy smoking aggravated chronic bronchitis. After a serious illness in November 1928 he convalesced at Bognor, which later gained the suffix Regis. He took to his bedroom at Sandringham House on 15 January 1936 and died on 20 January; his eldest son succeeded him as Edward VIII.

He enjoyed stamp collecting and game shooting and lived a conventional life. The historian David Cannadine describes him and Queen Mary as an inseparably devoted couple who upheld character and family values. In a series of crises he acted as a force for neutrality and moderation, seeing his role as mediator rather than final decision maker.
george-washington: George Washington was born on 22 February 1732 (11 February 1731 in the old style calendar) at Popes Creek in Westmoreland County, Virginia, the first of six children of Augustine and Mary Ball Washington. When his father died in 1743 he inherited Ferry Farm and ten slaves, while his half-brother Lawrence inherited the estate renamed Mount Vernon. Without the formal schooling his half-brothers had in England, he learned mathematics and land surveying and became a talented draftsman and mapmaker.

Lawrence's service as adjutant general of the Virginia militia inspired him to seek a commission. His report was published in Virginia and London. On 6 January 1759 he married Martha Dandridge Custis, a wealthy widow, and became one of the wealthiest men in Virginia.

After the war began with Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775, the Second Continental Congress created the Continental Army on 14 June, and John Adams nominated Washington as its commander-in-chief. He led a poorly organised force against disciplined British troops. He won at Boston in March 1776 but was forced to retreat from New York City in November. He crossed the Delaware River and won at Trenton in late 1776 and Princeton in early 1777, then lost at Brandywine and Germantown. In 1781 he led a combined French and American force to a decisive victory at Yorktown, and the Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognised American independence.

He presided over the Constitutional Convention of 1787. Elected unanimously by the Electoral College in 1789 and 1792, he was inaugurated on 30 April 1789 at Federal Hall in New York City. President against grander styles proposed by the Senate. He stayed neutral in the rivalry between Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton in his cabinet, and adopted neutrality during the French Revolution while supporting the Jay Treaty with Britain.

Washington's farewell address of 1796 stressed national unity and the dangers of regionalism, partisanship and foreign influence. In 1798 President Adams made him commanding general of the army during the Quasi-War, though he did not take the field. He died on 14 December 1799, and Henry Lee III eulogised him as first in war, first in peace and first in the hearts of his countrymen.

At least 577 slaves lived and worked at Mount Vernon during his lifetime. From the 1760s he gradually grew to oppose slavery, partly because his shift from tobacco to grain left him with a costly surplus of slaves, and in a letter of 1778 he wrote of his desire to get quit of Negroes. His will provided for the eventual manumission of his slaves.
georges-clemenceau: Georges Benjamin Clemenceau was born on 28 September 1841 in Mouilleron-en-Pareds in the Vendée, a remote, rural and poor department. His father, Benjamin Clemenceau, came from a line of physicians but lived off his lands, was a political activist and was arrested in 1851 and 1858. He instilled in his son a love of learning, devotion to radical politics and a hatred of Catholicism. In Paris the young Clemenceau co-founded a weekly, Le Travail, in 1861 and was held for 77 days in Mazas Prison in 1862 after posting notices calling a demonstration. He qualified as a doctor of medicine on 13 May 1865, and in 1869 he married Mary Eliza Plummer in New York City.

After the defeat at Sedan in 1870 Clemenceau became mayor of the 18th arrondissement of Paris and was elected to the National Assembly. When the Paris Commune seized power in March 1871 he tried without success to find a compromise between its leaders and the government. From 1876 he sat in the Chamber of Deputies for the 18th arrondissement, and his energy and cutting eloquence made him leader of the radicals. After his defeat in 1893 he confined himself for nearly a decade to journalism. On 13 January 1898 he published Émile Zola's J'Accuse...! on the front page of L'Aurore, which he owned and edited, and during the Dreyfus Affair he published 665 articles defending Dreyfus.

In 1906 he became Minister of the Interior, reformed the police, supported scientific policing under Alphonse Bertillon and founded the mobile squads nicknamed the Tiger's Brigades. After the war began, his newspaper was censored and, renamed L'Homme enchaîné, criticised the government's lack of transparency while defending the union sacrée. In November 1917, at one of the darkest hours of the war, he became prime minister, governing from the Ministry of War and discouraging internal disagreement. His government passed a general eight-hour day law in April 1919, extended to all classes of workers by later measures.

At the Paris Peace Conference Clemenceau sought the Rhine as France's frontier and was under strong pressure to make Germany's reparations bill large. On 19 February 1919 the anarchist Émile Cottin fired on his car, and a bullet that stayed in his body for the rest of his life struck him between the ribs. The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919, and he defended it in the French Parliament against critics who thought its compromises inadequate. He resigned as prime minister after the presidential election of 17 January 1920 and took no further part in politics.
He was a long-time friend of Claude Monet and persuaded him to complete his donation of the Water Lilies paintings to the French state. He died on 24 November 1929.
georges-danton: Georges Jacques Danton was born on 26 October 1759 in Arcis-sur-Aube, in Champagne, to Jacques Danton, a respectable but not wealthy lawyer, and Madeleine Camus. At thirteen he entered the seminary in Troyes and then a boarding school nearby. He settled in Paris in 1780 as a clerk, passed the barrister examination at Reims in 1783, and in 1787 became a prosecutor. That year he married Antoinette Gabrielle Charpentier, and the couple lived on the Left Bank near the Café Procope.

In the spring of 1789 Danton spoke to crowds at the Palais Royal, and his powerful voice earned him the nickname The Thunderer. He led the militia of the Cordeliers district and in 1790 became president of the Club de Cordeliers. After the monarchy was suspended in August 1792, the Girondin ministers wanted a man committed to the insurgents, and Danton was made Minister of Justice on 10 August. His part in the September Massacres has long been disputed. Against the invading armies he called for daring, and yet more daring.

In 1793 his wife died on 10 February while he was on a mission in Belgium. He supported the Revolutionary Tribunal in March and was among the first members of the Committee of Public Safety, installed on 6 April. In March 1793 the National Convention sent him to Leuven to investigate General Dumouriez. On 1 June he urged the Convention to break up the Commission of Twelve. He declined to rejoin the committee in September and withdrew to Arcis-sur-Aube in October.

Returning to Paris in November 1793, Danton attacked religious persecution and called for clemency, and a group called the Indulgents formed around him. Robespierre answered his plea for an end to the Terror on 25 December. He was accused of financial misdeeds, above all involvement in the scandal over the liquidation of the French East India Company, though no hard evidence against him is recorded. On 30 March 1794 two committees decided to arrest him, with Desmoulins and others. Tried from 3 to 5 April before the Revolutionary Tribunal, he was guillotined on 5 April 1794.

Historians have long disagreed about him. Thiers and Mignet saw a gigantic revolutionary, Lamartine a man without principles, and Robinet a generous patriot. He left little writing, so most evidence is secondhand. Georg Büchner made his last days the subject of the play Dantons Tod.
georges-lemaitre: Georges Henri Joseph Édouard Lemaître was born on 17 July 1894 in Charleroi, Belgium, the eldest of four children of an industrialist who owned a glassworks. He attended Jesuit schools and in 1911 began studying engineering at the Catholic University of Louvain. In the First World War he volunteered for the Belgian army, fought in the Battle of the Yser and received the Belgian War Cross. Afterwards he turned to physics and mathematics, took his doctorate in 1920 and prepared for the priesthood. He was ordained on 22 September 1923 by Cardinal Mercier, who supported his scientific work.

Lemaître spent 1923 to 1924 at Cambridge with Arthur Eddington and the next year at the Harvard College Observatory with Harlow Shapley. In 1927 he published a report arguing, independently of Alexander Friedmann, that the equations of general relativity implied a universe that is not static, and linking this to a proportional relation between the recession velocity of galaxies and their distance. It had little impact because the journal was little read, and Einstein is reported to have said his calculations were correct but his physics abominable. Edwin Hubble published better data in 1929, and in 2018 the International Astronomical Union recommended the name Hubble-Lemaître law.

In 1931 Lemaître proposed that the universe expanded from a single initial quantum, which he called the primeval atom, now regarded as the first formulation of the Big Bang theory. With Manuel Sandoval Vallarta he showed that cosmic rays are charged particles deflected by the Earth's magnetic field. He argued throughout his career for a positive cosmological constant and was an early user of computers in physics.

Lemaître held that science and religion were not in conflict but should not be mixed. He was professor of physics at Louvain from 1927 until he retired in 1964, and from 1960 president of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, a post he held until his death. The Royal Astronomical Society gave him its first Eddington Medal in 1953. In 1965 he learned of the discovery of the cosmic microwave background, which convinced most experts of the Big Bang's validity. He died on 20 June 1966.
georgetown-guyana: Georgetown is on the east bank of the Demerara River estuary, on Guyana's Atlantic coast, in flat coastal plains. The city is surrounded by cane fields and marshy swamps, with savannah to the east and south. Its land lies as much as 2 metres below the high-tide level, and a retaining wall known as the seawall keeps the ocean out, while a network of canals with kokers, or sluices, built by the Dutch and later the British, drains the city. It is laid out in a north-south, east-west grid interlaced with these canals. It has a hot, trade-wind tropical rainforest climate, moderated by the north-east trade winds, and rarely sees temperatures above 31 degrees Celsius.

In 1748 Governor Laurens Storm van 's Gravesande built a guard post at the mouth of the Demerara River, and English planters later built houses around it, forming a small village. The town was established in 1782 during a brief French occupation of the Dutch colony of Demerara, under the name Longchamps. In 1784 the name was changed to Stabroek, after Nicholaas Geelvinck, Lord of Stabroek, then President of the Dutch West India Company. In 1789 the population was 780, of whom 239 were white, but the town grew quickly, reaching around 8,500 by 1807. American traders built a wharf that became known as American Stelling.

Under British rule the city took the name Georgetown in 1812, in honour of King George III. A ward one fourth of a mile broad and one mile long retains the name Stabroek. Georgetown gained official city status on 24 August 1842, in the reign of Queen Victoria. A large fire, the Great Fire, caused widespread damage in 1945.

Georgetown is the capital and largest city of Guyana, the seat of its government and the home of the Secretariat of the Caribbean Community, CARICOM. The 2022 census recorded 125,683 people. It is known for its colonial architecture, with many wooden buildings and markets. These include the tall painted-timber St. George's Anglican Cathedral, State House (built 1852), the neo-Gothic City Hall (1889), the Victoria Law Courts (1887), the Parliament Building (1829-1834) and Stabroek Market (1792), whose cast-iron clock tower dominates the skyline. The Georgetown Cenotaph, built in 1923, is the site of Remembrance Day services each November.
georgian-orthodox-church: The Georgian Orthodox Church is an autocephalous Eastern Orthodox church in full communion with the other Orthodox churches. It asserts an apostolic foundation and traces its roots to the Christianization of Iberia and Colchis, in modern eastern and western Georgia, by the apostle Andrew in the 1st century and by Saint Nino in the 4th. Modern historians consider the Andrew account mythical, the product of a late tradition from 9th-century Byzantine legends. In the 4th and 5th centuries the Church of Iberia was strictly subordinate to Antioch, where its bishops were consecrated, and around 480 the Byzantine government recognised its chief prelate as a catholicos instead of an archbishop.

Between the 11th and early 13th centuries the Bagrationi dynasty united western and eastern Georgia in one kingdom, relying on the church's prestige and granting it tax immunity and large appanages. In 1103 King David the Builder convened the council of Ruisi-Urbnisi, which condemned Armenian Miaphysitism more strongly than before. Georgian monasticism began in the 6th century with the Thirteen Assyrian Fathers, who founded David Gareja, and its golden age lasted from the 9th to the 11th century, with monasteries abroad such as Iviron on Mount Athos.

The Mongol invasions of the 13th century and Tamerlane's in the 14th and 15th gravely disrupted Georgian Christianity. In the west the Catholicate of Abkhazia emerged under the kings of Imereti and lasted until 1795. After the Russian Empire annexed Kartl-Kakheti in 1801, its authorities abolished the church's autocephaly on 18 July 1811 and replaced the Georgian liturgy with Church Slavonic. On 25 January 1990 the Patriarch of Constantinople recognised autocephaly again.

The church is governed by the Holy Synod, the body of bishops, headed by the Catholicos-Patriarch of All Georgia. The first head of the church to carry the title of patriarch was Melkisedek I, from 1010 to 1033. Eastern Orthodoxy was the state religion for most of Georgia's history until 1921, when Soviet forces occupied the country. The constitution recognises the church's special role in Georgia's history and states its independence from the state, and relations are further regulated by the Concordat of 2002.
georgians: Georgians call themselves Kartveli, their land Sakartvelo and their language Kartuli. The Greeks and Romans knew western Georgians as Colchians and eastern Georgians as Iberians. Most historians agree that the ancestors of modern Georgians lived in the southern Caucasus and northern Anatolia from the Neolithic. Western tribes established the kingdom of Colchis, dated to about 1350 BCE, and eastern tribes formed their kingdom in the 7th century BCE. Between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE, Kartlian tribes consolidated around Mtskheta and founded the Kingdom of Kartli, or Iberia, under Pharnavaz I. By the mid-4th century both Lazica and Iberia were officially Christian.

Arabs invaded south-eastern Georgia in 645. The Bagrationi dynasty rose in the 9th century, and Bagrat III, supported by David III of Tao, was crowned first king of a unified Georgia in 1008. Under David IV (r. 1089–1125), who defeated Turkish forces at the Battle of Didgori in 1121, and Tamar (r. 1184–1213), Georgia reached its height, commonly called the Georgian Golden Age. Jalal ad-Din captured Tbilisi in 1226, and the Mongol invasions followed. The kingdom collapsed into anarchy by 1466 and split into three kingdoms and five principalities.

In 1783 the Treaty of Georgievsk made eastern Georgia a Russian protectorate under Heraclius II. Russia annexed eastern Georgia in 1801, abolished the Bagrationi dynasty and ended the autocephaly of the Georgian Orthodox Church. Georgia declared the Democratic Republic of Georgia on 26 May 1918, and the Red Army occupied it in February 1921. The Supreme Council declared independence from the Soviet Union on 9 April 1991.

Georgian is a Kartvelian language with no known relation to any other language family, with its own writing system and a written tradition dating back to the 5th century. Svans, Mingrelians and the Laz speak related Kartvelian languages. The Church was crucial to the development of a written language, and most of the earliest works were religious texts. Most Georgians are Eastern Orthodox Christians belonging to the Georgian Orthodox Church. There are about 5 million Georgians in the world.
georgy-lvov: Prince Georgy Yevgenyevich Lvov was born on 2 November 1861 (21 October, Old Style) in Dresden, into one of the oldest Russian noble families, which traced its roots to the Rurik princes of Yaroslavl. His reform-minded father spent almost all his income on his children's education. The family lived at Popovka in Tula Governorate, a few miles from Leo Tolstoy's home, and counted Tolstoy among their closest friends. After the abolition of serfdom they fell deep into debt, and chose to turn Popovka into a profitable farm, laying off their servants and working the land themselves while Georgy studied law at the University of Moscow. All debts were repaid by the late 1880s.

When war between Japan and Russia began in January 1904, thirteen provincial zemstvos formed a medical brigade of 360 doctors and nurses under Lvov to help the Red Cross on the Manchurian front. The relief mission won high praise from military leaders and made him a national hero. In 1906 he was elected to the First Duma for the Constitutional Democratic Party. In 1914 he became chairman of the All-Russian Union of Zemstvos, and in 1915 he was a leader of the Union of Zemstvos and a member of Zemgor, the committee that helped supply the army and tend the wounded in the First World War.

After the February Revolution and the abdication of Nicholas II, Lvov headed the Provisional Government founded by the Duma on 2 March 1917, serving as prime minister from 15 March to 20 July. His government introduced universal adult suffrage, freedom of press and speech, the abolition of capital punishment and the removal of legal restrictions of religion, class and race. Unable to rally enough support, he resigned in July 1917 in favour of his war minister, Alexander Kerensky.

After the October Revolution he was arrested but escaped, and in October 1918 travelled to the United States for the anti-Bolshevik Provisional Siberian Government, arriving after the First World War had ended. He moved to France, headed the Russian political meeting in Paris from 1918 to 1920, lived in poverty, wrote his memoirs and died in March 1925.
german-empire: The German Confederation had been created by the Congress of Vienna on 8 June 1815. After the liberal Revolutions of 1848 were crushed, Otto von Bismarck's pragmatic Realpolitik took their place. He sought to extend Hohenzollern hegemony across the German states, which meant excluding Prussia's main German rival, Austria. The Second Schleswig War against Denmark in 1864, the Austro-Prussian War in 1866 and the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871 fed a growing pan-German ideal and brought victory for the Kleindeutsche Lösung, the Lesser German solution.

The empire was founded on 18 January 1871, when the south German states, except for Austria, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, joined the North German Confederation. Wilhelm I, King of Prussia, became German Emperor, Berlin remained the capital, and Bismarck became chancellor. It was a federal constitutional monarchy of 25 states, and Prussia held about two thirds of its population and territory.

Bismarck served as chancellor from 1871 to 1890. His tenure began with relatively liberal measures and shifted toward conservatism, marked by the Kulturkampf against the Catholic Church. He enacted universal male suffrage in 1871 and created pioneering social programmes in the 1880s. In 1879 he concluded the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary, which became the Triple Alliance with Italy in 1882. In the 1880s the empire entered the colonial race, acquiring territories in Africa, the Pacific and China.

Wilhelm I died on 9 March 1888. His son Frederick, who had incurable cancer of the larynx, died on 15 June 1888 after 99 days, and Wilhelm II became emperor. Wishing to rule in his own right, he came into conflict with Bismarck, who resigned in March 1890. Wilhelm II then pursued Weltpolitik, a more aggressive course that abandoned Bismarck's alliance system and left Germany increasingly isolated.

After the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the Kaiser gave Austria-Hungary full support against Serbia, a blank check in the term of the historian Fritz Fischer. The German plan to take Paris quickly failed, and the Western Front became a stalemate. In October 1918 the armies were in retreat and the allies had collapsed. The empire fell in the November revolution of 1918 with the abdication of Wilhelm II.

The Treaty of Versailles imposed reparations of 132 billion gold marks and limited the army to 100,000 men. The economic devastation that followed, and the humiliation felt by the German population, are considered leading factors in the rise of Adolf Hitler and Nazism. Many historians have stressed a German Sonderweg, or special path, as a root of the catastrophe of the 20th century. Large parts of the empire now belong to Poland, Russia and France.
german-revolution-of-1918-1919: The First World War exposed weaknesses in the German Empire's social and political structures. The Allied blockade from 1914 to 1919 cut off imported food and led to widespread hunger as early as the Turnip Winter of 1916 and 1917, while profiteering, inflation and class antagonism rose. The initial enthusiasm for the war waned. After the Russian Revolution of October 1917, the moderate Social Democratic Party leadership drew a line between itself and the Bolsheviks, and fear of civil war on the Russian model shaped its choices. When the request for a ceasefire came, the war-weary population wanted only peace, and Wilson's Fourteen Points fed the belief that a democratic Germany would get a just peace.

The revolution began on 29 October 1918, when sailors at Kiel mutinied against an unauthorized naval order to sail against the British Royal Navy. By 7 November it controlled all the large coastal cities and had spread to Cologne and Munich, where Kurt Eisner proclaimed the People's State of Bavaria on 8 November. By the end of the month the dynastic rulers of the other German states had abdicated without bloodshed. On 9 November Chancellor Prince Max of Baden announced that the Emperor had renounced the throne and handed the chancellorship to Friedrich Ebert, and a republic was proclaimed. Wilhelm II fled to Holland the next day.

On 10 November the Council of the People's Deputies was formed as a provisional government of the two main socialist parties under Ebert, who kept most of the imperial officer corps and administration in place. The split between moderate and radical socialists turned violent. The Spartacist uprising of January 1919 failed and led to the murders of Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht by members of the Freikorps. Local soviet republics appeared in Bavaria, Bremen and Würzburg and were put down.

On 19 January 1919 Germans voted for a constituent national assembly, in an election that included women for the first time. It met at Weimar from 6 February and accepted the Treaty of Versailles on 16 June. The revolution is generally said to end on 11 August 1919, when the Weimar Constitution was adopted. It ended the monarchies of the Empire and the states, abolished hereditary titles of nobility and introduced equal suffrage, creating a representative democracy new to Germany.

It left much of the military hierarchy and imperial civil service, including the judiciary, untouched, and many who stayed were monarchists. Far-right extremists used the stab-in-the-back myth to blame communists, socialists and Jews for the defeat. The Kapp Putsch of March 1920 collapsed within days under a general strike, and the Nazi Beer Hall Putsch of 9 November 1923 was stopped in Munich. The Weimar Republic eventually ended with the ascent of Hitler.
germania: Roman geographers placed Germania roughly between the Rhine in the west and the Vistula in the east, from the upper Danube northwards along the North and Baltic seas to the known parts of southern Scandinavia. The free lands are also called Magna Germania, and by modern scholars Germania Libera or the Germanic Barbaricum. The origin of the name Germani is uncertain. Tacitus wrote that the name had once belonged only to the Tungri, west of the Rhine, and was later extended to supposedly related peoples beyond it.

The country held many peoples with little unity among them, and river names suggest that another Indo-European group lived there, probably under Germanic domination. Archaeologically it corresponds, from the 1st to the 4th century CE, to the Roman Iron Age: largely agrarian, without cities or coinage of its own. Amber was a primary export, and Roman luxury goods were imported on a large scale and have been found as far away as Scandinavia and western Russia.

Julius Caesar met peoples from beyond the Rhine during the Gallic Wars and called their homeland Germania, a name the Romans appear to have borrowed from the Gauls. Augustus later carried Roman arms as far as the Elbe and in 7 BCE created a short-lived province, Germania Antiqua, before the victory of Arminius ended the attempt. The Rhine became the frontier. Germani such as the Ubii and Sicambri were settled on the Roman bank, which was heavily affected by the Revolt of the Batavi under Gaius Julius Civilis in 69–70 CE.

Under the Flavian dynasty the two provinces were organised, Germania Inferior with its headquarters at Colonia, the modern Cologne, and Germania Superior at Mogontiacum. The Romans also occupied the land between the Rhine, Main and Danube, known as the Agri Decumates. In the 3rd century confederations such as the Alemanni and Franks emerged and raided the provinces, and around 280 CE the Agri Decumates were evacuated and taken by the Alemanni. In 406 a large number of people fleeing the Huns crossed the Rhine, and Roman rule there eventually collapsed.

Much of Germania, including all the former Roman provinces, was eventually incorporated into the Frankish Empire and later East Francia. The name survived in learned use: it is attested in Old English translations of Bede and Orosius, and since the 17th century the usual English name of Germany has been derived from it, as are the names of that country in many other languages.
germanicus: Germanicus was born in Rome on 24 May 15 BCE to Nero Claudius Drusus and Antonia the Younger, and his younger siblings were Livilla and the future emperor Claudius. His grandparents included the triumvir Mark Antony and Octavia Minor on his mother's side. His father's victories in Germania earned the name Germanicus, which was awarded to the father after his death in 9 BCE. In 4 CE his uncle Tiberius adopted him, and he entered the gens Julia as Germanicus Julius Caesar. He married Agrippina the Elder, a granddaughter of Augustus, and was the father of Caligula and the maternal grandfather of Nero.

He became quaestor in 7 CE, five years before the legal age, and was sent to Illyricum to help Tiberius suppress the Pannonian and Dalmatian rebellion, where he defeated the Mazaei. In 12 CE he was consul, and in 13 CE Augustus appointed him commander on the Rhine, with eight legions, about one third of the Roman army. When Augustus died in 14 CE the legions of the Lower Rhine mutinied over unpaid bonuses, and Germanicus dealt with them. Their attempt to proclaim him emperor failed, since he stayed loyal and led them against the German tribes instead.

He campaigned in Germania from 14 to 16 CE, avenged the defeat in the Teutoburg Forest and recovered two of the three legionary eagles lost there. On 26 May 17 he held a triumph in which Thusnelda, the wife of Arminius, and her three-year-old son were led among the captives, although Arminius himself was never taken. In 18 CE he was given command in the east with imperium maius, reorganized the provinces of Asia Minor and incorporated Cappadocia and Commagene.

In the east he quarrelled with Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso, the governor of Syria whom Tiberius had appointed. Germanicus fell ill at Antioch, became convinced that Piso was poisoning him, and renounced their friendship. He died on 10 October 19. Several sources blamed Piso, acting on the orders of Tiberius, but this was never proven. Piso died before his trial in the Senate ended, ostensibly by suicide, and Tacitus supposes that Tiberius may have had him killed.

Tacitus described Germanicus as a fine general, kind and temperate. The historian Anthony A. Barrett accepts that he was an able general. Ancient writers often contrasted him as a tragic hero with Tiberius as a tyrant. In 4 CE Germanicus also wrote a Latin version of Aratus's Phainomena, which survives.
germany: Ancient humans were present in what is now Germany at least 600,000 years ago. Germanic peoples expanded from southern Scandinavia and northern Germany, and the Celtic-speaking peoples of the south were later assimilated by them. Under Augustus, the Roman Empire created a short-lived province of Germania between the Rhine and Elbe rivers, and in 9 CE Arminius defeated three Roman legions in the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, an outcome that dissuaded the Romans from conquering Germania. After the invasion of the Huns in 375 and the decline of Rome from 395, the Franks established the Frankish Kingdom.

Charlemagne founded the Carolingian Empire in 800, and after its division in 843 the Kingdom of Germany and the Holy Roman Empire emerged from the eastern successor kingdom of East Francia. Northern German regions became the centre of the Protestant Reformation in the 16th century. After the Holy Roman Empire's dissolution in 1806 the German Confederation was formed in 1815, and Prussia led unification into the German Empire in 1871. The Weimar Republic replaced the Empire after World War I. The Nazi rise to power in 1933 led to a totalitarian dictatorship under Adolf Hitler, which resulted in World War II and the Holocaust.

In 1949, after the war and Allied occupation, Germany was organised into two polities with limited sovereignty: the Federal Republic of Germany, or West Germany, and the German Democratic Republic, or East Germany. The first was a founding member of the European Economic Community, while the second was a communist Eastern Bloc state and a founding member of the Warsaw Pact. The former East German states joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990, and Germany regained its full sovereignty on 15 March 1991.

Germany covers 357,022 square kilometres between the Baltic Sea and the North Sea in the north and the Alps in the south, and its highest point is the Zugspitze at 2,963 metres. It is a federal parliamentary republic of sixteen Länder under the Basic Law of 1949, and Berlin is the capital and most populous city. The census of 2023 recorded a population of 84.7 million. Four national minorities live in the country: a Danish minority, the Sorbs, the Roma and Sinti, and the Frisians.
gers: The Gers is a department in the region of Occitania, in south-western France. It is bordered by the departments of Hautes-Pyrénées and Pyrénées-Atlantiques to the south, Haute-Garonne and Tarn-et-Garonne to the east, Lot-et-Garonne to the north and Landes to the west. Its inhabitants are called Gersois and Gersoises, after the Gers River. The landscape is one of sleepy bastide villages and rolling hills, with the Pyrenees visible to the south. Annual rainfall varies from more than 900 mm in the south-west to less than 700 mm in the north-east, around Auch, Condom and Lectoure. Winters are mild and summers hot and dry.

The Gers is one of the original 83 departments created during the French Revolution, on 4 March 1790. It was formed from parts of the former provinces of Guyenne and Gascony. In 1808 it lost Lavit, on its north-eastern side, to the newly created department of Tarn-et-Garonne.

The culture is largely agricultural, with weight placed on local food and drink: Armagnac brandy, Côtes de Gascogne wine, Floc de Gascogne, foie gras and wild mushrooms. Maize, colza, sunflowers and grain are the main crops. Gascon, a dialect of Occitan, is spoken only by a minority. The department is among the most thinly peopled and most rural areas in Western Europe, with about 31 people per square kilometre and a population of 192,645 in 2023.

Alexandre Dumas, père, made the Gersois d'Artagnan the fourth musketeer of The Three Musketeers, and a museum to d'Artagnan stands in the village of Lupiac. A horse race at the Auteuil Hippodrome is named after André Boingnères, a local race-horse owner and mayor of Termes-d'Armagnac from 1951 to 1976.
getulio-vargas: Getúlio Dornelles Vargas was born on 19 April 1882 in São Borja, Rio Grande do Sul, near the border with Argentina, into a powerful local family. He joined the army in 1898 and studied at the military college at Rio Pardo until 1901, when he and twenty other cadets were forced out after a protest over a lack of water. After law school he became state attorney of Rio Grande do Sul through his party and his father, and in 1911 he married Darci Lima Sarmanho. He was a state deputy, took part in the state's 1923 civil war, and became a national deputy that year. He was finance minister under Washington Luís and in 1928 became president of Rio Grande do Sul.

In the First Republic an alliance of São Paulo and Minas Gerais held power. When President Luís named another paulista, Júlio Prestes, as his successor, he broke that arrangement, and Prestes was declared winner of the 1930 election amid claims of fraud on both sides. After the assassination of Vargas's running mate João Pessoa the opposition took up arms. Vargas's provisional presidency began on 3 November 1930. He governed by decree, imprisoned opponents and created a Ministry of Labor, brought unions under state control, and introduced the secret vote and women's suffrage. He survived the Constitutionalist Revolution of 1932 and was elected president in 1934.

Citing a possible communist insurrection, Vargas seized powers in 1937 and began the Estado Novo. Opponents were arrested or exiled and the press censored. In May 1938 armed Integralists attacked the presidential palace and besieged him for hours. The Estado Novo's chief social reforms were a minimum-wage law and a single labor code. Brazil declared war on Italy and Germany on 21 August 1942 after attacks on its ships. As discontent grew, Vargas abolished censorship in 1945, but the military feared he would seize absolute power and forced him from office on 29 October.

Vargas ran in 1950 as candidate of the Brazilian Labor Party and took office on 31 January 1951. He pursued a nationalist economic policy and founded Petrobras. A crisis followed the murder of an Air Force officer outside the home of his adversary Carlos Lacerda, which implicated the chief of Vargas's personal guard. Generals demanded his resignation, and on 24 August 1954 he shot himself in the chest at Catete Palace. Many historians regard him as the most influential Brazilian politician of the twentieth century, and he was nicknamed the Father of the Poor.
ghana: Ghana lies on the Gulf of Guinea, a few degrees north of the Equator, and covers 239,567 square kilometres with an Atlantic coastline of about 560 kilometres. It borders Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso and Togo. The land consists of low coastal plains, forested hills in the centre, and savanna in the north. The Prime Meridian passes through Tema, near Accra. Lake Volta, formed by the Akosombo Dam completed in 1965, is the largest reservoir in the world by surface area. The highest point is Mount Afadja, at 885 metres, in the Akwapim-Togo Range.

The earliest kingdoms to emerge were Bonoman in the south, existing in the 11th century, and the Kingdom of Dagbon in the north. From the 17th century Akan states, mainly based on gold trading, emerged from what is believed to have been the Bonoman area; they included Adansi, Asante, Denkyira, Akyem and Akwamu. By the 19th century the south was included in the Asante Kingdom, whose government grew from a loose network into a centralised kingdom with a specialised bureaucracy centred on Kumasi.

The Portuguese came to the Gold Coast in the 15th century to trade, and in 1481 King John II of Portugal commissioned Diogo de Azambuja to build Elmina Castle. The Dutch joined the gold trade by 1598 and captured Elmina in 1617. The British eventually controlled the coast by the 19th century. The modern borders took shape after more than a century of colonial resistance and joined four British territories: the Gold Coast, Ashanti, the Northern Territories and British Togoland.

On 6 March 1957 Ghana became the first colony in Sub-Saharan Africa to achieve sovereignty. Under President Kwame Nkrumah it became influential in decolonisation and the Pan-African movement. Ghana alternated between civilian and military governments until January 1993, when the Fourth Republic began after elections in late 1992.

The name comes from Wagadu, an empire of west Africa from the 3rd to 12th centuries that Arab traders called Ghana; it is thought to derive from the title Kaya Maghan, meaning ruler of gold. According to Jack Goody, the idea that the Akan descended from the medieval empire lacked linguistic and historical evidence, yet became influential among nationalist intellectuals. The name was adopted as a symbol of precolonial prestige before independence. English is the official language.
ghana-empire: It is uncertain among historians when Ghana's ruling dynasty began. The first identifiable mention is by al-Khwārizmī in 830, and the 11th-century Cordoban scholar al-Bakri gave further information. Ghana meant warrior or war chief and was the title of the rulers, who were also called Kaya Maghan, king of gold. Soninke oral tradition names Dinga as the ancestor, who killed a serpent deity, Bida, and whose son Dyabe founded Wagadu. Medieval Arabic chronicles proposed Soninke, Wangara or Sanhaja Berber origins for the rulers, while archaeology since the mid 20th century has led scholars to favour a local origin: the Dhar Tichitt site shows a complex culture there by 1600 BCE.

Towards the end of the 3rd century CE a wet period in the Sahel opened new land, and the introduction of the camel turned irregular trade routes into a network between North Africa and the Niger. Wagadu made its profits from a monopoly on gold heading north and salt heading south, though it did not control the goldfields.

In 734 the Umayyad Caliphate sent an expedition against the Sous and the Sudan, and al-Bakri noted that descendants of its troops still lived in Ghana and followed the native religion. When Muslim merchants first crossed the desert, Ghana was the most powerful state in the Sahel. As the Sahel dried, the centres of trade moved south to the Niger and west to the Senegal, which strengthened Ghana's vassals and weakened its core. Awdaghost, then a seat of the king, fell to the Almoravids in 1054, and the country converted to Islam around 1076. In 1083 it asked the Almoravids to help it attack Tadmekka.

By 1203 the Sosso had risen against their masters and conquered Ghana, creating a short-lived empire. Ibn Khaldun wrote that the people of Mali vanquished the Susu and acquired both their kingdom and that of Ghana. Maurice Delafosse assigned the date 1235 to this event, but it is arbitrary.

Kingship was matrilineal and traditionally passed to the son of the king's sister. Al-Bakri described a capital of two towns about 10 km apart, so built up between that they might be said to have merged. The royal town, El-Ghaba, had a stone wall, a sacred grove where priests lived and the king's palace, and the other town was almost entirely Muslim, with twelve mosques, scholars and jurists. The usual identification is Koumbi Saleh, excavated by French teams from the 1920s, but scholars increasingly dispute it. Contemporary sources suggest an army reliant on infantry with swords, spears and bows.
ghent: Ghent lies at the confluence of the Scheldt and the Leie, in the East Flanders province of the Flemish Region of Belgium. Archaeological evidence shows human presence there from the Stone Age and Iron Age. Most historians derive the older name, Ganda, from a Celtic word meaning confluence or river mouth, while other sources connect it with an obscure deity named Gontia. The rivers flowed through land that flooded periodically, and these water-meadows were well suited to grazing sheep, whose wool fed the city's cloth trade.

Around 650 Saint Amand founded two abbeys in Ghent, St. Peter's and St. Bavo's, and around 800 Louis the Pious appointed Einhard, the biographer of Charlemagne, abbot of both. The city grew from the abbeys and a commercial centre, and Vikings plundered it in 851 and 879. Under the protection of the County of Flanders it flourished from the 11th century as a small city-state. By the 13th century it was the biggest city in Europe north of the Alps after Paris, with up to 65,000 people within its walls, and the leading centre of woollen cloth manufacture; by the middle of that century the industry employed 4,000 weavers and 1,200 fullers.

In 1453 Ghent suffered a heavy defeat at the Battle of Gavere at the hands of Philip the Good, after high taxes had led to rebellion. Afterwards the political and social centre of the Low Countries began to shift from Flanders towards Brabant. After the Revolt of Ghent in 1539, Charles V, a native of the city, made its nobles walk before him barefoot with a noose around the neck, so that its people have since been called Stroppendragers, or noose bearers. St. Bavo's Abbey was torn down and replaced with a fortress for Spanish troops. The Eighty Years' War ended Ghent's role as a centre of international importance.

Ghent's textile industry flourished again in the 18th and 19th centuries, and in 1800 Lieven Bauwens introduced the first mechanical weaving machine on the European continent after smuggling plans out of England. The Treaty of Ghent, adopted on Christmas Eve 1814, formally ended the War of 1812 between Great Britain and the United States. The city was occupied by the Germans in both world wars but escaped severe destruction, and was liberated on 6 September 1944.

Ghent is the capital and largest city of its province and the third largest city in Belgium, a port and university city. Much of its medieval architecture survives, including St. Bavo's Cathedral with the Ghent Altarpiece, the belfry, the Gravensteen castle and the buildings along the old Graslei harbour. UNESCO recognised its béguinages as World Heritage Sites in 1998, and the belfry and adjacent cloth hall in 1999.
giacomo-puccini: Giacomo Puccini was born in Lucca, then in the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, the sixth of nine children of Michele Puccini and Albina Magi. His great-great-grandfather, also named Giacomo, had made the family a local musical dynasty as maestro di cappella of the Cattedrale di San Martino, a post passed down through his son Antonio, his grandson Domenico and Michele. Each studied music at Bologna and composed church music, and Domenico and Michele also wrote operas. Michele's funeral was an occasion of public mourning.

At the Milan Conservatory, Puccini studied under Ponchielli and Bazzini. His thesis piece, the Capriccio sinfonico, was performed on 14 July 1883 and favourably reviewed. His first opera, Le Villi, was entered for a competition run by the publisher Sonzogno but was disqualified because its manuscript was illegible. The publisher Giulio Ricordi then commissioned Edgar, which premiered at La Scala on 21 April 1889 to a lukewarm response and never became popular. Ricordi kept Puccini on and continued his allowance. Manon Lescaut was completed with the librettists Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa.

La bohème, based on Henri Murger's La Vie de Bohème, premiered in Turin in 1896 under Arturo Toscanini and was soon performed in leading opera houses in Europe and the United States. Tosca followed in 1900, arguably his first venture into verismo, the realistic depiction of life including violence. Madama Butterfly, first given at La Scala on 17 February 1904, was greeted with hostility, probably owing to inadequate rehearsals; Puccini withdrew it and revised it, and a fifth version of 1907 became the standard one.

La fanciulla del West, from a play by David Belasco, premiered at the Metropolitan Opera in New York on 10 December 1910, the first world premiere of an opera there. La rondine was first given at Monte Carlo on 27 March 1917, and Il trittico, three one-act operas, in New York in 1918. Puccini left Turandot unfinished; Franco Alfano completed the last two scenes from his sketches.

In 1903 Puccini was seriously injured in a car crash on the road from Lucca to Torre del Lago, where he had a villa on the lake from about 1900, and he was found to have a form of diabetes. Late in 1923 he began to complain of a sore throat, and doctors diagnosed throat cancer and recommended an experimental radiation treatment in Brussels. He died there on 29 November 1924, aged 65, of complications after the treatment. News reached Rome during a performance of La bohème, which was stopped while the orchestra played Chopin's Funeral March. He is buried in a chapel at the Villa Puccini.
gian-lorenzo-bernini: Gian Lorenzo Bernini was born on 7 December 1598 in Naples, the sixth of thirteen children of Angelica Galante and the Mannerist sculptor Pietro Bernini, who came from Florence. He was recognised as a prodigy at eight, and Pope Paul V is said to have remarked that the child would be the Michelangelo of his age. In 1606 his father received a papal commission and moved the family to Rome, where he continued his son's training. Under the patronage of the wealthy Cardinal Scipione Borghese the young Bernini rose rapidly as a sculptor.

Pope Gregory XV gave Bernini the rank of Cavaliere in 1621. From 1623 to 1644 he enjoyed a near monopoly of patronage from Urban VIII and the Barberini family, who first set him to architecture. His first fountain, the Barcaccia at the foot of the Spanish Steps, commissioned in 1627, was a low-lying boat that made the most of Rome's weak water pressure. After Urban's death Innocent X, an enemy of the Barberini, left him in eclipse for four years, partly because of the failed bell towers of St. Peter's, which Bernini had designed.

Under Alexander VII, who planned to make Rome a world capital, Bernini was chief collaborator, and St. Peter's Square was built from 1656 to 1667. In 1665 political pressure sent him to Paris to work for Louis XIV on the Louvre, and he stayed from April to October. Later he refurbished the Ponte Sant'Angelo under Clement IX, and in 1674 he made the statue of the Blessed Ludovica Albertoni in six months.

Bernini was first and foremost a sculptor, and the latest catalogue of his sculpture lists 143 entries, from 1610 to a marble Salvator Mundi bust of 1679. He also designed tomb monuments, among them those of Urban VIII and Alexander VII in St. Peter's, painted perhaps 150 canvases of which 35 to 40 survive, and wrote, directed and acted in plays, mostly Carnival satires. The art historian Irving Lavin called his ability to combine sculpture, painting and architecture into one whole the unity of the visual arts.

He worked until two weeks before his death, from a stroke, on 28 November 1680. Few artists have so shaped the appearance of a city as he did Rome, and sculptors and architects studied his work for decades afterwards.
gibraltar: Gibraltar lies near the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, on the Bay of Gibraltar, close to where the Mediterranean Sea meets the Atlantic Ocean at the Strait of Gibraltar. Its territory covers 6.8 square kilometres and shares a land border of 1.2 kilometres with Spain. The Rock of Gibraltar dominates the landscape, and the town stands at its foot. The name comes from the Arabic Jabal Ṭāriq, the Mount of Tariq, after the eighth-century North African commander Tariq ibn Ziyad, who began the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula across the strait in 711.

Neanderthals lived in Gorham's Cave about 50,000 years ago, and Homo sapiens went on using the caves of Gibraltar from about 40,000 years ago to about 5,000 years ago. Neolithic pottery found in the caves is mostly of the Almerian culture of Andalusia. There is little evidence of habitation in the Bronze Age, when people had largely stopped living in caves.

The Almohads founded Gibraltar as a permanent watchtower in 1160. In the Late Middle Ages control passed between the Nasrids, Castilians and Marinids, and the place gained strategic weight with the destruction of nearby Algeciras around 1375. It became part of the Crown of Castile again in 1462. Anglo-Dutch forces captured it from Spain in 1704, during the War of the Spanish Succession, and it was ceded to Great Britain in perpetuity by the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.

Its control of the narrow entrance to the Mediterranean made it an important base for the Royal Navy, particularly during the Napoleonic Wars and the Second World War. Gibraltar was declared a crown colony on 25 June 1830. Water was a constant concern: with no rivers or streams, the town relied on wells, cisterns and rainwater, and in the late nineteenth century a Sanitary Commission introduced large-scale desalination and giant catchments after cholera and yellow fever had spread. In 1969 Francisco Franco closed the land frontier with Spain, and it reopened in 1982.

Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory with almost complete internal self-government through an elected parliament, while the United Kingdom remains responsible for defence and foreign policy. Spain asserts a claim to the territory; Gibraltarians overwhelmingly rejected Spanish sovereignty in a referendum in 1967 and shared sovereignty in 2002. English is the language of government, commerce and education, and many Gibraltarians also speak Spanish and a local dialect called Llanito. About 38,000 people live there, and their ancestry includes Genoese, Maltese, Portuguese, Sephardic Jewish and Moroccan as well as Spanish and British.
gifu: Gifu is the capital of Gifu Prefecture, on the northern edge of the Nōbi Plain. The Nagara River cuts the city in half, and its alluvial plain is fertile but prone to flooding in typhoons, so dykes and levees have been built. Mount Kinka, 329 metres high beside the river, is one of the city's main symbols and carries Gifu Castle. Traditional industries include Mino washi paper and agriculture, and the city is part of the Chūkyō metropolitan area centred on Nagoya.

Two sites in the city, Ryomonji and Kotozuka, have produced large burial mounds of the late Yayoi period. In the Sengoku period it was said that whoever controls Gifu controls Japan, since its central location suited those seeking to unify the country. The Toki clan held Mino Province for over 200 years until Saitō Dōsan, a Toki vassal, rebelled and took control in 1542, building Inabayama Castle on Mount Inaba. Oda Nobunaga, who followed Dōsan in the castle, gave the castle and the surrounding town the name Gifu. The castle was first built by the Nikaidō clan in the Kamakura period and has been rebuilt many times, the present one in 1956.

In the Edo period the nearby post towns of Kanō-juku and Gōdo-juku on the Nakasendō provided traffic and were later absorbed by Gifu, which became a city in 1889. Its first major industry was textiles, and for a long time it rivaled Tokyo and Osaka as a centre of Japanese fashion. In the Pacific War, Gifu was an industrial centre, and the air raid of 9 July 1945 caused 1,383 casualties, 863 of them deaths, and affected 20,426 buildings. It merged with Yanaizu in 2006.

Cormorant fishing on the Nagara River is the city's best-known attraction and is said to date back more than 1,300 years. Six fishing masters work the river together from 11 May to 15 October, catching ayu sweetfish. Temples tied to Saitō Dōsan and Oda Nobunaga include Jōzai-ji, where Dōsan's remains are interred, and Sōfuku-ji, with its Blood Ceiling.
gilan: Gilan Province lies in the north-west of Iran, along the south-western Caspian Sea, west of Mazandaran, east of Ardabil and north of Zanjan and Qazvin; in the north it borders Azerbaijan. Its capital is Rasht, and its main port is Bandar-e Anzali, formerly Bandar-e Pahlavi. The climate is humid subtropical, with the heaviest rainfall in Iran, generally around 1,400 mm a year. Large parts of the province are mountainous and forested, and the coastal plain is used mainly for rice paddies. Gilaks and Talysh form the majority of the population; the Gilaki language belongs to the north-western Iranian branch.

The Gelae, or Gilites, seem to have entered the region south of the Caspian coast in the second or first century BCE; Pliny identified them with the Cadusii, though they were more likely a separate people from the Dagestan region. Gilan was the home of the Ziyarid and Buyid dynasties in the mid-10th century. Its Deylamite warriors resisted the Arabs, who never conquered the region, and under the Buyid ruler Mu'izz al-Dawla the Deylamites took Baghdad in 945. After the Turkish invasions ended the Deylamite states, local rulers governed independently until the Mongol Ilkhan Öljeitü conquered the region in 1307.

Silk made Gilan wealthy from the 15th century, and it was the major exporter of silk in Asia from the 16th century until the mid 19th century. Shah Abbas I ended the rule of Khan Ahmad Khan, the last semi-independent ruler, and annexed the province, and Georgians, Circassians and Armenians settled there under the Safavids. Russia held Gilan for about ten years after the war of 1722 to 1723, and Russian influence lasted until 1946. A disease of silkworms in the mid 19th century caused hardship and a turn to rice and tea.

In the late 1910s Mirza Kuchik Khan led the Jangal movement, and in 1920, in alliance with the Bolsheviks against British forces, the Jangalis helped found the Persian Socialist Soviet Republic, which lasted from June 1920 until September 1921. After the Soviets withdrew support, the Jangalis were defeated and control returned to Tehran. Gilan is one of the 31 provinces of Iran. Rasht is known as the City of Rain, and the coast draws domestic and international visitors.
gilgit: Gilgit lies in the broad Gilgit Valley near the confluence of the Gilgit and Hunza rivers, southwest of the Karakoram range. It has a cold desert climate with little rainfall, and its irrigation comes from rivers fed by melting snow. The economy has mainly rested on agriculture, with wheat, maize and barley the main crops. The earliest known mention of the name is the Hatun Rock Inscription of the 7th century CE, which gives it as Giligitta, and al-Biruni recorded it in Arabic as klkt in the 11th century.

Gilgit was an important city on the Silk Road, along which Buddhism spread, and the Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang passed through it. In the 600s and 700s, according to Chinese records, a Buddhist dynasty called Little Balur governed it, believed to be the Patola Shahis. China held suzerainty in the mid-600s, and the Tibetan Empire took the region in the late 600s and held it until the late 800s. Later the Trakhan dynasty ruled until the death of Raja Abbas about 1810, its best known ruler being Queen Dadi Jawari in the 17th century, who built irrigation canals.

In 1846 Gilgit was transferred from the Sikhs to the British and sold to Gulab Singh of Jammu under the Treaty of Amritsar, and Dogra troops took over. The people drove them out in 1852, but Dogra forces from Ranbir Singh retook the town in 1860. In 1877 the British India Government established the Gilgit Agency to guard against the advance of Russia. On 1 November 1947 Major William Brown of the Gilgit Scouts mutinied and overthrew the governor, Ghansara Singh. A provisional government lasted 16 days, and Pakistan's political agent took over the administration on 16 November.

Gilgit is the capital and most populous city of the Pakistani-administered territory of Gilgit-Baltistan, renamed from the Northern Areas in 2009. It lies about 10 kilometres from the Karakoram Highway, which links it to Kashgar in China and to Chitral, Skardu, Peshawar and Islamabad, and it is a hub for trekking and mountaineering in the Karakoram.
giorgione: Little is known of Giorgione's life beyond what Giorgio Vasari records in his Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects. He came from Castelfranco Veneto, about 40 km inland from Venice, and the name Giorgione may be translated as Big George. Stylistic evidence supports Carlo Ridolfi's statement that he trained in Venice under Giovanni Bellini. In 1500 he was chosen to paint portraits of the Doge Agostino Barbarigo and the condottiere Consalvo Ferrante, and in 1504 he was commissioned to paint an altarpiece in the cathedral of Castelfranco. In 1507 and 1508 he worked on the exterior frescoes of the rebuilt Fondaco dei Tedeschi, having already decorated the exteriors of several Venetian palaces; very little of this work survives.

Apart from the altarpiece and the frescoes, his surviving works are small paintings made for wealthy collectors to keep at home, mostly under 60 cm in either dimension. He was the first major Italian painter to concentrate on this market. In the Castelfranco Madonna the landscape background gains an importance that was new in Venetian art. He painted pictures that told no story, embodying moods of lyrical or romantic feeling, and used the soft modelling called sfumato at about the time Leonardo da Vinci did.

The Tempest has been called the first landscape in Western painting. Its subject is unclear, and radiography shows the man at the left was once a seated female nude. The Sleeping Venus in Dresden was left unfinished, and Titian is generally agreed to have painted its landscape. None of his paintings is signed and only the portrait of Laura bears a reliable date, 1 June 1506. Attributions are therefore disputed: the Pastoral Concert in the Louvre is now widely given to Titian. Charles Hope wrote in 2012 that only three paintings have clear early evidence of his authorship, though he is generally credited with between twenty and forty.

Giorgione died of the plague on 17 September 1510. He was usually thought to have died on the island of Poveglia in the Venetian lagoon, but an archival document published in 2011 places his death on Lazzareto Nuovo. Isabella d'Este asked in October 1510 for a painting by him, and the reply a month later said it was not to be had at any price. Titian finished some of his paintings, though which ones remains controversial. Giorgione influenced Titian, Sebastiano del Piombo and Palma il Vecchio, and he was among the first Italians to paint landscapes with figures as independent pictures with no devotional, allegorical or historical purpose.
giovanni-battista-tiepolo: Born in Venice, Giovanni Battista Tiepolo was the youngest of six children of Domenico Tiepolo, a small shipping merchant, and Orsetta Tiepolo. His family bore the patrician name without claiming noble descent. In 1710 he became a pupil of Gregorio Lazzarini, but he was at least as strongly influenced by Sebastiano Ricci, Giovanni Battista Piazzetta, Tintoretto and Veronese. His earliest known works are apostles painted in 1715 and 1716 at Santa Maria dei Derelitti in Venice, and he painted his first fresco in 1716 on a church ceiling at Biadene, near Treviso. In 1719 he married Maria Cecilia Guardi, sister of the painters Francesco and Giovanni Antonio Guardi. They had nine children, and two sons, Giovanni Domenico and Lorenzo, worked as his assistants.

In about 1719-20 he painted the Triumph of Aurora and the Myth of Phaethon for the villa of Giambattista Baglione at Massanzago, a fluid spatial illusion that became a recurring theme. Commissions from the Dolfin family followed, including cycles for the archbishop's palace at Udine, completed in 1726 to 1728, and ten large canvases of Roman history for Ca' Dolfin in Venice. He used a cooler palette than earlier Venetian painters to give a convincing effect of daylight. Later works include the ceiling of the Gesuati in Venice and the story of Cleopatra at the Palazzo Labia, painted from 1745 to 1750. He also produced two sets of etchings, the Capricci and the Scherzi di fantasia.

In November 1750 he arrived in Würzburg at the invitation of Prince-Bishop Karl Philipp von Greifenclau. He frescoed the Kaisersaal with his sons, then painted the ceiling over Balthasar Neumann's staircase, finished in November 1753. This Allegory of the Planets and Continents covers 677 square metres and includes portraits of Tiepolo, his son Giandomenico and Neumann.

After returning to Venice in 1753 he was elected President of the Academy of Padua and painted villas such as the Villa Valmarana and the Villa Pisani at Stra. King Charles III of Spain commissioned him to decorate the throne room of the Royal Palace of Madrid with the Apotheosis of Spain. In Spain he met the opposition of Anton Raphael Mengs, the champion of Neoclassicism, and his canvases for the church of San Pascual at Aranjuez were replaced by works by Mengs.

Tiepolo died in Madrid on 27 March 1770 and is buried in Madonna dell'Orto in Venice. The rise of Neoclassicism slowly ended the Rococo style associated with him but did not damage his reputation. In 1878 Mark Twain wrote in his diary, Tiepolo is my artist.
giovanni-boccaccio: Boccaccio was the son of the Florentine merchant Boccaccino di Chellino and an unknown woman, and was probably born out of wedlock. He grew up in Florence, where his father worked for the Compagnia dei Bardi, and may have been tutored by Giovanni Mazzuoli, who gave him an early introduction to the works of Dante. In 1326 his father was appointed head of a bank and the family moved to Naples. Boccaccio disliked banking and studied canon law at the Studium for six years, while pursuing scientific and literary studies and meeting scholars and the Neapolitan nobility.

In Naples Boccaccio began what he considered his true vocation, poetry. Il Filostrato and the Teseida of this period were the sources for Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde and The Knight's Tale. He returned to Florence in early 1341, after tensions between the Angevin king and Florence, and his father, who had gone bankrupt, died in 1349. He began the Decameron around 1349; the choice of a hundred tales and the frame story of three men and seven women dates from this time. It was largely complete by 1352 and revised in 1370-1371.

From 1350 he was closely involved with humanism and with the Florentine government, which sent him on missions to Romagna, Brandenburg, Milan and Avignon. He housed Leontius Pilatus and encouraged his tentative translations of Homer, Euripides and Aristotle. In October 1350 he welcomed Francesco Petrarch to Florence, and Petrarch became his teacher and friend. Their discussions fed the Genealogia deorum gentilium, completed in 1360, a reference work on classical mythology that defended the study of ancient literature against clerical intellectuals who wished to limit it. In 1360 he began De mulieribus claris, biographies of 106 women, completed in 1374, and in 1373 he lectured on Dante, which produced his Esposizioni sopra la Commedia di Dante.

Illness troubled Boccaccio's last years. He died on 21 December 1375 in Certaldo, where he is buried, and his library passed to the monastery of Santo Spirito in Florence. He is counted with Dante and Petrarch as one of the Three Crowns of Italian literature. Pietro Bembo made his style a model of Italian prose in the sixteenth century, and he influenced Chaucer, Miguel de Cervantes and Lope de Vega.
giovanni-giustiniani-longo: Giustiniani, born in 1418, belonged to the House of Giustiniani and was probably a native of Chios. That he lived as a mercenary suggests he was not the first-born son of his family. He left no testimony of his reasons for going to Constantinople. Reportedly Emperor Constantine XI promised him sovereignty over the island of Lemnos in case of victory.

Constantine XI gave him the rank of protostrator. Why he in particular was chosen is unclear; one explanation offered is that the emperor distrusted the city's large and discontented Venetian population and preferred a Genoese. Giustiniani trained the recruits, strengthened the fortifications and brought back men who had fled to monasteries to escape military duty. Drawing on the siege of 1422, he concentrated the defence on the outer walls. Some 8,000 to 9,000 people were available to defend the city, and his own post was at the lowest-lying section of the walls, between the gates of St. Romanos and Charisius.

After Sultan Mehmed II arrived on 6 April, Giustiniani led sorties that destroyed Ottoman troops, siege works and artillery, until their cost in lives caused them to be given up. Against the Ottoman guns, which included a cannon 6 metres long, he had the walls covered with soft surfaces and the breaches filled with debris, into which the cannonballs sank. On 18 April his men repelled the first assault, by Janissaries and archers at a narrow breach, after four hours.

In the final assault of 29 May two waves were beaten back before the Janissaries attacked a line held by no more than 3,000 exhausted troops. The accounts differ on his wound: a cannon shot or a crossbow bolt struck his arm, chest or leg. He was taken to his ship and sailed away with his men when the fall of the city became known. He died on 1 June and was buried in the church of San Domenico in the Castle of Chios. The tomb is lost, possibly destroyed in the earthquake of 1881, though descriptions of its inscription survive.

Sources hostile to the Genoese, above all the Venetian eyewitness Nicolò Barbaro, claim that he was lightly wounded or not at all and left his post out of fear. The charges of cowardice and treason spread so widely that the Republic of Genoa denied them in letters to the chanceries of England, France, the Duchy of Burgundy and others. The historians Marios Philippides and Walter Hanak rebut Barbaro, citing several other sources that record an injury.
giuseppe-garibaldi: Garibaldi was born and christened Joseph-Marie Garibaldi on 4 July 1807 in Nice, to a Ligurian family of coastal traders, which drew him to a life at sea. He lived in the Pera district of Istanbul from 1828 to 1832, teaching Italian, French and mathematics. In April 1833, in the port of Taganrog in the Russian Empire, he met Giovanni Battista Cuneo, a member of Giuseppe Mazzini's Young Italy movement, which sought Italian unification as a liberal republic. After taking part in an uprising in Piedmont he was sentenced to death, escaped and sailed to South America, where he spent 14 years in exile.

In Brazil he joined the rebels known as the Ragamuffins in the war of 1835, taking up their cause of an independent Riograndense Republic and later a Catarinense Republic. There he met Ana Maria de Jesus Ribeiro da Silva, known as Anita, who joined him aboard his ship in 1839 and fought beside him. He also became involved in the Uruguayan Civil War, raising an Italian force that wore red shirts.

He returned to Italy in 1848, offered his services to Charles Albert of Sardinia, who treated him with distrust, and then helped the provisional government of Milan. In 1849 he took command of the defence of the Roman Republic against a French force. Forced to emigrate again, he spent the next years in Tangier, New York and, in 1854, on Tyneside, where working men welcomed him.

In 1859 he led the Hunters of the Alps to victories over the Austrians at Varese and Como. On 5 May 1860 he left Quarto, near Genoa, with the volunteers known as the Thousand or the Redshirts, on two ships, and landed at Marsala in Sicily on 11 May. The expedition ended with the annexation of Sicily, southern Italy, the Marche and Umbria to the Kingdom of Sardinia before the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861. In 1866 he led some 40,000 men into the Trentino and defeated the Austrians at Bezzecca; ordered to halt, he telegraphed the reply Obbedisco, meaning I obey. His last campaign was with the Army of the Vosges in the Franco-Prussian War.

Ill with arthritis, Garibaldi died on 2 June 1882. He had asked for a simple funeral and cremation, which were not respected, and he was buried on his farm on the island of Caprera. His popularity, skill in rousing the common people and military exploits are credited with making Italian unification possible; to achieve it he gave up his ambition of a republic. Abraham Lincoln, Victor Hugo, Charles Dickens and Friedrich Engels were among his admirers, and a bust of him stands outside the old Supreme Court Chamber in the United States Capitol.
giuseppe-verdi: Verdi was the first child of Carlo Giuseppe Verdi and Luigia Uttini, an innkeeper and a spinner according to the baptismal register of 11 October 1813. He was born at Le Roncole, near Busseto, then in the Taro department of the First French Empire, and from the age of four had private lessons in Latin and Italian. He learned the organ and showed so much interest in music that his parents gave him a spinet. With the help of a local patron, Antonio Barezzi, he received a musical education. In 1835 he became director of the Busseto school, and the La Scala impresario Bartolomeo Merelli agreed to stage his first opera, Oberto, in November 1839.

Nabucco, in 1842, made his reputation, and I Lombardi alla prima crociata followed in 1843. Verdi then wrote twenty operas over sixteen years, a period he later called sixteen years in the galleys. Rigoletto, based on Victor Hugo's Le roi s'amuse, was written for Venice in 1851, and with Il trovatore and La traviata it cemented his fame. Censors objected to Stiffelio and Rigoletto, and Verdi refused to compromise on the hunchbacked hero of the latter.

After La traviata he wrote only six new stage works in eighteen years, up to Aida, and he returned happily to his estate at Sant'Agata. In 1859 he began to take an active interest in Italian politics, and he served briefly as an elected politician. After the success of Otello in 1887 he said that having massacred so many heroes and heroines he had the right to laugh a little, and with a libretto by Boito he wrote the comedy Falstaff, of 1893.

Critics divide Verdi's work into early, middle and late periods. Macbeth of 1847 has been called his first masterpiece, and his late masterpieces are the Requiem of 1874 and the operas Otello and Falstaff. He was influenced by Rossini, Bellini and Donizetti and by the French Grand opera of Meyerbeer and Spontini.

Historians debate how political his operas were. The chorus Va, pensiero from Nabucco became an anthem of Italian patriots, and from 1859 the slogan Viva VERDI was used as an acronym for Viva Vittorio Emanuele Re D'Italia. The music historian Philip Gossett notes that myths exaggerating his early nationalism circulated in the nineteenth century: the audience is said to have demanded an encore of Va, pensiero at its Milan premiere, but the piece encored was in fact the hymn Immenso Jehova.
glasgow: Glasgow lies on the banks of the River Clyde in west central Scotland, with the Kelvin as an important tributary. The name is Brittonic in origin, from glas, meaning grey-green or grey-blue, and a second element meaning hollow, giving a sense of green hollow; it is often said to mean dear green place, and the dear green place remains an affectionate name for the city. The area around Glasgow has hosted communities for millennia and the Romans built outposts there and the Antonine Wall.

Glasgow grew from a small rural settlement near its cathedral into a medieval bishopric and burgh, and was raised to the status of Royal Burgh in 1611. Its early trade was in agriculture, brewing and fishing, and from 1668 the magistrates created a deep water port at Port Glasgow, down the Clyde, because the river was then too shallow for seagoing merchant ships.

After the Acts of Union in 1707 Glasgow became prominent as a hub of trade with the Americas, in sugar, tobacco, cotton and manufactured goods. The city prospered from the triangular trade and the Atlantic slave trade on which it depended, and its merchants dealt in slave-produced crops. From 1717 to 1766 Scottish slave ships, mainly sailing from Greenock and Port Glasgow, carried approximately 3,000 enslaved Africans to the Americas. By the late 18th century more than half of the British tobacco trade was concentrated on the Clyde. The city became a major centre of the Scottish Enlightenment.

As the population grew, about 4,000 people died in an outbreak of cholera in 1848–1849, which led to the Loch Katrine aqueduct, 26 miles long, opened by Queen Victoria in 1859. The population reached 1,034,174 in 1921 and peaked at 1,127,825 in 1938, and boundary extensions between 1912 and 1936 tripled the city's area. In the First World War approximately 18,000 Glaswegian soldiers were lost. Clearance of poor inner-city areas such as the Gorbals and resettlement in new towns including Cumbernauld and East Kilbride reduced the population from the 1960s.

Glasgow is the most populous city in Scotland and one of its 32 unitary council areas, administered by Glasgow City Council. Its cultural institutions include the Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, the Hunterian Museum and Art Gallery, the Burrell Collection, Scottish Opera and Scottish Ballet, and it was European Capital of Culture in 1990. St. Mungo's Cathedral, of the 13th century, and Provand's Lordship, of the 15th, are the two main landmarks of the medieval city.
goa: Goa lies on the southwestern coast of India, in the Konkan region, separated from the Deccan highlands by the Western Ghats. It covers 3,702 square kilometres, and its highest point, Sonsogor, rises to 1,167 metres. The climate is tropical monsoon, with over 90 per cent of the rain falling from June to September. Rock engravings at Usgalimal and Kajur are among the earliest known traces of human life in India.

In the 3rd century BCE Goa belonged to the Maurya Empire under Ashoka. Between the 2nd century BCE and the 6th century CE it was ruled by the Bhojas of Goa, then by the Chalukyas of Badami from 578 to 753 and the Rashtrakutas from 753 to 963. The Kadambas, who followed as feudatories of the Chalukyas of Kalyani, patronised Jainism.

In 1510 the Portuguese defeated the Bijapur sultan Yusuf Adil Shah with the help of a local ally, Thimmayya or Timoji, and set up a permanent settlement at Old Goa. Under Afonso de Albuquerque the city became capital of the Estado da Índia. The Goa Inquisition was established in 1560 and abolished in 1812, and the first printing press in India produced its first books in 1556. Old Goa was abandoned in the 19th century after outbreaks of disease. On 19 December 1961 the Indian Army invaded in Operation Vijay and annexed Goa, and on 30 May 1987 it became India's twenty-fifth state.

Goa is a state of India with Panaji as its capital and Vasco da Gama as its largest city. Konkani is its sole official language, with Marathi also permitted for official purposes. The census of 2011 counted 1,458,545 people, 66.1 per cent of them Hindu and 25.1 per cent Christian. The Bom Jesus Basilica and the churches and convents of Old Goa form its World Heritage Site; the basilica holds the remains of Saint Francis Xavier. Goan cooking, based on rice, fish and coconut, is heavily influenced by Portuguese cuisine.
gorgan: The present city of Gorgan is the capital of Golestan province and lies about 400 km north-east of Tehran and some 30 km from the Caspian Sea. North of it stretches the wide Dasht-e Gorgan, the Plain of Gorgan. The city has hot, humid summers and cool, wet winters, with about 584 millimetres of rain a year, while the Gorgan valley has a semi-arid climate. Some 150 km to the east is the Golestan National Park.

More than 50 archaeological sites lie on the Gorgan Plain, among them Tureng Tepe and Shah Tepe, with remains from the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods. According to the Greek historian Arrian, Zadracarta was the largest city of Hyrcania and the site of its royal palace. Hyrcania became part of the Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great or his successor Cambyses. The Great Wall of Gorgan was built in the Parthian and Sasanian periods, and under the Sasanians the name Gurgan was used for a city, a provincial capital and a province.

The region kept its independence as a Zoroastrian state even after the Arab conquest of Persia in the 7th century. In 1210 the city was invaded and sacked by the army of the Kingdom of Georgia under the Mkhargrdzeli brothers. Old Gorgan was destroyed during the Mongol invasion of the 13th century, and the centre of the region moved to Astarabad, which is the city now called Gorgan. Astarabad was an important political and religious city in the Qajar era.

The census of 2016 counted 350,676 people in the city, against 269,226 in 2006. It has several universities, among them Golestan University and Gorgan University.
